meta.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
meta.subject: Chemistry

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Cyclohexane is an example of which class of organic compound?
options: Heterocyclic compound
Open-chain compound
Aromatic compound
Alicyclic compound
questions.explanation: Cyclohexane is a saturated ring of six carbon atoms with no delocalised π system, so it is classed as an alicyclic (aliphatic cyclic) compound — it behaves chemically like an open-chain alkane rather than like benzene.
questions.hint: Does the ring contain a benzene-like delocalised electron cloud, or is it just a saturated carbon ring?
distractor_logic: Aromatic wrongly assumes any ring is aromatic.
Heterocyclic wrongly assumes a ring atom other than carbon is present.
Open-chain ignores that the compound is cyclic.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: A compound such as butane, whose carbon atoms form a continuous chain with no ring, is described as:
options: Heterocyclic
Aromatic
Alicyclic
Open-chain (acyclic)
questions.explanation: Open-chain (acyclic) compounds have carbon atoms linked in straight or branched chains without closing into a ring; butane, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, is a classic example.
questions.hint: Is there a ring anywhere in the structure?
distractor_logic: Alicyclic/aromatic/heterocyclic all require a closed ring, which butane does not have.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: When selecting the parent chain in IUPAC nomenclature, the first criterion is that the chain must contain:
options: The maximum number of double bonds only
The lowest possible locants regardless of chain length
The maximum number of substituents
The maximum number of carbon atoms
questions.explanation: The parent chain is chosen as the longest continuous carbon chain (containing the maximum number of skeletal atoms, and if there is a choice, the one with the maximum number of multiple bonds); this is the very first rule applied before any locant rule.
questions.hint: Chain-selection rules are applied in order — which property is checked before locants are even considered?
distractor_logic: Double bonds and substituents are secondary tie-breaking criteria used only when two chains are equally long.
Lowest locants is applied after the chain is already fixed.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: The IUPAC suffix used to indicate a carbon–carbon triple bond in the parent chain is:
options: -yne
-yl
-ene
-ol
questions.explanation: A triple bond is indicated by replacing the '-ane' ending of the corresponding alkane with '-yne', e.g. ethyne, propyne.
questions.hint: Think of the word 'alkyne'.
distractor_logic: -ene marks a double bond, -yl marks a substituent group, -ol marks an alcohol.
None denote a triple bond.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: In IUPAC nomenclature, the principal characteristic group present in a molecule is expressed in the name as a:
options: Separate word after the name
Locant with no suffix or prefix
Suffix
Prefix only
questions.explanation: The senior-most (principal) characteristic group is always cited as a suffix attached to the parent name (e.g. '-ol' for –OH, '-al' for –CHO); every other group present is cited only as a prefix.
questions.hint: Which functional group gets to 'name' the compound, and how is that reflected grammatically?
distractor_logic: Prefix only describes how non-principal groups are cited, not the principal one.
The other options ignore the suffix convention entirely.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: While numbering the parent chain of a polyfunctional compound, the lowest locant is given first to:
options: The double bond, regardless of any functional group present
The principal characteristic group
The substituent with the largest number of carbon atoms
Whichever substituent is alphabetically first
questions.explanation: Numbering rules are applied in a strict hierarchy: the principal characteristic group (expressed as suffix) gets the lowest possible locant first; only if there is still a choice do multiple bonds, then substituents, get considered.
questions.hint: Which part of the molecule is 'senior' in the naming hierarchy — the suffix group or the prefixes?
distractor_logic: Alphabetical order and chain size govern the order substituents are cited, not the numbering priority.
Multiple bonds are considered only after the principal group is fixed.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Isomers that have the same molecular formula but differ only in the arrangement of the carbon skeleton (e.g. n-butane and isobutane) are called:
options: Functional isomers
Position isomers
Metamers
Chain isomers
questions.explanation: Chain isomerism arises purely from a different arrangement (branching pattern) of the carbon skeleton while the functional group and its position stay conceptually equivalent; n-butane and 2-methylpropane are the textbook pair.
questions.hint: n-butane is a straight chain, isobutane is branched — what has changed between them?
distractor_logic: Position isomers differ in the location of a group on an identical skeleton.
Functional isomers have different functional groups altogether.
Metamers differ in the alkyl groups flanking the same functional group.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: 1-propanol and 2-propanol have the same molecular formula and the same functional group (–OH) but the –OH is attached at different carbon atoms. This is an example of:
options: Tautomerism
Position isomerism
Chain isomerism
Functional group isomerism
questions.explanation: When the carbon skeleton and functional group are identical but the functional group sits on a different carbon, the compounds are position isomers.
questions.hint: Is the skeleton branching different, or just where the –OH sits on the same skeleton?
distractor_logic: Chain isomerism would require a different skeleton.
Functional isomerism would require a different functional group (e.g. an ether).
Tautomerism involves rapid interconversion, not a fixed structural difference.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: The inductive effect is transmitted through a chain of carbon atoms via:
options: Space, with no involvement of bonds
π-bonds only, and it does not weaken with distance
Hydrogen bonds exclusively
σ-bonds, and it weakens rapidly with distance
questions.explanation: The inductive effect is a permanent, weak electron-displacement along the σ-bond framework caused by electronegativity differences; its influence falls off sharply and is usually negligible beyond the third carbon from the substituent.
questions.hint: Is this effect carried by the single-bond skeleton or by delocalised π electrons?
distractor_logic: π-bonds only describes resonance/conjugation, not induction.
'no weakening with distance' contradicts the defining short-range nature of the inductive effect.
Hydrogen bonding is unrelated.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Among the halogens, which shows the strongest −I (electron-withdrawing inductive) effect when directly attached to a carbon chain?
options: Cl
F
Br
I
questions.explanation: Inductive effect strength tracks electronegativity for atoms of similar size in the same period/group comparison used at this level: F is the most electronegative halogen, so it withdraws electron density most strongly through the σ-framework, giving the order F > Cl > Br > I.
questions.hint: Which halogen is the most electronegative?
distractor_logic: Cl, Br, and I are progressively less electronegative than F, so each withdraws electron density less strongly by induction.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Different resonance structures of the same molecule differ from each other only in the:
options: Molecular formula
Position of electrons (the positions of atomic nuclei stay fixed)
Position of atomic nuclei
Number of atoms present
questions.explanation: Resonance structures (canonical forms) are hypothetical structures that differ only in how electrons (usually π or lone-pair electrons) are distributed; the actual molecule is a single hybrid, not a mixture, and the atomic skeleton never moves between the canonical forms.
questions.hint: Do the atoms shift position, or only the electrons drawn in the Lewis structures?
distractor_logic: Moving nuclei would make these different compounds, not resonance forms of the same molecule.
Molecular formula and atom count are identical across all canonical structures by definition.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: A more stable contributing (canonical) resonance structure generally has:
options: More covalent bonds and less charge separation
Fewer covalent bonds and more charge separation
Negative charge on the more electronegative atom is always forbidden
No relationship to the number of covalent bonds
questions.explanation: Canonical structures with a greater number of covalent bonds and minimal separation of unlike charges contribute more to the resonance hybrid and are considered more stable/major contributors.
questions.hint: Recall the standard rules for ranking resonance contributors by stability.
distractor_logic: The reverse relationship (fewer bonds, more charge separation) describes a less stable, minor contributor.
Negative charge on an electronegative atom is actually favoured, not forbidden.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: The electromeric effect is observed only:
options: In ionic compounds only
In saturated molecules with no multiple bonds
In the presence of an attacking reagent, at the moment of reaction
Permanently, whether or not a reagent is present
questions.explanation: The electromeric effect is a temporary, complete transfer of a shared pair of π electrons to one atom of a multiply-bonded pair, triggered only when an attacking reagent approaches; once the reagent is removed, the molecule reverts to its original electron distribution.
questions.hint: Compare this to the inductive effect — which one is 'always on' and which one only switches on momentarily?
distractor_logic: It requires a multiple bond (C=C, C=O, etc.), so it cannot occur in fully saturated molecules.
Unlike the inductive effect, it is not permanent.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Compared with the inductive effect, the electromeric effect is:
options: Transmitted only through σ-bonds
Permanent and always present
Independent of the presence of a multiple bond
Temporary and operative only during a reaction
questions.explanation: Inductive effect is a weak but permanent polarisation through σ-bonds; electromeric effect is a strong, instantaneous, temporary polarisation of a π-bond that occurs only in the presence of an attacking reagent and disappears once the reagent leaves.
questions.hint: Which effect 'switches off' as soon as the reagent is gone?
distractor_logic: 'Permanent and always present' describes the inductive effect, not the electromeric effect.
It operates through π-bonds, not σ-bonds, and strictly requires a multiple bond to exist.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Hyperconjugation requires the presence of:
options: A C–H (or C–C) σ bond on a carbon directly attached to an atom bearing a positive charge, a free radical, or a multiple bond
A C–H bond that is at least three carbons away from the charged/unsaturated centre
Two adjacent negative charges
A lone pair on oxygen or nitrogen only
questions.explanation: Hyperconjugation is the delocalisation of electrons from a σ (usually C–H) bond on a carbon directly attached (alpha) to an electron-deficient centre, a radical, or a π system, into the adjacent empty/partially-filled p orbital or π* system.
questions.hint: Which carbon's C–H bonds actually participate — the one right next to the charge, or one further away?
distractor_logic: Bonds far from the reactive centre cannot overlap effectively and do not contribute.
Hyperconjugation involves σ C–H/C–C bonds, not isolated lone pairs, and does not require two negative charges.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Hyperconjugation is also known by which alternative name?
options: True resonance
No-bond resonance
Tautomeric resonance
Steric resonance
questions.explanation: Hyperconjugation is called 'no-bond resonance' because one of its canonical (hyperconjugative) structures shows a C–H bond fully broken with the electrons shown as a π bond and a bare proton, i.e. a structure with 'no bond' between that carbon and hydrogen.
questions.hint: One of the resonance structures literally shows the C–H bond disappearing — what would you call that?
distractor_logic: 'True resonance' misleadingly implies this is identical to ordinary π-electron resonance.
'steric' and 'tautomeric resonance' are not standard names used for this effect.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: For hydrogen bonding to occur, hydrogen must be covalently attached to a small, highly electronegative atom, typically:
options: Any halogen including I
Any atom regardless of electronegativity
F, O, or N
C, S, or P
questions.explanation: Hydrogen bonding requires H bonded to a small, highly electronegative atom — classically F, O, or N — so that the H carries a significant partial positive charge able to interact with a nearby lone pair.
questions.hint: Which three elements are always cited in the textbook definition of hydrogen bonding?
distractor_logic: Carbon, sulfur, phosphorus and the larger halogens (Cl, Br, I) are too large or insufficiently electronegative to support conventional hydrogen bonding.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Intramolecular hydrogen bonding (chelation), as seen in ortho-nitrophenol, tends to result in:
options: Complete loss of the H-bond donor's acidity
Lower boiling/melting point and lower water solubility than the corresponding isomer with intermolecular H-bonding
Higher boiling point than intermolecular hydrogen-bonded isomers
No effect on the physical properties of the compound
questions.explanation: Intramolecular H-bonding ties up the H-bond donor and acceptor within a single molecule, so the molecules cannot link extensively with each other or with water; this gives ortho-nitrophenol a lower boiling point, lower melting point, and lower water solubility than the para isomer, which forms intermolecular H-bonds.
questions.hint: Compare ortho- and para-nitrophenol — which one can form a chain of molecules held together by H-bonds, and which one 'uses up' its H-bond within itself?
distractor_logic: Intermolecular H-bonding (not intramolecular) is what raises boiling point by linking many molecules together.
Chelation clearly does affect physical properties and does not eliminate acidity.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Homolytic fission of a covalent A–B bond produces:
options: No new species; the bond simply reforms
Two identical cations
Two neutral free radicals, each carrying one electron of the shared pair
A cation and an anion
questions.explanation: In homolytic (symmetrical) fission, the shared electron pair splits evenly, one electron going to each fragment, generating two neutral species each with an unpaired electron — free radicals.
questions.hint: 'Homo-' means 'same' — how are the two electrons of the bond divided?
distractor_logic: A cation/anion pair is the result of heterolytic (unequal) fission, not homolytic.
Producing two cations would violate charge and electron conservation.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Heterolytic fission of a covalent bond A–B, where B is more electronegative, produces:
options: A carbanion A<sup>−</sup> and a cation B<sup>+</sup>
Two neutral fragments with no charge
Two free radicals A• and B•
A carbocation A<sup>+</sup> and an anion B<sup>−</sup> (both electrons go to B)
questions.explanation: In heterolytic fission the bonding pair moves entirely to the more electronegative/more stabilising atom; if B is more electronegative, both electrons stay with B (forming B<sup>−</sup>) while A is left electron-deficient (A<sup>+</sup>).
questions.hint: Which atom 'keeps' the electron pair when the bond breaks unevenly?
distractor_logic: Two free radicals or two neutral fragments describe homolytic fission, not heterolytic.
The option showing a carbanion A<sup>−</sup> and a cation B<sup>+</sup> has the charges reversed relative to which atom (the more electronegative B) actually retains the electron pair.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: The positively charged carbon of a simple carbocation is:
options: sp<sup>3</sup> hybridised and pyramidal
sp<sup>3</sup>d hybridised
sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised and planar, with an empty p orbital
sp hybridised and linear
questions.explanation: A carbocation carbon uses three sp<sup>2</sup> hybrid orbitals for its three sigma bonds, leaving an empty, unhybridised p orbital perpendicular to the plane of the molecule; the ion is therefore trigonal planar.
questions.hint: How many groups/bonds does the positively charged carbon actually have, and what geometry does that give?
distractor_logic: Sp<sup>3</sup>/pyramidal describes a carbanion (which has a lone pair).
Sp/linear and sp<sup>3</sup>d do not correspond to a three-bonded carbon centre.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: The stability order 3° > 2° > 1° > methyl for simple alkyl carbocations is mainly explained by:
options: Decreasing hyperconjugation with increasing alkyl substitution
Increasing −I effect with increasing alkyl substitution
Resonance, since all alkyl carbocations are resonance stabilised
Increasing +I effect and greater hyperconjugation (more alpha C–H bonds) with increasing alkyl substitution
questions.explanation: Each alkyl group attached to the cationic carbon donates electron density by +I effect and offers additional alpha C–H (or C–C) bonds for hyperconjugative donation into the empty p orbital; more alkyl substitution means more of both effects, stabilising the positive charge.
questions.hint: Do alkyl groups push or pull electron density, and does a tertiary carbon have more or fewer adjacent C–H bonds than a primary one?
distractor_logic: Plain alkyl carbocations are not resonance stabilised unless allylic/benzylic.
Hyperconjugation increases (not decreases) with more substitution.
Alkyl groups are +I (electron donating), not −I.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: The negatively charged carbon of a simple carbanion is:
options: sp<sup>3</sup> hybridised, roughly pyramidal, bearing a lone pair
sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised and planar with an empty p orbital
sp hybridised and linear
sp<sup>2</sup>d hybridised
questions.explanation: A carbanion carbon is tetrahedral-like (sp<sup>3</sup>) with three bond pairs and one lone pair, giving it a pyramidal shape similar to ammonia.
questions.hint: A carbanion has a lone pair instead of an empty orbital — what shape does that produce?
distractor_logic: Sp<sup>2</sup>/planar with an empty p orbital describes a carbocation, not a carbanion.
Sp/linear and sp<sup>2</sup>d do not apply to a four-electron-domain carbon.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: For simple alkyl carbanions, the stability order CH<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> > 1° > 2° > 3° is explained by:
options: Alkyl groups being +I (electron donating), which intensifies the already-negative charge and destabilises it as substitution increases
Alkyl groups being −I, which withdraws the negative charge and stabilises it as substitution increases
Hyperconjugation, which stabilises more-substituted carbanions the most
Resonance being stronger in more-substituted carbanions
questions.explanation: Alkyl groups donate electron density by the +I effect; on an already electron-rich carbanion centre, this additional electron donation increases charge density and destabilises the ion, so more alkyl substitution (more +I donors) makes the carbanion less stable, giving CH<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> as the most stable of this simple set.
questions.hint: If alkyl groups push electrons toward a centre that is already negative, does that help or hurt stability?
distractor_logic: Hyperconjugation classically stabilises electron-deficient/radical centres, not simple carbanions in the way described.
Plain alkyl carbanions have no resonance stabilisation.
Alkyl groups are electron-donating (+I), not electron-withdrawing (−I).

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Free radicals are formed as a result of:
options: Heterolytic fission of a covalent bond
Gain of a pair of electrons by a neutral atom
Homolytic fission of a covalent bond
Loss of a proton from a neutral molecule
questions.explanation: Homolytic (symmetrical) bond cleavage splits the shared electron pair equally between the two fragments, producing two species each with a single unpaired electron — free radicals.
questions.hint: Which type of fission leaves an odd (unpaired) electron on each fragment?
distractor_logic: Gaining an electron pair gives an anion, not a radical.
Heterolytic fission produces ions, not radicals.
Simple proton loss gives a carbanion (if from carbon) or a conjugate base, not a radical.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Because a free radical carries an unpaired electron, it is:
options: Paramagnetic
Always negatively charged
Always positively charged
Diamagnetic
questions.explanation: An unpaired electron gives a species a net magnetic moment, making free radicals paramagnetic; they are also electrically neutral overall, not charged.
questions.hint: Does an unpaired electron create a magnetic moment or cancel it out?
distractor_logic: Diamagnetism applies to species with all electrons paired.
Free radicals are neutral, not cations or anions, since fission was homolytic and no charge was created.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: A species that is electron-deficient and seeks out electron-rich centres in a reaction is called a(n):
options: Electrophile
Free radical
Nucleophile
Leaving group only, never a reactive species
questions.explanation: Electrophiles ('electron-loving') are electron-deficient species (cations or neutral molecules with an incomplete octet, or with a polarised, electron-poor centre) that attack sites of high electron density.
questions.hint: Break down the word: 'electro-' + '-phile' (lover of).
distractor_logic: Free radicals are defined by having an unpaired electron, not by being electron-deficient.
Leaving groups are a separate mechanistic concept.
Nucleophiles are electron-rich, the opposite behaviour.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Ammonia (NH<sub>3</sub>) typically behaves as a:
options: Free radical
Nucleophile, donating its lone pair on nitrogen
Neither electrophile nor nucleophile, since it is neutral
Electrophile, accepting an electron pair
questions.explanation: Nitrogen in NH<sub>3</sub> carries a lone pair of electrons that it can readily donate to an electron-deficient centre, which is the defining behaviour of a nucleophile; overall neutrality does not prevent a species from being nucleophilic.
questions.hint: Does nitrogen in ammonia have a lone pair to give away?
distractor_logic: Electrophiles accept electrons rather than donate them.
Being neutral does not stop a species from acting as a nucleophile (many good nucleophiles are neutral).
NH<sub>3</sub> has no unpaired electron, so it is not a radical.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: A reaction in which an atom or group of atoms in a molecule is replaced by another atom or group is called a(n):
options: Rearrangement reaction
Addition reaction
Substitution reaction
Elimination reaction
questions.explanation: Substitution reactions swap one atom/group for another, e.g. CH<sub>4</sub> + Cl<sub>2</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>Cl + HCl, where a hydrogen is replaced by chlorine.
questions.hint: Is something being swapped out, added across a bond, or removed to form a new bond?
distractor_logic: Rearrangement changes the skeleton without net substitution.
Elimination removes atoms/groups to form a multiple bond.
Addition involves combining across a multiple bond with no atoms lost.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: A reaction in which two or more molecules combine to form a single product, typically across a carbon–carbon multiple bond, with no atoms lost, is called a(n):
options: Oxidation reaction only
Elimination reaction
Substitution reaction
Addition reaction
questions.explanation: Addition reactions occur at sites of unsaturation (C=C, C≡C, C=O), where the π bond opens and new σ bonds form to incoming atoms/groups without expelling any part of the original molecule, e.g. CH<sub>2</sub>=CH<sub>2</sub> + HBr → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br.
questions.hint: Are atoms being lost from the molecule, or simply added on?
distractor_logic: 'oxidation only' is far too narrow a description.
Substitution replaces one group with another rather than adding across a multiple bond.
Elimination removes atoms to create unsaturation, the reverse process.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Sublimation is used to purify a solid that:
options: Decomposes well below its melting point
Has exactly the same volatility as its impurities
Passes directly from the solid to the vapour state on heating, leaving non-volatile impurities behind
Is highly soluble in every common solvent
questions.explanation: Sublimable solids (e.g. camphor, naphthalene, ammonium chloride) vaporise directly without passing through a liquid phase; heating the impure solid lets the pure compound sublime away and be recondensed, leaving non-volatile impurities in the residue.
questions.hint: What must be true of the compound's vapour pressure/behaviour on heating for this method to work at all?
distractor_logic: High solubility is the basis for crystallisation, not sublimation.
A compound that decomposes on heating cannot be purified by sublimation.
If the impurity is equally volatile, sublimation cannot separate them.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Crystallisation as a purification technique is based primarily on differences in the:
options: Vapour pressure of the compound and its impurities
Solubility of the compound and its impurities in a chosen solvent, especially with temperature
Adsorption of the compound and its impurities on a solid stationary phase
Boiling points of the compound and its impurities
questions.explanation: Crystallisation exploits the fact that a compound is far more soluble in a solvent at high temperature than at low temperature (or is more/less soluble than the impurities); cooling a hot saturated solution lets pure crystals separate out while impurities stay dissolved (or vice versa).
questions.hint: What property changes when you heat then cool a saturated solution, letting crystals form?
distractor_logic: Adsorption differences underlie chromatography.
Boiling-point differences are exploited in distillation.
Vapour-pressure differences are the basis of sublimation/distillation, not crystallisation.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Simple distillation is suitable for separating two miscible liquids that do not decompose on heating and whose boiling points differ by at least about:
options: 1–2 °C
Exactly 100 °C
25 °C or more
Boiling point difference is irrelevant to the method
questions.explanation: Simple distillation works well when the boiling points are sufficiently far apart (conventionally ≥ ~25 °C) that one liquid vaporises well before the other; when boiling points are closer together, fractional distillation (with a fractionating column) is needed instead.
questions.hint: If two liquids boil at nearly the same temperature, would a single simple vaporisation step cleanly separate them?
distractor_logic: A 1–2 °C gap is far too small for simple distillation and would instead need fractional distillation.
There is no fixed '100 °C' rule.
Boiling-point difference is in fact central to choosing this method.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Differential extraction (using a separating funnel) relies on the fact that a solute:
options: Has the same solubility in both solvents used
Adsorbs strongly onto a solid stationary phase
Sublimes readily on gentle heating
Is more soluble in one of two mutually immiscible solvents than in the other
questions.explanation: In differential extraction, a compound distributes unequally between two immiscible solvents (e.g. water and an organic solvent) according to its relative solubility in each; shaking the mixture in a separating funnel and letting the layers separate transfers most of the solute into the solvent it prefers.
questions.hint: Would extraction work at all if the compound liked both solvents equally?
distractor_logic: Sublimation is a different, solid-state technique.
Equal solubility in both solvents would give no net separation.
Adsorption on a stationary phase describes chromatography, not liquid–liquid extraction.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Adsorption chromatography separates the components of a mixture based on differences in their:
options: Boiling points as they are heated in sequence
Solubility in water alone
Degree of adsorption on a stationary adsorbent as they travel with a mobile phase
Molecular colour, since only coloured compounds can be chromatographed
questions.explanation: In adsorption chromatography, components of a mixture are adsorbed to different extents onto a stationary adsorbent (e.g. alumina, silica) while a mobile phase moves over it; weakly adsorbed components move faster and are eluted first, achieving separation.
questions.hint: What is the stationary phase actually doing to each component as the mobile phase flows past?
distractor_logic: Boiling-point separation is the basis of distillation, not chromatography.
The technique is not restricted to water-soluble or coloured compounds (though colour can help visualise separation, it is not required).

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: In column chromatography, as the mobile phase (eluant) flows down through the adsorbent-packed column, the component that is eluted first is generally the one that is:
options: Least strongly adsorbed on the stationary phase
Most highly coloured
Most strongly adsorbed on the stationary phase
Heaviest in molecular mass
questions.explanation: Components with the weakest interaction with (least adsorption on) the stationary adsorbent are carried down the column fastest by the mobile phase and emerge first; strongly adsorbed components lag behind.
questions.hint: Which component would the stationary phase 'hold onto' the least?
distractor_logic: Strong adsorption slows a component down rather than speeding it out first.
Molecular mass and colour are not the determining factors in elution order for adsorption chromatography.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: In Lassaigne's test, fusing an organic compound with sodium metal serves to:
options: Convert the compound into a coloured complex for visual identification without any further tests
Measure the boiling point of the compound
Convert covalently bound N, S, and halogens into water-soluble ionic sodium salts (NaCN, Na<sub>2</sub>S, NaX) that can be tested with simple ionic reactions
Directly char the compound to identify carbon and hydrogen only
questions.explanation: Sodium fusion converts the covalently bonded nitrogen, sulfur, and halogens present in an organic compound into inorganic, water-soluble ionic species (cyanide, sulfide, halide), which can then be detected by standard qualitative ionic tests on the resulting sodium fusion extract.
questions.hint: Why must covalent N/S/halogen first be turned into simple ions before they can be tested with everyday reagents like AgNO<sub>3</sub> or FeSO<sub>4</sub>?
distractor_logic: Boiling point is unrelated.
Charring for C/H estimation is a separate (quantitative, combustion-based) procedure.
The fusion extract itself is colourless and requires further specific tests, it is not a direct visual identification.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: In the test for nitrogen via Lassaigne's extract, formation of Prussian blue colouration upon treatment with FeSO<sub>4</sub> followed by acidification confirms the presence of:
options: Sulfur only
Phosphorus
Nitrogen (as sodium cyanide formed during fusion)
A halogen
questions.explanation: Sodium fusion converts organic nitrogen into NaCN; treating the extract with FeSO<sub>4</sub> and then acidifying forms ferric ferrocyanide, Fe<sub>4</sub>[Fe(CN)<sub>6</sub>]<sub>3</sub>, the Prussian blue precipitate, which is the standard confirmatory test for nitrogen.
questions.hint: What sodium salt does nitrogen get converted into during fusion, and which classic pigment does that salt help form with iron(II/III)?
distractor_logic: Halogens are confirmed with AgNO<sub>3</sub>.
Phosphorus is confirmed as a yellow ammonium phosphomolybdate precipitate — none of these give Prussian blue.
Sulfur is instead confirmed via a sodium nitroprusside test (violet colour) or lead acetate (black PbS).

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Carbon and hydrogen in an organic compound are estimated quantitatively by Liebig's method, which is based on:
options: Complete combustion of a known mass of the compound and weighing the CO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O produced
Precipitation of the compound as a silver salt
Measuring the volume of nitrogen gas liberated
Sodium fusion followed by titration
questions.explanation: In Liebig's method, a weighed sample is completely combusted in a stream of oxygen over CuO; the CO<sub>2</sub> produced is absorbed and weighed (giving the mass of carbon) and the H<sub>2</sub>O produced is absorbed and weighed separately (giving the mass of hydrogen), from which the percentage composition is calculated.
questions.hint: The method uses combustion — what two combustion products are collected and weighed?
distractor_logic: Sodium fusion followed by titration/precipitation and nitrogen-gas volume measurement describe methods for N, S, halogens (Kjeldahl, Carius, Dumas), not the carbon/hydrogen estimation method.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: The Dumas method for nitrogen estimation determines the percentage of nitrogen in an organic compound by:
options: Titrating the ammonia liberated after digestion with concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>
Precipitating nitrogen as AgCN and weighing it
Measuring the volume of N<sub>2</sub> gas liberated when the compound is heated with copper oxide (with excess CO<sub>2</sub> absorbed by KOH)
Weighing the CO<sub>2</sub> produced on combustion
questions.explanation: In the Dumas method, the compound is heated with copper oxide (and sometimes copper) in an atmosphere of CO<sub>2</sub>, converting nitrogen to N<sub>2</sub> gas; the gas mixture is passed through concentrated KOH, which absorbs CO<sub>2</sub>, leaving pure N<sub>2</sub> whose volume is measured and used to calculate percentage nitrogen.
questions.hint: This is the gas-volumetric method — which gas is collected over KOH solution?
distractor_logic: Weighing CO<sub>2</sub> describes the carbon estimation (Liebig's) method.
Titrating liberated ammonia after acid digestion describes Kjeldahl's method, an alternative nitrogen method, not Dumas.
There is no AgCN precipitation step.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Furan, a five-membered ring containing one oxygen atom and a delocalised π system, is best classified as:
options: An open-chain compound
A heterocyclic aromatic compound
A saturated heterocyclic compound
An alicyclic compound
questions.explanation: Furan's ring contains a non-carbon atom (oxygen) as a ring member, making it heterocyclic, and it possesses a delocalised, aromatic π system (6 π electrons including an oxygen lone pair), making it aromatic as well — so it is a heterocyclic aromatic compound.
questions.hint: First check: does the ring contain a non-carbon atom? Then check: is the ring system aromatic?
distractor_logic: 'saturated heterocyclic' is wrong because furan's ring is unsaturated/aromatic, not saturated.
Alicyclic wrongly ignores both the heteroatom and the aromaticity.
Open-chain ignores that it is a ring.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Naphthalene, made of two fused six-membered rings sharing a common edge, both with delocalised π systems, is classified as:
options: An alicyclic compound
An open-chain compound
An aromatic (polycyclic aromatic) hydrocarbon
A heterocyclic compound
questions.explanation: Naphthalene contains only carbon and hydrogen in fused rings that satisfy aromaticity criteria (planar, cyclic, conjugated, obeying the 4n+2 rule across the fused system), so it is classified as an aromatic hydrocarbon, specifically a polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH).
questions.hint: Are any ring atoms non-carbon? Are the rings fully conjugated and planar like benzene?
distractor_logic: Open-chain contradicts its clearly cyclic, fused structure.
Heterocyclic would require a non-carbon ring atom, which naphthalene lacks.
Alicyclic describes non-aromatic rings.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: What is the IUPAC name of CH<sub>3</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>–CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)–CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>3</sub>?
options: 2-Ethylbutane
3-Ethylbutane
3-Methylpentane
2-Methylpentane
questions.explanation: The longest chain has 5 carbons (pentane) with a methyl branch on C3, counting from either end (the locant is the same, 3, from both directions), giving 3-methylpentane.
questions.hint: Find the longest continuous chain first, then number from whichever end gives the branch the lowest locant.
distractor_logic: 2-Methylpentane misplaces the branch's locant.

'2-ethylbutane' and '3-ethylbutane' wrongly select a 4-carbon parent chain with an ethyl substituent instead of correctly identifying the 5-carbon parent chain, which is not the longest possible chain.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: What is the IUPAC name of CH<sub>2</sub>=CH–CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>3</sub>?
options: 1-Butyne
But-2-ene
But-1-ene
Propene
questions.explanation: The chain has 4 carbons with a double bond starting at C1 (numbering from the end nearer the double bond to give it the lowest locant), giving but-1-ene.
questions.hint: Count the carbons, locate the double bond, and number so the double bond gets the lowest locant.
distractor_logic: 1-butyne wrongly assumes a triple bond.
But-2-ene would place the double bond between C2 and C3, which is not this structure.
Propene has only 3 carbons, one fewer than this structure.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: What is the IUPAC name of CH<sub>3</sub>–CH(OH)–CH<sub>2</sub>–CHO?
options: 4-Hydroxybutanal
3-Oxobutan-1-ol
3-Hydroxybutanal
1-Hydroxybutanal
questions.explanation: The aldehyde (–CHO) outranks the alcohol (–OH) as the principal characteristic group, so it is expressed as the suffix '-al' and numbering starts from the CHO carbon as C1: C1(CHO)–C2(H<sub>2</sub>)–C3(OH)–C4(H<sub>3</sub>), giving the –OH at C3, i.e. 3-hydroxybutanal.
questions.hint: Which group is senior for naming purposes here — the aldehyde or the alcohol — and from which end should you start numbering to favour that group?
distractor_logic: 4-hydroxybutanal numbers from the wrong end (away from the senior CHO group).
1-Hydroxybutanal misplaces the OH position.
'3-oxobutan-1-ol' incorrectly makes the alcohol the suffix group when the aldehyde should outrank it.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: What is the IUPAC name of CH<sub>3</sub>–CO–CH<sub>2</sub>–COOH?
options: 2-Oxobutanoic acid
3-Oxobutanoic acid
3-Hydroxybutanoic acid
1-Oxobutanoic acid
questions.explanation: The carboxylic acid outranks the ketone, so –COOH is the suffix and C1; numbering C1(COOH)–C2(H<sub>2</sub>)–C3(C=O)–C4(H<sub>3</sub>) places the oxo (ketone) group at C3, giving 3-oxobutanoic acid, with the ketone cited as the prefix 'oxo-'.
questions.hint: The carboxylic acid must be C1 and named as the suffix '-oic acid'; where does the C=O of the ketone fall when you number from that end?
distractor_logic: The locant '1' would place the oxo group on the same carbon as the acid, which is structurally impossible here.
'Hydroxy' wrongly describes an –OH group, but this molecule has a ketone (C=O), not an alcohol.
'2-oxo' misplaces the ketone by one carbon.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: CH<sub>3</sub>–O–CH<sub>3</sub> (dimethyl ether) and CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH (ethanol) share the molecular formula C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O. What type of isomerism do they show?
options: Chain isomerism
Functional group isomerism
Metamerism
Position isomerism
questions.explanation: The two compounds belong to entirely different functional classes (ether vs alcohol) despite sharing a molecular formula, which is the defining feature of functional group isomerism.
questions.hint: Do these two molecules even have the same type of functional group, or completely different ones?
distractor_logic: Position isomerism requires the same functional group at a different location.
Chain isomerism requires the same functional group with a different carbon skeleton.
Metamerism applies to isomers of the same functional class (e.g. ethers) with different alkyl groups on either side, none of which fit an ether vs. an alcohol.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: n-Pentane (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>) and 2-methylbutane (isopentane) both have the molecular formula C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub>. What type of isomerism is this?
options: Chain isomerism
Functional group isomerism
Position isomerism
Metamerism
questions.explanation: Both compounds are alkanes (identical functional character: none) differing only in how the carbon skeleton is branched, which is chain isomerism.
questions.hint: Is any functional group or its position changing here, or just the branching of an otherwise identical carbon skeleton?
distractor_logic: There is no functional group to reposition (position isomerism) or change class (functional isomerism).
Metamerism specifically concerns different alkyl groups flanking a shared functional group such as an ether or ketone, which does not apply to two alkanes.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Acetic acid derivatives R–COOH with R = –CH<sub>2</sub>Cl, –CH<sub>2</sub>NO<sub>2</sub>, or –CH<sub>3</sub> show different acid strengths due to inductive effects on the adjacent carbon. Which substituted acid is expected to be the strongest acid?
options: O<sub>2</sub>N–CH<sub>2</sub>–COOH (nitroacetic acid)
CH<sub>3</sub>–COOH (acetic acid)
All three have identical acid strength
Cl–CH<sub>2</sub>–COOH (chloroacetic acid)
questions.explanation: −NO<sub>2</sub> is a stronger electron-withdrawing (−I) group than −Cl, so it pulls more electron density away from the carboxylate oxygen after deprotonation, stabilising the conjugate base more and making nitroacetic acid the strongest acid of the three; acetic acid (with an electron-donating methyl group) is the weakest.
questions.hint: Rank −NO<sub>2</sub>, −Cl, and −CH<sub>3</sub> by how strongly they withdraw electron density.
distractor_logic: The three clearly differ, so they cannot be identical.
Chloroacetic acid is more acidic than plain acetic acid but less than the nitro-substituted acid since −Cl is a weaker −I group than −NO<sub>2</sub>.
Acetic acid is the weakest since −CH<sub>3</sub> is electron-donating (+I), not withdrawing.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Of the alkyl groups –CH<sub>3</sub>, –C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>, –CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>, and –C(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>, which shows the strongest +I (electron-donating inductive) effect?
options: –CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> (isopropyl)
–C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub> (ethyl)
–C(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub> (tert-butyl)
–CH<sub>3</sub> (methyl)
questions.explanation: The +I effect of an alkyl group increases with the number of alkyl substituents attached to the donating carbon: tert-butyl (three methyls attached) donates electron density most strongly, giving the order tert-butyl > isopropyl > ethyl > methyl.
questions.hint: More branching around the carbon attached to the chain generally means a stronger electron-donating inductive effect.
distractor_logic: Methyl is the least branched and therefore the weakest +I donor of the set.
Ethyl and isopropyl fall in between tert-butyl and methyl in donating strength, not at the top.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: For acrolein, CH<sub>2</sub>=CH–CHO, which is a valid resonance (canonical) structure, obtained purely by moving electrons with the atomic skeleton fixed?
options: CH≡C–CH<sub>2</sub>–OH
CH<sub>3</sub>–CH=CH–OH
<sup>+</sup>CH<sub>2</sub>–CH=CH–O<sup>−</sup>
CH<sub>2</sub>=CH–CH<sub>2</sub>–OH
questions.explanation: Shifting the C=C π electrons toward the carbonyl carbon and the C=O π electrons fully onto oxygen (while keeping every atom in place) gives the delocalised canonical form <sup>+</sup>CH<sub>2</sub>–CH=CH–O<sup>−</sup>; this is a legitimate resonance contributor of the conjugated enal system.
questions.hint: A true resonance structure must have every atom in exactly the same position — only electrons (and formal charges) can move.
distractor_logic: The other three options all add a hydrogen atom that was not present in the original molecule (they are different, tautomeric or reduced molecules, not resonance forms), which is not allowed in resonance — resonance never changes atom positions or atom count.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: In phenol, resonance donation of the oxygen lone pair into the aromatic ring increases electron density mainly at which ring positions?
options: All six ring positions equally, including meta
Ortho and para positions
Only at the ipso (attached) carbon
Meta position only
questions.explanation: Drawing out the resonance structures of phenol shows the oxygen lone pair delocalising into the ring specifically onto the ortho and para carbons (each acquiring a partial negative charge in a canonical form), which is why phenol undergoes electrophilic substitution preferentially at those positions.
questions.hint: Draw the resonance structures of phenoxide-like delocalisation from oxygen — which carbons end up carrying the negative charge in the canonical forms?
distractor_logic: The ipso carbon is where oxygen is attached, not where the extra density appears.
The meta position does not receive direct resonance donation in any canonical structure.
The increase is not uniform across all six positions, it is specific to ortho/para.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: When an electrophile E<sup>+</sup> approaches CH<sub>2</sub>=CH<sub>2</sub> to initiate electrophilic addition, the electromeric effect involves:
options: Complete transfer of the π electron pair to one carbon, which bonds to E, leaving a carbocation on the other carbon
Equal sharing of the π electron pair between both carbons, with no bond formed to E
No change in the electron distribution of the double bond
Transfer of a σ electron pair from a C–H bond to the incoming electrophile
questions.explanation: As the electrophile approaches, the electromeric effect completely shifts the mobile π electron pair to one carbon of the double bond; that carbon forms a new bond to the electrophile E, while the other carbon is left electron-deficient as a carbocation intermediate.
questions.hint: In electrophilic addition, one carbon of the double bond ends up bonded to E and the other ends up positively charged — what happened to the shared π electron pair to cause that?
distractor_logic: 'no change' contradicts the entire premise of how addition reactions proceed.
Equal sharing would not create a carbocation at all.
The electromeric effect specifically involves π, not σ, electrons.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: The temporary shift of π electrons that assists HBr in adding across the double bond of propene (making the reaction proceed readily) is best classified as an example of the:
options: Electromeric effect
Hydrogen bonding effect
Van der Waals effect
Inductive effect
questions.explanation: This is a textbook case of the electromeric effect: the π electron pair of the C=C bond shifts completely toward one carbon only in the presence of the approaching electrophilic H of HBr, generating a carbocation that Br<sup>−</sup> then attacks.
questions.hint: This shift only happens because HBr is actively approaching — which effect is defined as operating only during a reaction, in the presence of a reagent?
distractor_logic: The inductive effect is permanent and weaker, not the sudden complete π-shift described here.
Hydrogen bonding and van der Waals forces are intermolecular attractions unrelated to electron shifts within a double bond.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: How many hyperconjugative (no-bond resonance) structures can be drawn for the tert-butyl cation, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C<sup>+</sup>?
questions.explanation: Hyperconjugation requires alpha C–H bonds on carbons directly attached to the cationic centre; each of the three methyl groups attached to the cationic carbon contributes 3 alpha hydrogens, giving 3 × 3 = 9 total alpha hydrogens and therefore 9 possible hyperconjugative structures.
questions.hint: Count the number of methyl groups directly attached to the C<sup>+</sup>, then count the alpha C–H bonds on each.
distractor_logic: 3 counts only a single methyl group.
12 overcounts, exceeding the actual number of alpha C–H bonds available (there are only 9 in total on the three methyls).
6 undercounts by ignoring one methyl group's contribution.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: For the ethyl cation, CH<sub>3</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> (positive charge on the terminal CH<sub>2</sub>), how many alpha hydrogens are available to stabilise the cation through hyperconjugation?
questions.explanation: The alpha carbon (the one directly attached to the cationic carbon) is the CH<sub>3</sub> group, which carries 3 C–H bonds, all capable of hyperconjugative overlap with the empty p orbital on the adjacent cationic carbon — giving 3 hyperconjugative structures.
questions.hint: Identify which carbon is 'alpha' to the positively charged carbon, then count its hydrogens.
distractor_logic: 2 undercounts the methyl group's hydrogens.
5 overcounts beyond what a single CH<sub>3</sub> group can supply.
0 wrongly assumes hyperconjugation is impossible here, when in fact this primary cation is stabilised (albeit weakly) exactly by this effect.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Between ortho-nitrophenol and para-nitrophenol, which has the lower boiling point, and why?
options: Both have identical boiling points since both contain the same functional groups
para-Nitrophenol, because it cannot form any hydrogen bonds at all
ortho-Nitrophenol, because its intramolecular H-bond (chelation) prevents intermolecular association
ortho-Nitrophenol, because it is a stronger acid than the para isomer
questions.explanation: In ortho-nitrophenol the –OH and the adjacent –NO<sub>2</sub> group are close enough to form a six-membered intramolecular hydrogen bond (chelation); this ties up the H-bond donor/acceptor within a single molecule, preventing the extensive intermolecular hydrogen-bond network that para-nitrophenol can form, so the ortho isomer boils at a distinctly lower temperature.
questions.hint: Which isomer's substituents are close enough in space to hydrogen-bond with each other rather than with a neighbouring molecule?
distractor_logic: Acid strength is not the reason for the boiling-point gap here.
The two isomers do not have identical boiling points precisely because of this structural difference.
Para-Nitrophenol can and does form intermolecular hydrogen bonds, so it is not simply 'no H-bonds'.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Ethanol (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH) and dimethyl ether (CH<sub>3</sub>OCH<sub>3</sub>) are isomers of identical molecular mass, yet ethanol boils at a much higher temperature. This is best explained by:
options: Ethanol has a larger molecular mass than dimethyl ether
Dimethyl ether undergoes intramolecular hydrogen bonding, lowering its boiling point
Dimethyl ether has stronger inductive effects than ethanol
Ethanol molecules can hydrogen-bond intermolecularly through their O–H groups, while dimethyl ether has no O–H to donate
questions.explanation: Ethanol has an O–H bond that can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, letting molecules link together extensively; dimethyl ether's oxygen can only accept hydrogen bonds (there is no O–H to donate), so it cannot form the same network, resulting in a much lower boiling point despite the identical molecular formula.
questions.hint: Does dimethyl ether have any O–H bond to hydrogen-bond with a neighbouring molecule?
distractor_logic: Dimethyl ether has no O–H hydrogens at all, so intramolecular H-bonding within it is not possible.
The two compounds have exactly the same molecular mass (both C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O), so that cannot be the explanation.
Inductive effects are not the determining factor for this large a boiling-point gap.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Under UV light, Cl<sub>2</sub> dissociates into two chlorine atoms: Cl<sub>2</sub> → 2Cl•. This bond cleavage is:
options: Homolytic fission, since the non-polar bond splits symmetrically to give two identical radicals
Heterolytic fission, since one chlorine keeps both electrons
Neither, since no bond is actually broken
Heterolytic fission, producing Cl<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>−</sup>
questions.explanation: The Cl–Cl bond is completely non-polar (both atoms identical), so under UV energy it splits symmetrically, each chlorine keeping one electron of the shared pair, producing two identical, neutral chlorine radicals — classic homolytic fission that initiates radical chain reactions.
questions.hint: Since both atoms in Cl<sub>2</sub> are identical, is there any reason for the electron pair to go unevenly to one atom?
distractor_logic: Cl<sup>+</sup>/Cl<sup>−</sup> would require heterolytic cleavage, which does not apply here.
The bond clearly is broken (that is the entire point of initiation in radical chain mechanisms).
Heterolytic fission requires an unequal distribution, which makes no sense for two identical atoms.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: The first step of the reaction (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C–Cl → (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C<sup>+</sup> + Cl<sup>−</sup> in aqueous solution involves:
options: No bond breaking; only a proton is transferred
Homolytic fission, producing a tert-butyl radical and a chlorine radical
Heterolytic fission, with both bonding electrons going to carbon
Heterolytic fission, with both bonding electrons going to the more electronegative chlorine
questions.explanation: Because chlorine is far more electronegative than carbon and the ionisation is assisted by a polar solvent, the C–Cl bond breaks unevenly: both electrons of the shared pair leave with chlorine, forming Cl<sup>−</sup>, while carbon is left as an electron-deficient carbocation, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C<sup>+</sup>.
questions.hint: The products are ions (a cation and an anion), not neutral radicals — which type of fission gives ionic products?
distractor_logic: The electrons go to the more electronegative chlorine, not to carbon, since carbon ends up positively charged.
Homolytic fission would give two neutral radicals, not the ionic products shown.
No bond is broken is directly contradicted by the C–Cl bond clearly cleaving.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Among CH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CH<sup>+</sup>, and (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C<sup>+</sup>, which carbocation is the most stable?
options: CH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> (methyl)
(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C<sup>+</sup> (tertiary)
(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CH<sup>+</sup> (secondary)
CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> (primary)
questions.explanation: Increasing alkyl substitution provides more +I donation and more alpha C–H bonds for hyperconjugation, so stability rises steadily from methyl (no stabilisation at all) through primary and secondary to tertiary, which is the most stable of this set.
questions.hint: Which cation has the most alkyl groups directly attached to the positively charged carbon?
distractor_logic: Methyl has no adjacent alkyl group at all, making it the least stable.
Primary and secondary cations are more stable than methyl but still less stable than tertiary, since they offer less +I donation and fewer hyperconjugative C–H bonds.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Which is more stable, the benzyl cation (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>) or the ethyl cation (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>)?
options: The ethyl cation, because primary cations are always more stable than benzylic ones
Both are equally stable since both are primary cations
The benzyl cation is less stable due to steric hindrance from the ring
The benzyl cation, because the positive charge is delocalised into the aromatic ring by resonance
questions.explanation: Although both cations have the positive charge on a carbon bonded to only one other carbon (formally 'primary'), the benzyl cation can delocalise its positive charge into the aromatic ring through resonance (onto the ortho and para ring carbons), which provides substantial extra stabilisation unavailable to a simple, non-conjugated ethyl cation.
questions.hint: Can the positive charge on the benzylic carbon be pushed into the ring by resonance? Can the ethyl cation's charge be delocalised anywhere?
distractor_logic: Formal degree of substitution alone (both 'primary') does not capture the resonance effect, so they are not equally stable.
Primary cations are not 'always' more stable than benzylic ones — resonance stabilisation in the benzyl case dominates over the simple hyperconjugative/inductive stabilisation available to ethyl.
Steric hindrance from the ring is not the determining factor for cation stability here.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Among CH<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup>, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CH<sup>−</sup>, and (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C<sup>−</sup>, which simple alkyl carbanion is the most stable?
options: CH<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> (methyl)
(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C<sup>−</sup> (tertiary)
CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup> (primary)
(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CH<sup>−</sup> (secondary)
questions.explanation: Alkyl groups are +I (electron-donating); on an already electron-rich carbanion, each additional alkyl group intensifies the negative charge density and destabilises the ion, so stability decreases with increasing substitution, making methyl carbanion the most stable of this simple alkyl set.
questions.hint: This is the reverse trend to carbocation stability — which end of the substitution scale is most stable here?
distractor_logic: Tertiary and secondary carbanions are destabilised by the extra +I donation from their additional alkyl groups relative to methyl.
Primary carbanion falls in between methyl and secondary/tertiary in stability, not at the top.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Which is more stable: a simple methyl carbanion (CH<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>) or the enolate-type carbanion formed by deprotonating acetone at the alpha carbon (CH<sub>3</sub>–CO–CH<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup>)?
options: The enolate-type carbanion, because the negative charge is delocalised by resonance onto the more electronegative oxygen of the adjacent carbonyl
The methyl carbanion, because carbanions next to a carbonyl group are always destabilised
Both are equally stable since both carry a single negative charge on carbon
The methyl carbanion, because resonance can only stabilise positive charges, never negative ones
questions.explanation: The carbanion adjacent to a C=O group can delocalise its negative charge through resonance onto the electronegative oxygen (forming an enolate), which is a strongly stabilising effect (further reinforced by the −I effect of the carbonyl); this makes it considerably more stable than an isolated, non-conjugated methyl carbanion.
questions.hint: Can the lone pair on the carbanion carbon next to C=O be pushed into resonance with the carbonyl, the way it can in an enolate?
distractor_logic: Being next to a carbonyl group stabilises, not destabilises, an adjacent carbanion through resonance.
Resonance readily stabilises negative charge (e.g. carboxylate, enolate), so that claim is false.
The two carbanions are clearly not equivalent because one benefits from resonance delocalisation and the other does not.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Which is more stable: a methyl radical (CH<sub>3</sub>•) or a tertiary radical ((CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C•)?
options: The tertiary radical, stabilised by +I effect and hyperconjugation from three attached methyl groups
The tertiary radical is less stable due to steric strain around the radical centre
Both are equally stable, since both carry a single unpaired electron
The methyl radical, since radicals are destabilised by alkyl substitution
questions.explanation: Like carbocations, radicals are stabilised by electron-donating alkyl groups through +I effect and by hyperconjugative overlap of adjacent C–H bonds with the singly occupied orbital; more alkyl substitution therefore increases radical stability, giving 3° > 2° > 1° > methyl.
questions.hint: Does this follow the same substitution-stability trend you would expect for a carbocation?
distractor_logic: Alkyl substitution stabilises, not destabilises, radicals.
Steric strain is a minor factor here and does not override the electronic stabilisation.
The two radicals are not equally stable because the tertiary one has far more hyperconjugative and inductive support.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Which is more stable: the allyl radical (CH<sub>2</sub>=CH–CH<sub>2</sub>•) or the n-propyl radical (CH<sub>3</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>•)?
options: The n-propyl radical, because primary radicals are always more stable than allylic ones
The allyl radical, because the unpaired electron is delocalised over two carbons by resonance with the adjacent double bond
Both are equally stable since both are primary radicals
The allyl radical is less stable because conjugation destabilises a radical centre
questions.explanation: The allyl radical's unpaired electron is delocalised over C1 and C3 through resonance with the adjacent C=C double bond, spreading the radical character over two carbons and lowering its energy substantially compared with the localised, non-conjugated n-propyl radical.
questions.hint: Is there a π bond next to the radical centre in the allyl case that could allow delocalisation, the way there is for the allyl cation?
distractor_logic: The two radicals are clearly not equal since only one has access to resonance delocalisation.
Formal 'primary' classification does not automatically make a radical more stable.
Conjugation with a π system stabilises, not destabilises, a radical centre through resonance.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Boron trifluoride, BF<sub>3</sub>, in which boron has only six electrons around it, typically behaves as a(n):
options: Neither electrophile nor nucleophile, since BF<sub>3</sub> is a stable, unreactive molecule
Nucleophile, donating a lone pair from fluorine
Electrophile (Lewis acid), accepting an electron pair to complete boron's octet
Free radical, due to an unpaired electron on boron
questions.explanation: Boron in BF<sub>3</sub> has an incomplete octet (only six electrons), making it strongly electron-deficient; it readily accepts an electron pair from a donor, behaving as a Lewis acid/electrophile, e.g. in forming BF<sub>3</sub>·NH<sub>3</sub> adducts.
questions.hint: Does boron in BF<sub>3</sub> have a full octet, or is it short of electrons?
distractor_logic: BF<sub>3</sub> does not have a lone pair on boron itself to donate, so it cannot be a nucleophile in that sense.
Boron has no unpaired electron here, so it is not a radical.
Being electron-deficient makes BF<sub>3</sub> quite reactive toward electron-pair donors, not inert.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: The cyanide ion, CN<sup>−</sup>, in reactions such as its attack on an alkyl halide, behaves as a(n):
options: Nucleophile, using the lone pair on carbon to attack an electron-deficient centre
Free radical, since it has an unshared electron
Electrophile, because it carries a negative charge
Neither, because CN<sup>−</sup> is unreactive
questions.explanation: CN<sup>−</sup> is negatively charged and carries a lone pair (largely on carbon) that it readily donates to an electron-poor carbon, the defining behaviour of a nucleophile; it is a classic reagent in substitution reactions such as R–X + CN<sup>−</sup> → R–CN + X<sup>−</sup>.
questions.hint: A negatively charged ion with a lone pair to give away — is that electron-seeking or electron-donating behaviour?
distractor_logic: It is, in fact, a well-known and reactive nucleophile, not unreactive.
CN<sup>−</sup> has all its electrons paired, so it is not a radical.
Negative charge is exactly why CN<sup>−</sup> is electron-rich and nucleophilic, not electrophilic (electrophiles are electron-poor).

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br + KOH (alcoholic) → CH<sub>2</sub>=CH<sub>2</sub> + KBr + H<sub>2</sub>O is an example of a(n):
options: Elimination reaction
Addition reaction
Substitution reaction
Rearrangement reaction
questions.explanation: A hydrogen and the bromine are removed from adjacent carbons to form a new C=C double bond (dehydrohalogenation); removing atoms to create unsaturation is the hallmark of an elimination reaction.
questions.hint: Is a new multiple bond being created by removing atoms, or is one atom simply being swapped for another?
distractor_logic: No skeletal rearrangement of carbons occurs in this reaction.
Substitution would replace Br with something else while keeping the molecule saturated, which does not match the alkene product formed here.
Addition is the reverse process (combining across a multiple bond).

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH + HBr → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br + H<sub>2</sub>O is an example of a(n):
options: Elimination reaction
Addition reaction
Substitution reaction
Free-radical polymerisation
questions.explanation: The –OH group of ethanol is replaced by –Br; one atom/group is swapped for another with no multiple bond created or destroyed, which is the definition of a substitution reaction.
questions.hint: Is a group being replaced, or is a new double bond being formed or broken?
distractor_logic: Addition requires a multiple bond to react across, which is absent here.
There is no chain polymerisation occurring in this simple single-molecule reaction.
Elimination would remove atoms to form unsaturation, the opposite of what happens.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: A solid organic compound known to sublime cleanly on gentle heating is contaminated with a non-volatile inorganic salt. Which technique should be tried first to purify it?
options: Sublimation
Simple distillation
Column chromatography
Steam distillation
questions.explanation: Since the compound sublimes and the impurity is non-volatile, gently heating the mixture lets the pure compound vaporise and recondense elsewhere (e.g. on a cold surface), cleanly leaving the non-volatile salt behind — the most direct and appropriate method here.
questions.hint: The compound's key property (subliming cleanly) matches exactly one purification technique named after that property.
distractor_logic: Simple distillation and steam distillation are designed for liquids, not solids that sublime.
Column chromatography could work but is unnecessarily elaborate when a simpler, purpose-built technique (sublimation) directly exploits the known property of the compound.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Two solid compounds have very similar solubility behaviour in all common solvents but noticeably different melting points. Which purification method is least likely to separate them well, and why?
options: Crystallisation, because it depends on differences in solubility, which are minimal here
Distillation, because it works only on solids
Sublimation, because it depends on solubility differences
Crystallisation, because it depends only on differences in melting point
questions.explanation: Crystallisation separates compounds based on how differently they dissolve (and precipitate out) in a solvent as conditions change; if two compounds have nearly identical solubility profiles, crystallisation will not discriminate between them well, regardless of any melting-point difference.
questions.hint: What physical property does crystallisation actually exploit to achieve separation — solubility, or melting point?
distractor_logic: Distillation is a technique for liquids (or volatile solids via related methods), the description given is inaccurate.
Sublimation depends on volatility, not solubility.
Crystallisation depends on solubility, not melting point, so that reasoning is incorrect even though the conclusion about crystallisation being unsuitable is right for the correct reason.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Two miscible liquids A (b.p. 60 °C) and B (b.p. 63 °C) need to be separated. Is simple distillation an appropriate method here?
options: Yes, because any boiling point difference at all is sufficient for simple distillation
No, because simple distillation only works on immiscible liquids
Yes, because simple distillation always gives perfect separation regardless of boiling points
No, because the boiling points are too close together; fractional distillation is needed instead
questions.explanation: With only a 3 °C gap between boiling points, the vapours of both liquids form together throughout the distillation, so a single simple-distillation step cannot cleanly separate them; a fractionating column, which provides repeated vaporisation-condensation cycles, is required instead.
questions.hint: How large a boiling-point gap does simple distillation generally need to work well, and is 3 °C anywhere close to that?
distractor_logic: Simple distillation is used for miscible liquids, not immiscible ones (immiscible liquids of different densities are more simply separated by a separating funnel).
No distillation method gives 'perfect' separation regardless of conditions.
A tiny boiling-point gap is exactly the situation where simple distillation fails.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: An organic solute is present in an aqueous reaction mixture and is known to be far more soluble in diethyl ether than in water. Which technique is best suited to isolate it?
options: Sublimation of the reaction mixture
Differential (solvent) extraction using ether and a separating funnel
Simple distillation of the aqueous mixture
Column chromatography without any solvent
questions.explanation: Shaking the aqueous mixture with an immiscible solvent (ether) in which the solute is much more soluble transfers most of the solute into the ether layer; the two immiscible layers are then separated using a separating funnel, isolating the solute efficiently — this is exactly differential/solvent extraction.
questions.hint: The key fact given is a large difference in solubility between two immiscible solvents — which technique is built directly around that property?
distractor_logic: Sublimation applies to solids that vaporise directly, not to a dissolved solute in water.
Chromatography does use solvents but is not the technique specifically designed for immiscible liquid–liquid partitioning.
Distillation targets differences in boiling point/volatility, not solubility differences between immiscible solvents.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: In a column chromatography experiment, compound X is adsorbed much more strongly onto the silica stationary phase than compound Y. Which of the two will elute (come out of the column) first?
options: Neither will elute; only non-adsorbed compounds can pass through a column
Both will elute at exactly the same time regardless of adsorption strength
Compound Y, since weaker adsorption lets it be carried along faster by the mobile phase
Compound X, since stronger adsorption always speeds up elution
questions.explanation: The mobile phase continuously carries components down the column, but strongly adsorbed components are repeatedly held back by the stationary phase; the more weakly adsorbed compound, Y, moves down (and elutes) faster, while the strongly adsorbed compound X lags behind.
questions.hint: Which compound does the stationary phase 'hold onto' less, letting it travel with the mobile phase more freely?
distractor_logic: Identical elution times would defeat the entire purpose of using differing adsorption strengths to separate the two compounds.
Stronger adsorption slows a compound down, it does not speed elution up.
Adsorbed compounds do still elute eventually as more mobile phase is passed through, they are not permanently trapped.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: A mixture of several structurally similar plant pigments, each with slightly different adsorption behaviour on alumina, needs to be separated into its individual components. Which technique is most directly suited to this task?
options: Column (adsorption) chromatography
Simple distillation
Sublimation
Crystallisation from a single solvent
questions.explanation: Adsorption chromatography, historically first used to separate coloured plant pigments (which is how the technique got its name), is specifically designed to exploit small differences in adsorption strength between structurally similar compounds, cleanly resolving them as bands along the column.
questions.hint: The problem statement explicitly mentions 'different adsorption behaviour' — which technique is built directly around that property?
distractor_logic: Distillation and sublimation both rely on volatility, which is largely irrelevant for these non-volatile pigment molecules.
Crystallisation depends on solubility differences and would struggle with structurally similar pigments that likely have very similar solubility profiles.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: A compound's Lassaigne extract gives a deep Prussian-blue colouration with FeSO<sub>4</sub>/FeCl<sub>3</sub> and dilute H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, but gives no precipitate with AgNO<sub>3</sub> and no black precipitate with lead acetate. What does this indicate about the compound's elemental composition?
options: It contains both nitrogen and sulfur
It contains sulfur, but no nitrogen
It contains a halogen, but no nitrogen
It contains nitrogen, but no halogen and no sulfur
questions.explanation: Prussian-blue colouration specifically confirms nitrogen (via NaCN formed during fusion); a negative AgNO<sub>3</sub> test rules out halogens (no AgX precipitate), and a negative lead acetate test rules out sulfur (no black PbS precipitate) — so only nitrogen is present among these three elements.
