questions.hint: Match each test result to the single element it is designed to confirm or rule out: Prussian blue → ?, AgNO<sub>3</sub> precipitate → ?, black PbS → ?
distractor_logic: A halogen would give a precipitate with AgNO<sub>3</sub>, which was not observed.
Sulfur would instead give a black precipitate with lead acetate (absent here) or a violet colour with sodium nitroprusside, not Prussian blue.
Since the sulfur test was negative, 'both nitrogen and sulfur' is inconsistent with the data.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: A compound's sodium fusion extract, when acidified with acetic acid and treated with lead acetate solution, gives a black precipitate. This indicates the presence of:
options: A halogen, as silver halide
Nitrogen, as Prussian blue
Phosphorus, as ammonium phosphomolybdate
Sulfur, as insoluble black lead sulfide (PbS)
questions.explanation: Sodium fusion converts organic sulfur into Na<sub>2</sub>S; treating the acidified extract with lead acetate precipitates black, insoluble lead sulfide (PbS), the standard confirmatory test for sulfur.
questions.hint: What black, insoluble metal sulfide would form if the fusion converted the sulfur present into sulfide ions?
distractor_logic: Nitrogen is instead confirmed by a Prussian-blue colour with iron salts, not a lead-acetate black precipitate.
Phosphorus requires a separate oxidative fusion and gives a yellow precipitate with ammonium molybdate, not a black one.
Halogens give a precipitate with AgNO<sub>3</sub>, not lead acetate.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: In Liebig's combustion method, a 0.30 g sample of an organic compound gives 0.44 g of CO<sub>2</sub> and 0.18 g of H<sub>2</sub>O. What is the percentage of carbon in the compound?
questions.explanation: Mass of carbon = 0.44 g CO<sub>2</sub> × (12/44) = 0.12 g. Percentage of carbon = (0.12 g / 0.30 g) × 100 = 40%.
questions.hint: First find the mass of carbon from the mass of CO<sub>2</sub> using the molar-mass ratio 12/44, then divide by the sample mass and multiply by 100.
distractor_logic: 44% mistakes the mass of CO<sub>2</sub> itself (or the CO<sub>2</sub> percentage) for the carbon percentage.
33% and 12% arise from arithmetic slips in applying the 12/44 mass ratio or in the final division by sample mass.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: In the Dumas method, 0.25 g of an organic compound gives 33.6 mL of N<sub>2</sub> gas measured at STP (after CO<sub>2</sub> is absorbed by KOH). What is the percentage of nitrogen in the compound? (Use %N = 28 × V<sub>N<sub>2</sub></sub>(mL) / (22400 × mass in g) × 100)
questions.hint: Plug the given volume and mass directly into the Dumas formula and simplify step by step.
distractor_logic: 33.6% simply restates the volume figure without applying the formula.
11.2% and 22.4% come from common slips such as using half or the wrong multiple of the molar volume (22400 mL) in the calculation.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: What is the correct IUPAC name of CH<sub>3</sub>–CH(Cl)–CH(OH)–COOH?
options: 2-Hydroxy-3-chlorobutanoic acid, numbered from the methyl end
2-Chloro-3-hydroxybutanoic acid
3-Hydroxy-2-chlorobutanoic acid
3-Chloro-2-hydroxybutanoic acid
questions.explanation: –COOH outranks –OH and –Cl, so it must be C1. Numbering from the acid end: C1(COOH)–C2(CHOH)–C3(CHCl)–C4(CH<sub>3</sub>). Substituents are cited alphabetically (chloro before hydroxy) with their correct locants: 3-chloro-2-hydroxybutanoic acid.
questions.hint: Fix C1 at the carboxylic acid carbon first (it is always senior to –OH and –Cl), then read off the locants of the other two groups in that direction, and cite them alphabetically.
distractor_logic: '2-Chloro-3-hydroxy...' and '3-hydroxy-2-chloro...' swap the two locants, misassigning which substituent sits closer to the acid carbon.

The option explicitly numbered from the methyl end deliberately numbers from the wrong end, which would make the principal group's own carbon fail to be C1 — a violation of the numbering priority rule.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: What is the correct IUPAC name of CH<sub>2</sub>=CH–CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)–CHO?
options: 2-Methylbut-1-enal
1-Methylbut-3-enal
2-Methylbut-3-enal
3-Methylbut-1-enal
questions.explanation: The aldehyde carbon must be C1: C1(CHO)–C2(CH–CH<sub>3</sub>)–C3(CH=)–C4(=CH<sub>2</sub>). The double bond spans C3–C4, cited by its lower locant as '-3-enal', and the methyl substituent sits at C2, giving 2-methylbut-3-enal.
questions.hint: The –CHO carbon is always C1 — number outward from there and locate both the branch and the double bond relative to that fixed starting point.
distractor_logic: '3-Methylbut-1-enal' and '2-methylbut-1-enal' misplace the double bond at C1–C2, which does not exist in this structure.
'1-methylbut-3-enal' incorrectly puts a substituent locant on C1, the very carbon that is already fully accounted for by the aldehyde suffix.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: What is the correct IUPAC name of CH<sub>3</sub>–CO–CH<sub>2</sub>–CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)–CH<sub>2</sub>–OH?
options: 1-Hydroxy-2-methylpentan-4-one
5-Hydroxy-4-methylpentan-2-one
5-Hydroxy-2-methylpentan-4-one
2-Hydroxy-4-methylpentan-5-one
questions.explanation: In the seniority order for principal characteristic groups, a ketone outranks an alcohol, so the C=O must be the suffix ('-one') and –OH is cited only as the prefix 'hydroxy-'. The parent chain has 5 carbons: C1(CH<sub>3</sub>)–C2(C=O)–C3(CH<sub>2</sub>)–C4(CH–CH<sub>3</sub>)–C5(CH<sub>2</sub>OH); numbering from the methyl end gives the ketone its lowest possible locant (2, versus 4 if numbered from the other end), fixing the methyl branch at C4 and –OH at C5: 5-hydroxy-4-methylpentan-2-one.
questions.hint: Check the seniority order first — between a ketone and an alcohol, which one is entitled to be the suffix and therefore to get the lowest locant?
distractor_logic: '5-hydroxy-2-methylpentan-4-one' keeps the correct substituent locants but assigns the wrong locant (4 instead of 2) to the suffix ketone, again failing to give the principal group the lowest number.
'2-Hydroxy-4-methylpentan-5-one' numbers from the wrong end, giving the ketone (the senior group) the higher locant 5 instead of the mandatory lower one.
'1-hydroxy-2-methylpentan-4-one' misreads which carbon bears which substituent, effectively reversing the structure.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Which is the correct IUPAC name for CH<sub>3</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>–C(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>–OH?
options: 2,2-Dimethylpropan-1-ol
2,2-Dimethylbutan-1-ol
3,3-Dimethylbutan-1-ol
2-Ethyl-2-methylpropan-1-ol
questions.explanation: The –OH carbon must be C1. Tracing the longest chain from C1 through the quaternary carbon and into the ethyl group (not stopping at a methyl branch) gives a 4-carbon parent: C1(CH<sub>2</sub>OH)–C2(C(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>)–C3(CH<sub>2</sub>)–C4(CH<sub>3</sub>), i.e. butan-1-ol with two methyl substituents at C2: 2,2-dimethylbutan-1-ol.
questions.hint: At the quaternary carbon, four different paths are possible for the 'longest chain' — which one, when followed, actually gives the greatest total number of carbons in the main chain?
distractor_logic: '3,3-Dimethylbutan-1-ol' misassigns the locant of the branch point.

'2-ethyl-2-methylpropan-1-ol' wrongly stops the parent chain at 3 carbons (propan-1-ol) and treats the longer continuation as an 'ethyl' substituent instead of extending the main chain, violating the longest-chain rule.
'2,2-dimethylpropan-1-ol' drops a carbon altogether, undercounting the chain by one.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: What is the correct IUPAC name of CH<sub>3</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>–CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)–CH<sub>2</sub>–CH(OH)–CH<sub>3</sub>?
options: 4-Methylhexan-2-ol
4-Methylhexan-5-ol
2-Methylhexan-4-ol
3-Methylhexan-5-ol
questions.explanation: –OH is the principal group and must receive the lowest possible locant. Numbering from the end nearer the –OH (the right-hand CH<sub>3</sub> end) gives: C1(CH<sub>3</sub>)–C2(CHOH)–C3(CH<sub>2</sub>)–C4(CH–CH<sub>3</sub>)–C5(CH<sub>2</sub>)–C6(CH<sub>3</sub>), placing –OH at C2 (far lower than numbering from the other end, which would give C5) and the methyl branch at C4: 4-methylhexan-2-ol.
questions.hint: Try numbering from both ends and compare the locant given to the –OH group each time — which direction gives the lower number for the suffix group?
distractor_logic: '3-Methylhexan-5-ol' and '4-methylhexan-5-ol' both number from the wrong end, giving –OH the higher locant (5) instead of the mandatory lower one (2).
'2-methylhexan-4-ol' swaps which substituent is the branch and which is the suffix-bearing carbon, misreading the structure entirely.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: The name '2-ethyl-3-methylpentane' is proposed for a certain C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub> alkane. Is this an acceptable IUPAC name, and if not, what is the correct one?
options: Not acceptable — the correct name is 2,3-dimethylhexane
Acceptable as written, since pentane with an ethyl and a methyl substituent correctly describes the molecule
Not acceptable — the correct name is 3-ethyl-2-methylpentane, only the substituent order needs fixing
Not acceptable — a longer 6-carbon chain exists through the ethyl branch, so the correct name is 3,4-dimethylhexane
questions.explanation: Tracing all possible chains through the structure shows that starting from the far end of the pentane chain and running through the ethyl substituent instead of stopping at C2 gives a continuous run of 6 carbons (hexane), longer than the 5-carbon 'pentane' chain originally chosen. On this correct 6-carbon parent chain, what were the C1 methyl and the C3 methyl branch now both appear as methyl substituents at positions 3 and 4, giving 3,4-dimethylhexane — the true longest-chain parent must always be selected first, so 'ethyl-methylpentane' was an invalid choice from the outset.
questions.hint: Whenever a substituent itself is a chain of 2 or more carbons (like ethyl), always check whether continuing the count through that branch, instead of stopping at the point of attachment, gives an even longer parent chain than the one you started with.
distractor_logic: 'Acceptable as written' ignores the fundamental longest-chain rule, which must be checked before any substituents are named.
'2,3-dimethylhexane' finds the correct 6-carbon parent but misplaces the two methyl locants.
Simply reordering the substituent names in 'ethyl-methylpentane' does not fix the underlying problem, which is the choice of parent chain itself, not the citation order.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: How many structurally isomeric alcohols (excluding ethers) are possible for the molecular formula C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O?
questions.explanation: The four possible alcohols are: butan-1-ol, butan-2-ol, 2-methylpropan-1-ol (isobutanol), and 2-methylpropan-2-ol (tert-butanol) — two from the straight-chain skeleton (chain-position variants) and two from the branched (2-methylpropane) skeleton.
questions.hint: First list the two possible carbon skeletons for 4 carbons (straight-chain and branched), then place –OH at every distinct position on each skeleton.
distractor_logic: 3 undercounts by missing one of the two branched-skeleton alcohols.
5 overcounts by double-listing a position or including a non-distinct structure.
2 accounts only for the straight-chain skeleton, ignoring the branched one entirely.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Diethyl ether (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>–O–CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>) and methyl propyl ether (CH<sub>3</sub>–O–CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>) share the molecular formula C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O and the same functional class (ether). What type of isomerism do they show?
options: Chain isomerism
Position isomerism
Metamerism
Functional group isomerism
questions.explanation: Both compounds are ethers (the same functional class) that differ only in how the total alkyl carbon count is distributed on either side of the oxygen (2+2 vs 1+3); this specific pattern — same functional group, different alkyl groups flanking it — defines metamerism.
questions.hint: Are these two ethers different classes of compound, or the same class with a different split of carbons around the oxygen?
distractor_logic: Position isomerism requires a fixed skeleton with the functional group moved to a different carbon, which does not describe two different ethers.
Chain isomerism would require a branched vs unbranched skeleton within a single continuous chain, not a redistribution around a heteroatom.
Functional group isomerism would require different functional classes altogether (e.g. an ether vs an alcohol), but both compounds here are ethers.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: How many structurally isomeric ketones are possible for the molecular formula C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O?
questions.explanation: The three possible ketones are pentan-2-one (CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>), pentan-3-one (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>), and 3-methylbutan-2-one (CH<sub>3</sub>COCH(CH<sub>3</sub>)CH<sub>3</sub>); the neopentane-type skeleton cannot host a ketone since its only internal carbon is already fully substituted with four alkyl groups and cannot bear a C=O.
questions.hint: Systematically place the carbonyl at every distinct internal position on both the straight-chain and the singly-branched 5-carbon skeleton; check whether the doubly-branched (neopentane) skeleton can even accommodate a C=O.
distractor_logic: 2 undercounts by missing the branched isomer (3-methylbutan-2-one).
4 overcounts, since the fully branched neopentane-type skeleton cannot bear a ketone at all (its central carbon has no room for a double-bonded oxygen).
1 accounts for only a single straight-chain possibility, ignoring both the second straight-chain position and the branched isomer.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Among the isomeric ketones of molecular formula C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O, how many are metamers of pentan-3-one (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>–CO–CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>)?
options: 2 (pentan-2-one and 3-methylbutan-2-one)
1 (pentan-2-one)
0, since pentan-3-one has no metamers among these isomers
3, all other C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O ketones are its metamers
questions.explanation: Metamerism strictly applies to unbranched alkyl groups redistributed around the same functional group. Pentan-3-one (ethyl + ethyl) and pentan-2-one (methyl + propyl) are both unbranched-alkyl ketones differing only in that distribution, so they are metamers. 3-Methylbutan-2-one has a branched skeleton, which makes it a chain isomer of the pentanones, not a metamer.
questions.hint: Metamerism is specifically about redistributing unbranched alkyl groups around a functional group — does the third ketone in this set have a branched or unbranched skeleton?
distractor_logic: Claiming all three are metamers ignores the distinction between chain isomerism (branching) and metamerism (unbranched redistribution).
Including 3-methylbutan-2-one over-counts, since its branching makes it a chain isomer rather than a metamer.
Claiming zero metamers ignores that pentan-2-one clearly qualifies.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Consider 2-chlorobutanoic acid, 3-chlorobutanoic acid, and 4-chlorobutanoic acid (chlorine on C2, C3, and C4 respectively of the same butanoic-acid chain). Based purely on the distance-dependence of the inductive effect, what is the expected order of acid strength?
options: All three are equally acidic, since each contains exactly one chlorine atom
2-Chloro > 3-chloro > 4-chloro
3-Chloro > 2-chloro > 4-chloro
4-Chloro > 3-chloro > 2-chloro
questions.explanation: The −I effect of chlorine is transmitted through σ bonds and weakens sharply with distance from the –COOH group. Chlorine on C2 (closest to the acidic proton's carbon) withdraws electron density most effectively, stabilising the conjugate base the most and giving the strongest acid; the effect progressively weakens as chlorine moves to C3 and then to the more distant C4.
questions.hint: The inductive effect is short-range — does moving the chlorine farther from the –COOH group strengthen or weaken its influence on acidity?
distractor_logic: Treating all three as equally acidic ignores the entire premise that inductive effect strength depends on proximity, not just presence.
Placing 3-chloro first ignores that C2 is even closer to the acidic centre than C3.
The reverse order incorrectly assumes the inductive effect gets stronger with distance.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Acetic acid, chloroacetic acid (ClCH<sub>2</sub>COOH), dichloroacetic acid (Cl<sub>2</sub>CHCOOH), and trichloroacetic acid (Cl<sub>3</sub>CCOOH) are compared for acid strength. What is the correct order, strongest to weakest?
options: All four are equally acidic since they share the same carboxylic acid group
Trichloroacetic acid > dichloroacetic acid > chloroacetic acid > acetic acid
Acetic acid > chloroacetic acid > dichloroacetic acid > trichloroacetic acid
Chloroacetic acid > trichloroacetic acid > dichloroacetic acid > acetic acid
questions.explanation: Each additional chlorine on the alpha carbon adds its own −I effect, and these effects are cumulative; trichloroacetic acid, with three electron-withdrawing chlorines pulling density away from the O–H bond and stabilising the resulting carboxylate, is the strongest acid, while unsubstituted acetic acid (with only electron-donating –CH<sub>3</sub>-type character, i.e. no withdrawing group at all) is the weakest.
questions.hint: More −I-donating chlorines on the same carbon should have an additive effect on withdrawing electron density — which compound has the most chlorines, and which has none?
distractor_logic: Putting chloroacetic acid first ignores that two or three chlorines withdraw even more density than one.
The reverse order incorrectly treats chlorine substitution as acid-weakening rather than acid-strengthening.
Equal acidity ignores that the presence and number of −I substituents is exactly what differentiates these four acids.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Methylamine (CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>) and aniline (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>) are compared for basicity. Which is more basic, and why?
options: Aniline, because resonance always increases the basicity of an attached amine group
Methylamine, because in aniline the nitrogen lone pair is delocalised into the aromatic ring by resonance, making it far less available to accept a proton
Both are equally basic, since both have a lone pair on nitrogen
Aniline, because the aromatic ring's +I effect donates electron density to nitrogen, making the lone pair more available
questions.explanation: In aniline, the nitrogen lone pair conjugates with the aromatic ring (delocalising into the ortho/para positions through resonance), which spreads out and reduces its availability for bonding to a proton; this resonance effect dominates over any weak inductive donation from the ring, making aniline a substantially weaker base than the simple alkyl amine methylamine, whose lone pair is fully localised on nitrogen.
questions.hint: Does the nitrogen lone pair in aniline stay entirely on nitrogen, the way it does in methylamine, or can it delocalise elsewhere?
distractor_logic: The two amines are clearly not equally basic given the very different behaviour of their lone pairs.
The claim that resonance 'always increases' basicity is backwards — resonance delocalisation of a lone pair generically reduces (not increases) its availability to act as a base.
Benzene rings are not simple +I donors in this sense and do not increase basicity by resonance.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: In the acetate ion, CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>−</sup>, experimental evidence shows both carbon–oxygen bonds are of equal length, intermediate between a typical C=O double bond and a C–O single bond. What best explains this?
options: Hydrogen bonding between the two oxygens equalises the bond lengths
The two bonds cannot actually be equal; this is purely a measurement artefact
One C–O bond is a pure single bond and the other a pure double bond, and they simply average out experimentally due to rapid rotation
Two equivalent resonance structures delocalise the negative charge equally over both oxygens, so the true structure is a hybrid with equal, intermediate bond character at both C–O bonds
questions.explanation: Acetate has two equivalent canonical (resonance) structures, each placing the C=O on one oxygen and the C–O<sup>−</sup> on the other; since both structures contribute equally to the true hybrid, both bonds acquire identical, intermediate bond order and length — a classic experimental signature of resonance delocalisation, not an artefact or a rotational average.
questions.hint: If a molecule really did have one true single and one true double bond, would their measured lengths be identical, or different?
distractor_logic: Hydrogen bonding between the two oxygens (which are on the same ion and not bonded to H in this anion form) is not the correct explanation.
Equal bond lengths are a real, well-established structural feature, not a measurement error.
There is no rotation occurring about these bonds in the way implied, and 'averaging' a genuinely different single and double bond would not give a clean, single intermediate length.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: When buta-1,3-diene (CH<sub>2</sub>=CH–CH=CH<sub>2</sub>) reacts with one equivalent of HBr, both the 1,2-addition product (3-bromobut-1-ene) and the 1,4-addition product (1-bromobut-2-ene) are obtained. What best explains why both products can form from a single mechanistic pathway?
options: Protonation at C1 generates a resonance-stabilised allylic carbocation delocalised over C2 and C4, so Br<sup>−</sup> can attack at either position
The electromeric effect only ever produces the 1,2-product; the 1,4-product forms by a completely different, non-electromeric route
HBr adds twice, once at each double bond, giving a dibromide that is misinterpreted as two separate products
The two products arise from two entirely separate, unrelated mechanisms with no common intermediate
questions.explanation: H<sup>+</sup> adds to the terminal C1, and the electromeric shift of the remaining π system generates a carbocation that is delocalised (by resonance) over C2 and C4 of the allylic system; because the positive charge has real character at both C2 and C4, the nucleophile Br<sup>−</sup> can attack either carbon, giving the 1,2- or 1,4-addition product respectively from the very same intermediate.
questions.hint: After the proton adds to C1, is the resulting positive charge stuck on one single carbon, or can it be drawn as delocalised over more than one carbon by resonance?
distractor_logic: The electromeric effect (which generates the delocalised cation in the first place) is exactly what makes both 1,2- and 1,4-attack possible from one pathway, not just the 1,2-product.
The two products genuinely share a single common allylic cation intermediate, so they are not from unrelated mechanisms.
This is addition of one equivalent of HBr to the diene system, not a double addition producing a dibromide.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Explain, in mechanistic terms, why electrophilic addition of HBr to propene (CH<sub>3</sub>–CH=CH<sub>2</sub>) follows Markovnikov's rule, giving 2-bromopropane as the major product.
options: The electromeric shift places H<sup>+</sup> on C2, generating a primary carbocation at C1, which is more stable and reacts faster with Br<sup>−</sup>
Markovnikov's rule has no mechanistic basis; it is purely an empirical rule unrelated to carbocation stability
The electromeric shift of the π electrons places H<sup>+</sup> on the terminal CH<sub>2</sub>, generating the more stable secondary carbocation at C2, which Br<sup>−</sup> then attacks
Br<sup>−</sup> attacks the double bond first, before any proton transfer occurs, making the mechanism unrelated to electron displacement effects
questions.explanation: The temporary (electromeric) shift of the double-bond π electrons allows the electrophilic proton to add to the terminal, less-substituted carbon (C1), because this leaves the positive charge on C2, which becomes a secondary carbocation stabilised by +I effect and hyperconjugation from two adjacent methyl-type carbons; this more stable intermediate forms preferentially, and Br<sup>−</sup> then combines with it to give 2-bromopropane as the major product.
questions.hint: Markovnikov addition proceeds through whichever carbocation is more stable — work out which carbon ends up positively charged if H adds to the terminal CH<sub>2</sub>, and how substituted that carbon is.
distractor_logic: The accepted mechanism is stepwise electrophilic addition (H<sup>+</sup> first, then Br<sup>−</sup>), not simultaneous or Br<sup>−</sup>-first attack.
Markovnikov's rule does have a clear mechanistic (carbocation-stability) basis, it is not merely empirical.
Placing H<sup>+</sup> on C2 would leave the charge on the terminal carbon (C1), giving a less stable primary cation, the opposite of what actually happens.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Compare 2-methylpropene, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C=CH<sub>2</sub>, with but-1-ene, CH<sub>2</sub>=CH–CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>3</sub>, by counting the alpha hydrogens available for hyperconjugation with the C=C double bond in each, and use this to predict which alkene is more stable.
options: Both alkenes have exactly the same number of alpha hydrogens and are equally stable
Alpha-hydrogen count is irrelevant to alkene stability; only ring size matters
But-1-ene has more alpha hydrogens than 2-methylpropene and is therefore more stable

2-Methylpropene has 6 alpha hydrogens (from its two methyl groups) versus only 2 for but-1-ene (from its single CH<sub>2</sub>), so 2-methylpropene is more stabilised by hyperconjugation and is the more stable alkene
questions.explanation: In 2-methylpropene, the sp<sup>2</sup> carbon bearing the two methyl groups provides 3 + 3 = 6 alpha C–H bonds available for hyperconjugative overlap with the π system; in but-1-ene, only the single CH<sub>2</sub> group adjacent to the double bond (at C3) contributes its 2 hydrogens as alpha hydrogens. The greater number of hyperconjugative structures in 2-methylpropene provides more stabilisation, consistent with the general rule that more highly substituted alkenes are more stable.
questions.hint: Identify the sp<sup>3</sup> carbons directly attached to each double bond, then count how many C–H bonds each contributes.
distractor_logic: Alpha-hydrogen counting is a genuine, standard method for comparing alkene stability via hyperconjugation, and ring size is not even relevant since neither compound is cyclic.
But-1-ene, being only monosubstituted at the double bond, in fact has fewer alpha hydrogens than the disubstituted 2-methylpropene, not more.
The alpha-hydrogen counts are clearly different (6 vs 2), so the alkenes are not equally stabilised.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Compare the tertiary cation (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C<sup>+</sup>–CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> (2-methylbutan-2-yl cation) with the secondary cation (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CH<sup>+</sup> (isopropyl cation) by counting alpha hydrogens available for hyperconjugation, and state which cation is more stable.
options: Neither cation is stabilised by hyperconjugation, since only alkenes (not cations) show this effect
Both cations have exactly 6 alpha hydrogens and are equally stable

The tertiary cation has 8 alpha hydrogens (3 + 3 from two methyls, 2 from the ethyl's CH<sub>2</sub>) versus 6 for the isopropyl cation (3 + 3 from its two methyls), so the tertiary cation is more stable
The isopropyl cation has more alpha hydrogens and is therefore more stable
questions.explanation: The tertiary cation is attached to three groups — two methyls (3 alpha H each) and one ethyl (whose attached CH<sub>2</sub> contributes 2 alpha H) — giving 3 + 3 + 2 = 8 alpha hydrogens in total. The isopropyl cation is attached to two methyl groups (3 alpha H each, the third substituent being a plain H with no alpha C–H to contribute) for 3 + 3 = 6 alpha hydrogens. More alpha hydrogens means more hyperconjugative (no-bond resonance) structures and therefore greater stabilisation, so the tertiary cation is more stable.
questions.hint: List every group directly attached to the positively charged carbon in each cation, then count the C–H bonds on each of those groups.
distractor_logic: The isopropyl cation, having fewer substituents overall, cannot have more alpha hydrogens than the tertiary cation.
The two counts (8 vs 6) are clearly different, so the cations are not equally stabilised.
Hyperconjugation is a well-established stabilising effect for carbocations and free radicals as well as alkenes, not exclusive to alkenes.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Rank the following carbocations in decreasing order of stability: (i) benzyl cation, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>; (ii) allyl cation, CH<sub>2</sub>=CH–CH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>; (iii) tert-butyl cation, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C<sup>+</sup>; (iv) ethyl cation, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>.
options: Benzyl > allyl > tert-butyl > ethyl
tert-Butyl > benzyl > allyl > ethyl
Allyl > tert-butyl > benzyl > ethyl
Ethyl > allyl > benzyl > tert-butyl
questions.explanation: Benzyl and allyl cations are resonance-stabilised, spreading the positive charge over several atoms; benzyl is generally considered slightly more stabilised than allyl because the aromatic ring offers three (nearly) equivalent delocalised resonance contributors (into both ortho positions and the para position) versus only two for the simple allyl system. Both resonance-stabilised cations outrank the purely hyperconjugation/induction-stabilised tertiary alkyl cation (tert-butyl), which in turn is far more stable than the essentially unstabilised primary ethyl cation.
questions.hint: Separate the cations into two groups first — those with resonance delocalisation available (through a π system) and those relying only on alkyl-group induction/hyperconjugation — then rank within and across the groups.
distractor_logic: Placing tert-butyl above benzyl or allyl ignores that resonance delocalisation across a π system generally provides more stabilisation than purely alkyl-based hyperconjugation/induction.
Placing allyl above tert-butyl but below no resonance-stabilised species is inconsistent since it omits ranking benzyl correctly relative to allyl.
Placing ethyl above allyl or benzyl ignores that ethyl has essentially no special stabilisation at all.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Rank the following carbanions in decreasing order of stability: (i) O<sub>2</sub>N–CH<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup> (nitromethyl carbanion); (ii) C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup> (benzyl carbanion); (iii) CH<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> (methyl carbanion).
options: O<sub>2</sub>N–CH<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup> > C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup> > CH<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>
CH<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> > C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup> > O<sub>2</sub>N–CH<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup>
C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup> > O<sub>2</sub>N–CH<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup> > CH<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>
All three carbanions are equally stable since each carries a single negative charge on carbon
questions.explanation: The nitro group is both a powerful −I (inductive) withdrawer and, crucially, can accept the carbanion's lone pair directly into resonance with its own π system (delocalising negative charge onto its oxygens), making the nitromethyl carbanion by far the most stable. The phenyl ring of the benzyl carbanion also delocalises the charge by resonance into the ring, but less effectively than the strongly electron-accepting nitro group. The plain methyl carbanion, with no resonance or significant inductive stabilisation available, is the least stable (most basic/reactive) of the three.
questions.hint: Which substituent can pull the carbanion's negative charge into its own resonance system most effectively — a nitro group, a phenyl ring, or nothing at all?
distractor_logic: The three are clearly not equally stable, since only two of them have any resonance stabilisation available at all, and to different extents.
Ranking benzyl above nitromethyl underestimates how much more strongly the nitro group withdraws and delocalises electron density than a phenyl ring.
Reversing the order ignores that both the nitro group and the phenyl ring stabilise (not destabilise) an adjacent carbanion through resonance.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Rank the following free radicals in decreasing order of stability: (i) allyl radical, CH<sub>2</sub>=CH–CH<sub>2</sub>•; (ii) tert-butyl radical, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C•; (iii) methyl radical, CH<sub>3</sub>•.
options: Allyl > tert-butyl > methyl
tert-Butyl > allyl > methyl
Methyl > allyl > tert-butyl
Methyl > tert-butyl > allyl
questions.explanation: The allyl radical is stabilised by resonance delocalisation of the unpaired electron over two carbons through the adjacent π system, which provides greater stabilisation than the purely hyperconjugative/inductive stabilisation of the tertiary alkyl radical; the methyl radical, with no adjacent alkyl groups or π system at all, is the least stable of the three. This ordering is consistent with the lower C–H bond dissociation energy observed at allylic positions compared with tertiary alkyl positions.
questions.hint: Which radical has a π system right next to the radical centre that its unpaired electron can delocalise into by resonance?
distractor_logic: Placing tert-butyl above allyl underestimates how much resonance delocalisation stabilises a radical compared with hyperconjugation alone.
Both orders that place methyl first ignore that methyl has no stabilising groups attached at all and should be the least, not the most, stable of the set.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Compare a secondary allylic carbocation, CH<sub>3</sub>–CH=CH–<sup>+</sup>CH–CH<sub>3</sub> (pent-3-en-2-yl cation), with the tertiary, non-allylic tert-butyl cation, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C<sup>+</sup>. Which is generally considered more stable, and why?
options: The tert-butyl cation, because tertiary character always dominates over allylic resonance regardless of degree
Both are equally stable, since 'stability' depends only on the degree (1°/2°/3°) of the carbon bearing the charge, not on resonance

The secondary allylic cation, because resonance delocalisation of the positive charge over two carbons typically outweighs the purely hyperconjugative/inductive stabilisation available to a localised tertiary cation
The secondary allylic cation is less stable because it is only 'secondary', and degree of substitution is the sole factor governing carbocation stability
questions.explanation: Even though the pent-3-en-2-yl cation is formally a secondary carbocation, its positive charge is delocalised by resonance over two carbons (through the adjacent double bond), which generally provides more stabilisation than the purely localised (though tertiary) hyperconjugative/inductive stabilisation of tert-butyl cation; as a result, secondary allylic (and benzylic) carbocations are typically ranked above simple tertiary alkyl carbocations in stability.
questions.hint: Does resonance delocalisation across a π system tend to outweigh simply having more alkyl groups directly attached, when comparing carbocation stability?
distractor_logic: Formal degree of substitution (1°/2°/3°) is a useful first guide but is not the sole factor once resonance becomes available — the presence of an adjacent π system changes the comparison substantially, which the last two options wrongly ignore.
Claiming tertiary character 'always' dominates ignores the well-established teaching that allylic/benzylic resonance can outstrip simple tertiary hyperconjugation.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: A crude solid mixture contains: (a) a sublimable volatile impurity, (b) the desired compound, which is very soluble in hot ethanol but only sparingly soluble in cold ethanol, and (c) a non-volatile, water-soluble inorganic salt. What is the correct sequence of steps to obtain the pure desired compound?
options: Gently heat to sublime away the volatile impurity, wash the remaining solid with water to remove the inorganic salt, then recrystallise the residue from hot ethanol
Wash the crude mixture with water first, then sublime, and skip recrystallisation entirely
Recrystallise the whole crude mixture from hot ethanol first, then attempt to sublime away the inorganic salt afterward
Dissolve everything in hot ethanol immediately, including the volatile impurity and the salt, and cool to crystallise the product directly
questions.explanation: Removing the easily separable volatile impurity by sublimation first avoids complicating the subsequent steps; washing with water next removes the water-soluble inorganic salt (assuming the organic product is not appreciably water-soluble) while leaving the organic solid behind; finally, recrystallising from hot ethanol — exploiting the compound's known high solubility hot and low solubility cold — delivers the compound in pure, crystalline form.
questions.hint: Tackle the easiest, most selective separation first (the one exploiting a property none of the other components share), then work down to the step that finally purifies the target compound itself.
distractor_logic: Dissolving everything together and crystallising directly ignores that the volatile impurity and inorganic salt would remain mixed in with the crystallised product without prior removal.
Recrystallising before removing the sublimable and inorganic impurities risks contaminating the crystals or complicating the recrystallisation.
The inorganic salt is not volatile, so sublimation alone cannot remove it, meaning skipping the water wash defeats the purpose.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: A liquid organic compound decomposes on being heated to its normal atmospheric boiling point, but it is reasonably volatile in the presence of steam and is immiscible with water. Which technique should be used to purify it, and why does this technique avoid decomposition?
options: Ordinary simple distillation, since decomposition is not actually a real concern for any compound immiscible with water

Steam distillation, because the mixture boils (and the compound distils over) once the combined vapour pressures of water and the compound equal atmospheric pressure, which happens at a temperature below the compound's own (decomposition) boiling point
Simple distillation at reduced pressure only, since lowering pressure alone is sufficient regardless of the presence of steam
Fractional distillation, since the issue is really one of closely spaced boiling points rather than thermal stability
questions.explanation: In steam distillation, the two immiscible liquids (water and the organic compound) each contribute their own vapour pressure independently; the mixture boils once their combined vapour pressures equal the external (atmospheric) pressure, which occurs at a temperature below 100 °C and well below the compound's own normal boiling point. This lets the thermally unstable compound distil over, carried by the steam, without ever reaching the higher temperature at which it would decompose.
questions.hint: In steam distillation, does the compound need to reach its own full boiling point to be carried over, or does the presence of steam let it distil at a lower combined temperature?
distractor_logic: Reduced-pressure distillation on its own (without steam) is a genuinely different technique and is not what is described or required here.
The problem is thermal instability, not merely closely spaced boiling points, so fractional distillation does not address the actual issue.
The premise explicitly states the compound decomposes at its normal boiling point, so plain simple distillation would still cause decomposition.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Compounds X (bearing a polar –OH group) and Y (a simple hydrocarbon) are separated on an alumina column. Which compound is adsorbed more strongly and elutes later, and what change to the mobile phase would help elute it sooner?
options: X is adsorbed more strongly (due to stronger polar interactions with the alumina surface) and elutes later; increasing the polarity of the eluting solvent would help elute X sooner
Both compounds are adsorbed equally, since adsorption chromatography depends only on molecular size, not polarity
Y is adsorbed more strongly and elutes later; increasing the polarity of the eluting solvent would help elute Y sooner
X is adsorbed more strongly and elutes later; decreasing the polarity of the eluting solvent would help elute X sooner
questions.explanation: Polar compounds like X interact more strongly with the polar alumina surface (via dipole and hydrogen-bonding-type interactions) than a non-polar hydrocarbon like Y, so X is retained longer and elutes later; increasing the polarity of the mobile phase lets it compete more effectively with the stationary phase for the polar compound, weakening its adsorption and helping X move down the column and elute sooner.
questions.hint: Polar stationary phases like alumina interact more strongly with polar solutes — and a more polar mobile phase can 'out-compete' the stationary phase for those solutes.
distractor_logic: Adsorption chromatography depends substantially on polarity (and other functional-group interactions), not merely molecular size.
Decreasing (not increasing) mobile-phase polarity would make it even harder to displace a strongly retained polar compound, slowing its elution further rather than speeding it up.
Y, being non-polar, has weaker interactions with the polar alumina and should elute first, not last.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: A 0.25 g sample of an organic compound containing only C, H, and O gives 0.55 g of CO<sub>2</sub> and 0.30 g of H<sub>2</sub>O on complete combustion. Determine the empirical formula of the compound.
options: C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O
C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O
C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O<sub>2</sub>
C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O
questions.explanation: Mass of C = 0.55 × 12/44 = 0.15 g → %C = 60%. Mass of H = 0.30 × 2/18 = 0.0333 g → %H = 13.33%. %O (by difference) = 100 − 60 − 13.33 = 26.67%. Moles: C = 60/12 = 5, H = 13.33/1 = 13.33, O = 26.67/16 = 1.667. Dividing by the smallest (1.667): C = 3, H = 8, O = 1, giving the empirical formula C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O.
questions.hint: Work out %C and %H from the combustion products first, get %O by subtracting from 100, then convert each percentage to a mole ratio and divide through by the smallest value.
distractor_logic: C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O and C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O come from small errors in the mole-ratio division (rounding the H or C ratio incorrectly).
C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O<sub>2</sub> comes from mis-splitting the oxygen mole count or misapplying the H/O ratio during simplification.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: In a Kjeldahl nitrogen estimation, the ammonia liberated from 0.7 g of an organic compound is absorbed in 50 mL of 1 N H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>; the excess (unreacted) acid requires 40 mL of 1 N NaOH for neutralisation. Calculate the percentage of nitrogen in the compound. (%N = 1.4 × N × (V<sub>1</sub> − V<sub>2</sub>) / W)
questions.explanation: (V<sub>1</sub> − V<sub>2</sub>) = 50 − 40 = 10 mL of acid actually neutralised by the liberated NH<sub>3</sub>. %N = 1.4 × 1 × 10 / 0.7 = 14/0.7 = 20%.
questions.hint: First find how much acid was actually consumed by the ammonia (the difference between the acid taken and the alkali used to back-titrate the excess), then plug that volume directly into the Kjeldahl formula.
distractor_logic: 10% comes from using the wrong volume difference (e.g. dividing 10 mL incorrectly by 2 somewhere in the calculation).
28% comes from doubling the correct answer, e.g. by mis-handling the 1.4 factor.
14% comes from forgetting to divide by the sample mass (0.7 g) and simply reading off the numerator.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: In Carius method halogen estimation, 0.15 g of an organic chlorine compound gives 0.12 g of AgCl. Calculate the percentage of chlorine in the compound. (Atomic masses: Ag = 108, Cl = 35.5; molar mass of AgCl = 143.5)
questions.hint: First convert the mass of AgCl into the mass of chlorine it actually contains using the atomic-mass-to-molar-mass ratio 35.5/143.5, then express that as a percentage of the original sample mass.
distractor_logic: 23.7% and 15.8% arise from small arithmetic slips in applying the 35.5/143.5 mass ratio or in the final division.
35.5% mistakes the atomic mass of chlorine itself for the calculated percentage, skipping the actual calculation entirely.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: In Carius method sulfur estimation, 0.157 g of an organic sulfur compound gives 0.4813 g of BaSO<sub>4</sub> precipitate. Calculate the percentage of sulfur in the compound. (Atomic mass of S = 32; molar mass of BaSO<sub>4</sub> = 233)
questions.hint: Convert the mass of BaSO<sub>4</sub> into the mass of sulfur it contains using the 32/233 mass ratio, then divide by the sample mass and multiply by 100.
distractor_logic: 32.0% mistakes the atomic mass of sulfur itself for the answer.
21.0% comes from a slip such as halving the correct result or misapplying the mass ratio.
48.1% comes from misreading the BaSO<sub>4</sub> mass as the percentage directly.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: An organic compound has the empirical formula CH<sub>2</sub>O and a vapour density of 30. What is its molecular formula?
options: CH<sub>2</sub>O
C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>O<sub>2</sub>
C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O<sub>3</sub>
C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>4</sub>
questions.explanation: Molecular mass = 2 × vapour density = 2 × 30 = 60. Empirical formula mass of CH<sub>2</sub>O = 12 + 2 + 16 = 30. n = molecular mass / empirical formula mass = 60/30 = 2. Molecular formula = (CH<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>2</sub> = C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>O<sub>2</sub>.
questions.hint: First convert vapour density into molecular mass (molecular mass = 2 × VD), then divide by the empirical formula mass to find the whole-number multiplier n.
distractor_logic: CH<sub>2</sub>O itself is only the empirical formula (n = 1), which does not match the given molecular mass of 60.

C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O<sub>3</sub> and C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>4</sub> correspond to n = 3 and n = 4, which would require molecular masses of 90 and 120 respectively, not the 60 implied by the given vapour density.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Rank the following in decreasing order of stability: p-methoxybenzyl cation, benzyl cation, p-nitrobenzyl cation.
options: All three are equally stable, since all are benzylic cations
p-Methoxybenzyl > benzyl > p-nitrobenzyl
p-Nitrobenzyl > benzyl > p-methoxybenzyl
benzyl > p-methoxybenzyl > p-nitrobenzyl
questions.explanation: The para substituent conjugates directly with the delocalised positive charge. –OCH<sub>3</sub> is a resonance electron donor (+M), pushing extra electron density into the ring and further stabilising the cation beyond plain benzyl; –NO<sub>2</sub> is a resonance electron acceptor (−M), withdrawing density from an already electron-poor ring and strongly destabilising the cation. Hence p-methoxybenzyl > benzyl > p-nitrobenzyl.
questions.hint: At the para position, does –OCH<sub>3</sub> feed electron density into the ring, or pull it out? What about –NO<sub>2</sub>?
distractor_logic: Equal stability ignores that para-conjugated substituents have a large, well-documented effect on benzylic cation stability.
Ranking plain benzyl above the methoxy derivative ignores that +M donation stabilises the cation further.
Reversing the order confuses donor and acceptor behaviour.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Rank in decreasing order of stability: cumyl cation ((C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>)(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C<sup>+</sup>), benzyl cation (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>), allyl cation (CH<sub>2</sub>=CH–CH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>).
options: Cumyl > benzyl > allyl
Benzyl > cumyl > allyl
Allyl > benzyl > cumyl
Cumyl > allyl > benzyl
questions.explanation: Cumyl cation combines aromatic-ring resonance delocalisation with the +I effect and hyperconjugation of two attached methyl groups (it is both benzylic and tertiary), making it the most stable. Benzyl has only resonance stabilisation into a single ring with no extra alkyl support, and allyl has resonance stabilisation over a smaller, non-aromatic two-carbon system with the weakest delocalisation of the three, so it ranks last.
questions.hint: Which cation combines resonance delocalisation AND extra hyperconjugative/inductive support from alkyl groups, and which has only a smaller, non-aromatic resonance system?
distractor_logic: Placing allyl or benzyl above cumyl ignores that cumyl benefits from both resonance and additional alkyl stabilisation simultaneously.
Ranking benzyl above cumyl ignores the extra methyl-group support cumyl has that benzyl lacks.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Rank in decreasing order of stability: methoxymethyl cation (CH<sub>3</sub>O–CH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>), ethyl cation (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>), 2-chloroethyl cation (Cl–CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>).
options: All three are equally stable, since all are primary cations
Ethyl > methoxymethyl > 2-chloroethyl
Methoxymethyl > ethyl > 2-chloroethyl
2-Chloroethyl > ethyl > methoxymethyl
questions.explanation: In methoxymethyl cation, a full lone pair on oxygen delocalises directly into the empty p orbital of the adjacent cationic carbon by resonance (forming an oxocarbenium-type structure), which is a very strong stabilising interaction — stronger than simple alkyl +I. Plain ethyl cation has only weak +I stabilisation from its methyl group. 2-Chloroethyl cation is destabilised by the −I effect of the nearby chlorine, which withdraws electron density from the already electron-deficient cationic carbon, making it the least stable.
questions.hint: Which substituent can donate a full lone pair directly into the empty orbital by resonance, and which one withdraws electron density instead?
distractor_logic: Treating all as equal ignores that formal 'primary' classification says nothing about resonance or inductive substituent effects nearby.
The reverse order confuses electron-donating oxygen with electron-withdrawing chlorine.
Ranking ethyl highest ignores that oxygen lone-pair donation by resonance is a stronger stabiliser than a simple alkyl +I effect.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Which is more stable, and why: the oxocarbenium-type cation CH<sub>3</sub>O–C<sup>+</sup>(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>, or the simple tert-butyl cation, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C<sup>+</sup>?
options: The methoxy-substituted cation is less stable because oxygen is highly electronegative and withdraws electron density inductively
The tert-butyl cation, because three methyl groups always out-stabilise a single oxygen substituent
The methoxy-substituted cation, because full resonance donation of the oxygen lone pair into the empty p orbital is a stronger stabilising interaction than hyperconjugation from a methyl group alone
Both are equally stable, since both cationic carbons are attached to three groups
questions.explanation: When oxygen is directly attached to the cationic carbon, its lone pair can be donated fully into the empty p orbital by resonance, forming a new O=C double-bond character (an oxocarbenium ion); this direct resonance donation is a much stronger stabilising interaction than the weaker hyperconjugative overlap of C–H bonds available to a purely alkyl-substituted cation like tert-butyl.
questions.hint: When a heteroatom with a lone pair is directly bonded to the cationic carbon, can it stabilise the charge more directly than an alkyl group's C–H bonds can?
distractor_logic: Equal stability ignores the qualitative difference between a lone pair donor and simple alkyl hyperconjugation.
While oxygen is indeed electronegative and does withdraw by induction, this is far outweighed here by its resonance donation once directly bonded to the cationic centre.
'Three methyl groups always win' ignores that direct lone-pair resonance donation is generally a stronger effect than hyperconjugation.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Rank in decreasing order of stability: benzyl cation, p-nitrobenzyl cation, m-nitrobenzyl cation.
options: Benzyl > p-nitrobenzyl > m-nitrobenzyl
p-Nitrobenzyl > m-nitrobenzyl > benzyl
Benzyl > m-nitrobenzyl > p-nitrobenzyl
m-Nitrobenzyl > benzyl > p-nitrobenzyl
questions.explanation: A nitro group at the para position directly conjugates with the ring's resonance pathway that carries positive charge to the ortho/para carbons, so it strongly withdraws electron density right where it is most needed — strongly destabilising. A nitro group at the meta position is not part of that same resonance pathway, so it can only act through its (comparatively weaker) inductive −I effect, giving milder destabilisation. Unsubstituted benzyl, with no electron-withdrawing group at all, is the most stable of the three.
questions.hint: Draw the resonance structures of the benzylic cation — does the positive charge ever appear at the meta position, the way it does at ortho/para?
distractor_logic: Placing p-nitrobenzyl or m-nitrobenzyl above benzyl ignores that both nitro-substituted cations are destabilised relative to the unsubstituted case.
Ranking m-nitrobenzyl above benzyl ignores that even the weaker inductive effect of a meta-nitro group is still net destabilising, not stabilising.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Rank in decreasing order of stability: 1,1-dimethylallyl cation ((CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C<sup>+</sup>–CH=CH<sub>2</sub>), allyl cation (CH<sub>2</sub>=CH–CH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>), tert-butyl cation ((CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C<sup>+</sup>).
options: tert-Butyl > allyl > 1,1-dimethylallyl
1,1-Dimethylallyl > allyl > tert-butyl
Allyl > 1,1-dimethylallyl > tert-butyl
tert-Butyl > 1,1-dimethylallyl > allyl
questions.explanation: 1,1-Dimethylallyl cation combines both tertiary character (two methyl groups providing +I and hyperconjugation) and allylic resonance delocalisation, making it the most stable. Plain allyl cation, though only formally primary, benefits from resonance delocalisation, which generally outweighs the purely hyperconjugative/inductive stabilisation available to a simple tertiary alkyl cation such as tert-butyl, placing allyl above tert-butyl.
questions.hint: Which cation combines both a high degree of substitution AND resonance delocalisation, and between resonance alone versus tertiary hyperconjugation alone, which tends to provide more stabilisation?
distractor_logic: Ranking tert-butyl above allyl ignores the generally accepted teaching that allylic resonance stabilisation outweighs simple tertiary hyperconjugation.
Ranking allyl above the combined 1,1-dimethylallyl cation ignores that the latter has every stabilising feature allyl has, plus more.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Rank in decreasing order of stability: pentadienyl cation (CH<sub>2</sub>=CH–CH=CH–CH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>), allyl cation (CH<sub>2</sub>=CH–CH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>), n-propyl cation (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>).
options: n-Propyl > allyl > pentadienyl
All three are equally stable, since all are formally primary cations
Allyl > pentadienyl > n-propyl
Pentadienyl > allyl > n-propyl
questions.explanation: Pentadienyl cation has an extended, doubly-conjugated system that delocalises the positive charge over three carbons (C1, C3, and C5) through three resonance contributors, providing more stabilisation than the allyl cation's simpler two-carbon, two-contributor delocalisation. The n-propyl cation has no adjacent π system at all and no resonance stabilisation, making it by far the least stable of the three.
questions.hint: Count how many resonance contributors (positions bearing partial positive charge) each cation's conjugated system can support.
distractor_logic: Equal stability ignores that only two of the three cations have any resonance delocalisation at all, and to very different extents.
The reverse order incorrectly treats more extensive delocalisation as destabilising rather than stabilising.
Ranking allyl above pentadienyl ignores that the extra conjugation in the pentadienyl system spreads the charge even further.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Which is more stable, and why: p-methylbenzyl cation (a benzyl cation with an extra –CH<sub>3</sub> at the para position) or plain benzyl cation?
options: Both are equally stable, since the methyl group is too far from the cationic centre to have any effect
p-Methylbenzyl cation is less stable because steric bulk from the extra methyl group outweighs any electronic effect
Plain benzyl cation, because any substituent on the ring destabilises the benzylic cation regardless of its electronic character
p-Methylbenzyl cation, because the para-methyl group provides extra +I/hyperconjugative electron donation exactly where partial positive charge is delocalised by resonance
questions.explanation: The para position is one of the ring carbons that carries partial positive character in the resonance structures of a benzylic cation; a methyl group placed there donates additional electron density (by +I and hyperconjugation) exactly where it is needed, providing extra stabilisation beyond what plain, unsubstituted benzyl cation has.
questions.hint: Is the para position part of the resonance delocalisation pathway of the benzylic cation, and does a methyl group there donate or withdraw electron density?
distractor_logic: The para position is directly involved in the resonance delocalisation, so it is not 'too far' to matter.
Not every substituent destabilises a benzylic cation — electron-donating groups like methyl help stabilise it.
Steric effects are a minor secondary consideration here, not the dominant factor for a small, flat substituent like methyl at a remote ring position.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Rank in decreasing order of stability: 1-phenylethyl cation (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>–CH<sup>+</sup>–CH<sub>3</sub>), benzyl cation (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>), isopropyl cation ((CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CH<sup>+</sup>).
options: Isopropyl > benzyl > 1-phenylethyl
1-Phenylethyl > benzyl > isopropyl
Isopropyl > 1-phenylethyl > benzyl
Benzyl > 1-phenylethyl > isopropyl
questions.explanation: 1-Phenylethyl cation combines benzylic resonance stabilisation with the extra hyperconjugative/inductive support of an additional methyl group (it is secondary and benzylic at once), making it the most stable. Plain benzyl cation has resonance stabilisation only, without the extra alkyl support. Isopropyl cation has only hyperconjugation/induction from its two methyl groups and no resonance delocalisation at all, making it the least stable of the three.
questions.hint: Which cation has both a resonance-donating aromatic ring AND an extra alkyl group providing hyperconjugation, and which has neither of those advantages?
distractor_logic: Ranking isopropyl above the resonance-stabilised cations ignores that resonance delocalisation generally provides more stabilisation than simple secondary hyperconjugation.
Ranking benzyl above 1-phenylethyl ignores that the latter has every stabilising feature benzyl has, plus an additional methyl group's hyperconjugative support.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Rank in decreasing order of stability: p-nitrobenzyl carbanion, benzyl carbanion, p-methoxybenzyl carbanion.
options: p-Methoxybenzyl > benzyl > p-nitrobenzyl
Benzyl > p-nitrobenzyl > p-methoxybenzyl
All three are equally stable, since all are benzylic carbanions
p-Nitrobenzyl > benzyl > p-methoxybenzyl
questions.explanation: A carbanion's negative charge is stabilised by a substituent that can accept (withdraw) electron density. Para –NO<sub>2</sub> both inductively withdraws and, crucially, accepts the delocalised negative charge into its own resonance system, strongly stabilising the carbanion. Para –OCH<sub>3</sub> is an electron donor, which pushes even more electron density toward an already electron-rich carbanion centre, destabilising it relative to plain benzyl carbanion.
questions.hint: For a negatively charged species, does an electron-withdrawing or an electron-donating para-substituent help stabilise the extra charge?
distractor_logic: Equal stability ignores the large difference in electronic character between –NO<sub>2</sub> and –OCH<sub>3</sub>.
The reverse order confuses which type of substituent helps stabilise excess negative charge.
Ranking benzyl above p-nitrobenzyl ignores that resonance/inductive withdrawal by the nitro group is stabilising, not neutral.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Rank in decreasing order of stability: fluoromethyl carbanion (F–CH<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup>), 2-fluoroethyl carbanion (F–CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup>), ethyl carbanion (CH<sub>3</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup>).
options: Fluoromethyl > 2-fluoroethyl > ethyl
All three are equally stable, since only one has no fluorine at all
Ethyl > 2-fluoroethyl > fluoromethyl
2-Fluoroethyl > fluoromethyl > ethyl
questions.explanation: Fluorine's strong −I effect withdraws electron density and stabilises an adjacent carbanion most effectively when it is directly on the carbanion carbon (fluoromethyl carbanion); when fluorine is one carbon further away (2-fluoroethyl), its inductive influence is weaker due to the extra bond distance; plain ethyl carbanion, with no electron-withdrawing group at all, is the least stable.
questions.hint: The inductive effect weakens quickly with distance — compare how many bonds separate the fluorine from the carbanion centre in each case.
distractor_logic: The reverse order ignores that fluorine's −I effect is stabilising, not destabilising, for a carbanion.
Equal stability ignores that only two of the three carbanions even have a stabilising fluorine present.
Ranking the more distant fluorine above the directly attached one ignores the sharp distance-dependence of the inductive effect.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Rank in decreasing order of stability: the enolate carbanion CH<sub>3</sub>–CO–CH<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup> (from acetone), the cyanomethyl carbanion NC–CH<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup>, and the ethyl carbanion CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup>.
options: Cyanomethyl > enolate > ethyl
Ethyl > enolate > cyanomethyl
Ethyl > cyanomethyl > enolate
Enolate > cyanomethyl > ethyl
questions.explanation: Both the carbonyl group and the nitrile group can accept the carbanion's negative charge into resonance, but a carbonyl (C=O) is a stronger resonance acceptor of adjacent negative charge than a nitrile (C≡N) at this level of comparison, making the enolate the most stable of the three. Ethyl carbanion, with no adjacent resonance-accepting group, is the least stable, since alkyl groups only destabilise (by +I) an already negative centre.
questions.hint: Both the C=O and C≡N groups can pull the carbanion's lone pair into resonance — which is generally the stronger electron-accepting group of the two?
distractor_logic: Placing ethyl above either resonance-stabilised carbanion ignores that it has no stabilising group at all.
Ranking cyanomethyl above the enolate reverses the generally accepted relative strength of carbonyl versus nitrile as a resonance acceptor for an adjacent carbanion.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Rank in decreasing order of stability: benzyl carbanion, methyl carbanion, tert-butyl carbanion.
options: tert-Butyl > benzyl > methyl
tert-Butyl > methyl > benzyl
Methyl > benzyl > tert-butyl
Benzyl > methyl > tert-butyl
questions.explanation: Benzyl carbanion is resonance-stabilised by delocalisation of the negative charge into the aromatic ring, making it the most stable of the three. Among the plain alkyl carbanions, methyl (with no attached alkyl groups donating extra +I density) is more stable than tert-butyl, whose three methyl groups intensify the already-negative charge through cumulative +I donation and destabilise it.
questions.hint: First separate out the resonance-stabilised carbanion from the two simple alkyl carbanions, then apply the usual alkyl-substitution trend (more substitution destabilises a carbanion) to rank the remaining two.
distractor_logic: Placing tert-butyl above benzyl or methyl ignores both that it has no resonance stabilisation and that its three alkyl groups actively destabilise it.
Ranking methyl above benzyl ignores that resonance delocalisation into an aromatic ring outweighs a simple alkyl carbanion's lack of destabilising substituents.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Rank in decreasing order of stability: p-nitrobenzyl carbanion, m-nitrobenzyl carbanion, benzyl carbanion.
options: m-Nitrobenzyl > p-nitrobenzyl > benzyl
p-Nitrobenzyl > m-nitrobenzyl > benzyl
Benzyl > p-nitrobenzyl > m-nitrobenzyl
Benzyl > m-nitrobenzyl > p-nitrobenzyl
questions.explanation: A nitro group at the para position can directly accept the carbanion's delocalised negative charge into its own resonance system, giving the strongest stabilisation. At the meta position, the nitro group is not part of that same resonance pathway and can only act by its weaker inductive −I effect, giving milder stabilisation. Unsubstituted benzyl carbanion, lacking any electron-withdrawing group, is the least stable of the three.
questions.hint: Draw the resonance structures that delocalise the carbanion's negative charge into the ring — does the meta position ever carry that charge, the way ortho/para positions do?
distractor_logic: The reverse order ignores that both nitro-substituted carbanions are stabilised, not destabilised, relative to plain benzyl.
Ranking m-nitrobenzyl above p-nitrobenzyl ignores that direct resonance acceptance (available only at para) is a stronger stabilising interaction than the weaker, purely inductive meta effect.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Rank in decreasing order of stability: dinitromethyl carbanion ((O<sub>2</sub>N)<sub>2</sub>CH<sup>−</sup>), nitromethyl carbanion (O<sub>2</sub>N–CH<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup>), methyl carbanion (CH<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>).
options: Dinitromethyl > nitromethyl > methyl
Nitromethyl > dinitromethyl > methyl
All three are equally stable, since carbanion stability does not depend on the number of substituents
Methyl > nitromethyl > dinitromethyl
questions.explanation: Each nitro group independently withdraws electron density and accepts negative charge by resonance; these effects are additive, so two nitro groups stabilise the carbanion more than one, and the unsubstituted methyl carbanion (with no electron-withdrawing group at all) is the least stable of the three.
questions.hint: If one electron-withdrawing group stabilises a carbanion, would adding a second one on the same carbon have an additive effect?
distractor_logic: Ranking nitromethyl above dinitromethyl ignores the additive nature of multiple −I/resonance-accepting substituents.
The reverse order ignores that more electron-withdrawing groups provide more (not less) stabilisation.
Claiming no dependence on substituent number directly contradicts the well-established cumulative nature of inductive/resonance withdrawal.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Rank in decreasing order of stability: benzyl carbanion, allyl carbanion (CH<sub>2</sub>=CH–CH<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup>), ethyl carbanion (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup>).
options: All three are equally stable, since none carries an electron-withdrawing substituent
Ethyl > allyl > benzyl
Benzyl > allyl > ethyl
Allyl > benzyl > ethyl
questions.explanation: Benzyl carbanion delocalises its negative charge into a full aromatic ring (a larger, more extensively conjugated system), giving it more resonance stabilisation than allyl carbanion, whose delocalisation is limited to a simple two-carbon system. Ethyl carbanion, with no adjacent π system at all, has no resonance stabilisation and is the least stable of the three.
questions.hint: Compare the size and extent of the conjugated system each carbanion's negative charge can delocalise into.
distractor_logic: Ranking allyl above benzyl ignores that an aromatic ring offers a larger delocalisation pathway than a simple allylic system.
Claiming equal stability ignores that resonance stabilisation, not just electron-withdrawing substituents, is itself a real stabilising factor for a carbanion.
The reverse order treats more extensive delocalisation as destabilising rather than stabilising.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Rank in decreasing order of stability: diphenylmethyl radical ((C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CH•), benzyl radical (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>•), allyl radical (CH<sub>2</sub>=CH–CH<sub>2</sub>•), tert-butyl radical ((CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C•).
options: tert-Butyl > allyl > benzyl > diphenylmethyl
Diphenylmethyl > benzyl > allyl > tert-butyl
tert-Butyl > diphenylmethyl > benzyl > allyl
Allyl > benzyl > diphenylmethyl > tert-butyl
questions.explanation: Diphenylmethyl radical delocalises its unpaired electron over two aromatic rings, giving it the most extensive resonance stabilisation of the four. Benzyl radical delocalises into a single ring, giving somewhat less stabilisation. Allyl radical is resonance-stabilised over a smaller, non-aromatic two-carbon system, providing less stabilisation than either aromatic case but still more than a purely hyperconjugation-stabilised tertiary alkyl radical like tert-butyl, which ranks last.
questions.hint: Rank by the extent of the conjugated (resonance-donating) system available to each radical — two rings, one ring, a simple allylic system, or none at all.
distractor_logic: Placing tert-butyl above any of the resonance-stabilised radicals ignores that resonance delocalisation generally outweighs simple alkyl hyperconjugation.
Placing allyl above the aromatic radicals ignores that a full aromatic ring offers more delocalisation than a two-carbon allylic system.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Rank in decreasing order of stability: triphenylmethyl radical ((C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C•), benzyl radical (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>•), methyl radical (CH<sub>3</sub>•).
options: Triphenylmethyl > benzyl > methyl
All three are equally stable, since all carry a single unpaired electron
Methyl > benzyl > triphenylmethyl
Benzyl > triphenylmethyl > methyl
questions.explanation: Triphenylmethyl radical is one of the most heavily resonance-stabilised simple organic radicals known, with the unpaired electron delocalised across three aromatic rings, making it far more stable than benzyl radical (delocalised over just one ring) or methyl radical (no delocalisation at all, the least stable of the three).
questions.hint: How many aromatic rings can each radical delocalise its unpaired electron into?
distractor_logic: Equal stability ignores the vastly different extents of resonance delocalisation available to each radical.
The reverse order ignores that more rings available for delocalisation means greater stabilisation, not less.
Ranking benzyl above triphenylmethyl underestimates how much additional stabilisation two extra phenyl rings provide.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Rank in decreasing order of stability: 2-methylallyl radical (CH<sub>2</sub>=C(CH<sub>3</sub>)–CH<sub>2</sub>•), allyl radical (CH<sub>2</sub>=CH–CH<sub>2</sub>•), sec-butyl radical (CH<sub>3</sub>–CH•–CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>).
options: sec-Butyl > allyl > 2-methylallyl
2-Methylallyl > allyl > sec-butyl
sec-Butyl > 2-methylallyl > allyl
Allyl > 2-methylallyl > sec-butyl
questions.explanation: 2-Methylallyl radical combines allylic resonance delocalisation with the extra +I/hyperconjugative support of the additional methyl substituent, making it the most stable. Plain allyl radical has resonance delocalisation alone. sec-Butyl radical, though a genuine secondary radical, has only hyperconjugation/induction (no resonance at all) available, making it the least stable of the three.
questions.hint: Which radical combines resonance delocalisation with an extra alkyl group's support, and which relies on hyperconjugation alone with no resonance?
distractor_logic: Placing sec-butyl above either allylic radical ignores that resonance stabilisation generally outweighs simple secondary hyperconjugation.
Ranking allyl above the methyl-substituted allylic radical ignores that the extra methyl group only adds further stabilisation on top of the same resonance system.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Despite looking more heavily substituted overall, which is actually more stable: isopropyl radical ((CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CH•) or neopentyl radical ((CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C–CH<sub>2</sub>•)? Base your answer on a careful count of alpha hydrogens available for hyperconjugation.
options: Both are equally stable, since neopentyl radical 'looks' more substituted overall

Isopropyl radical, because it is genuinely secondary with two methyl groups (6 alpha C–H bonds) providing hyperconjugation, whereas neopentyl radical's single alpha carbon is a fully substituted quaternary carbon with zero alpha C–H bonds available
Neopentyl radical, because its bulky tert-butyl group always provides more hyperconjugation than any secondary radical
Isopropyl radical is less stable because it has fewer total carbon atoms than neopentyl radical
questions.explanation: Neopentyl radical's radical-bearing carbon is only primary, and its single alpha carbon is the quaternary C(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub> carbon, which has no hydrogens left to offer for hyperconjugation at all (all four of its bonds go to carbon). Isopropyl radical, though smaller overall, is a genuine secondary radical with two methyl alpha carbons contributing 3 + 3 = 6 alpha C–H bonds, giving it real hyperconjugative stabilisation that neopentyl radical almost entirely lacks.
questions.hint: Identify the alpha carbon(s) directly attached to each radical centre, and check carefully how many actual C–H bonds remain on each alpha carbon — don't just judge by overall molecular bulk.
distractor_logic: The two radicals are clearly not equally stable once alpha-hydrogens are actually counted.
'Bulkier always wins' is exactly the trap this question is designed to catch — hyperconjugation depends on alpha C–H bonds specifically, not overall size.
Total carbon count is irrelevant to hyperconjugative stabilisation, which depends only on the immediate alpha carbon(s).

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Rank in decreasing order of stability: tert-pentyl radical ((CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C•–CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>), sec-butyl radical (CH<sub>3</sub>–CH•–CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>), n-propyl radical (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>•).
options: All three are equally stable, since none has resonance stabilisation
sec-Butyl > tert-pentyl > n-propyl
tert-Pentyl > sec-butyl > n-propyl
n-Propyl > sec-butyl > tert-pentyl
questions.explanation: This follows the standard degree-of-substitution trend for hyperconjugative/inductive stabilisation of radicals: tertiary > secondary > primary. tert-Pentyl radical (tertiary, three alkyl groups) is the most stable, sec-butyl (secondary, two alkyl groups) is intermediate, and n-propyl (primary, one alkyl group) is the least stable of the three.
questions.hint: Count how many alkyl groups are directly attached to the radical-bearing carbon in each case.
distractor_logic: Equal stability ignores that hyperconjugative/inductive stabilisation, not just resonance, still clearly differentiates these three radicals.
