The reverse order ignores the well-established trend that more alkyl substitution stabilises a radical via +I and hyperconjugation.
Placing sec-butyl above tert-pentyl ignores that the latter has one more stabilising alkyl group.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Rank in decreasing order of stability: 1-phenylethyl radical (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>–CH•–CH<sub>3</sub>), benzyl radical (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>•), isopropyl radical ((CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CH•).
options: Isopropyl > 1-phenylethyl > benzyl
Isopropyl > benzyl > 1-phenylethyl
1-Phenylethyl > benzyl > isopropyl
Benzyl > 1-phenylethyl > isopropyl
questions.explanation: 1-Phenylethyl radical combines aromatic resonance delocalisation with the extra hyperconjugative support of an additional methyl group, making it the most stable. Benzyl radical has resonance stabilisation alone. Isopropyl radical has only hyperconjugation/induction with no resonance, making it the least stable of the three.
questions.hint: Which radical combines a resonance-donating ring with an extra alkyl substituent, and which has neither a ring nor extra substitution beyond simple secondary character?
distractor_logic: Placing isopropyl above either resonance-stabilised radical ignores that resonance generally outweighs simple secondary hyperconjugation.
Ranking benzyl above 1-phenylethyl ignores that the latter has every stabilising feature benzyl has, plus more.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Despite having one extra carbon, which is actually less stable: sec-butyl radical (CH<sub>3</sub>–CH•–CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>) or isobutyl radical ((CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CH–CH<sub>2</sub>•)? Justify using an alpha-hydrogen count.
options: sec-Butyl radical is less stable because it has fewer total carbons contributing to hyperconjugation
Isobutyl radical is more stable because its branched alpha carbon always provides more hyperconjugation than a straight-chain one
Both radicals have exactly the same number of alpha hydrogens, so they are equally stable

Isobutyl radical is less stable: it is only primary, and its single alpha carbon (the isopropyl-type CH) has just 1 remaining alpha C–H bond, versus sec-butyl's 5 total alpha C–H bonds from its two alpha carbons
questions.explanation: sec-Butyl radical is secondary, with two distinct alpha carbons: a methyl group (3 alpha H) and the CH<sub>2</sub> of the ethyl portion (2 alpha H), totalling 5 alpha hydrogens. Isobutyl radical is only primary; its single alpha carbon, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CH–, already uses two of its four bonds on methyl groups and one on the radical-bearing CH<sub>2</sub>, leaving only 1 hydrogen on that alpha carbon. Even though isobutyl's alpha carbon is more branched, being the only alpha carbon severely limits its total alpha-H contribution, so sec-butyl (5 alpha H) is more stable than isobutyl (1 alpha H).
questions.hint: A primary radical has only one alpha carbon, no matter how branched that carbon is; a secondary radical has two alpha carbons. Count each alpha carbon's remaining hydrogens carefully rather than judging by how 'branched' the molecule looks.
distractor_logic: The two counts (5 vs 1) are clearly unequal.
This question specifically tests the trap of judging stability by apparent branching rather than actual alpha-H count.
Being 'branched' at the alpha carbon does not help if that branching uses up the very C–H bonds that would otherwise contribute to hyperconjugation.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: For vinylamine, CH<sub>2</sub>=CH–NH<sub>2</sub>, which of the following is a valid resonance (canonical) structure obtained by shifting only electrons, with every atom held in its original position?
options: <sup>+</sup>CH<sub>2</sub>–CH=NH<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup>, with positive charge on carbon and negative on nitrogen
CH<sub>3</sub>–CH=NH
CH<sub>2</sub>=CH–NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> with an extra proton
<sup>−</sup>CH<sub>2</sub>–CH=NH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>
questions.explanation: The nitrogen lone pair can be pushed into a new N=C π bond, displacing the original C=C π electrons fully onto the terminal carbon as a lone pair (negative charge); this gives <sup>−</sup>CH<sub>2</sub>–CH=NH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>, with every atom in its original position and only the electron distribution (and formal charges) changed.
questions.hint: A genuine resonance structure never adds or moves atoms — only electrons (shown as shifted bonds and lone pairs, and the resulting formal charges) may change.
distractor_logic: Adding an extra proton changes the molecular formula entirely, which resonance never does.
'CH<sub>3</sub>–CH=NH' adds a hydrogen atom that was not present in the original molecule, making it a different (tautomeric) structure, not a resonance form.
Reversing the charges (+ on carbon, − on nitrogen) pushes the electrons in the wrong direction, since nitrogen's lone pair is the one being donated, not accepted.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: For acetamide, CH<sub>3</sub>–CO–NH<sub>2</sub>, which is a valid resonance structure showing why the C–N bond has partial double-bond character and rotation about it is restricted?
options: CH<sub>3</sub>–CO–NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> with chlorine added
CH<sub>2</sub>=C(OH)–NH<sub>2</sub>, formed by moving a hydrogen from nitrogen to oxygen
CH<sub>3</sub>–C(–O<sup>−</sup>)=NH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>
CH<sub>3</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>–O–NH<sub>2</sub>
questions.explanation: The nitrogen lone pair delocalises into the carbonyl system, forming a new C=N π bond while the original C=O π electrons move fully onto oxygen as a lone pair (negative charge); this valid canonical form, CH<sub>3</sub>–C(–O<sup>−</sup>)=NH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>, explains both the restricted rotation about the C–N bond and why the amide nitrogen is a much weaker base than a simple amine nitrogen.
questions.hint: Which lone pair in the molecule is positioned to conjugate directly with the adjacent C=O group?
distractor_logic: 'CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>ONH<sub>2</sub>' rearranges the connectivity of atoms entirely, which resonance can never do.
Adding chlorine changes the molecular formula, which is not permitted in resonance.
Moving a hydrogen from nitrogen to oxygen produces a genuinely different molecule (a tautomer), not a resonance contributor of the same molecule.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Nitromethane, CH<sub>3</sub>–NO<sub>2</sub>, has two experimentally equal N–O bond lengths, intermediate between typical single and double bond lengths. Which pair of resonance structures best explains this?
options: CH<sub>3</sub>–N(=O)–OH, a single fixed structure with one double and one single N–O bond
CH<sub>3</sub>–N(=O)–O<sup>−</sup> ↔ CH<sub>3</sub>–N(–O<sup>−</sup>)=O, two equivalent structures each placing the double bond on a different oxygen
CH<sub>3</sub>–NO<sub>2</sub> has no resonance at all; the equal bond lengths are a coincidence of measurement
CH<sub>2</sub>=N(OH)–O<sup>−</sup>, formed by moving a hydrogen from carbon to oxygen
questions.explanation: The nitro group has two equivalent canonical structures, each with the N=O double bond on a different oxygen; because both structures contribute equally to the true resonance hybrid, both N–O bonds acquire identical, intermediate bond order and length — directly analogous to the two equal C–O bonds in a carboxylate ion.
questions.hint: If one oxygen genuinely had a fixed single bond and the other a fixed double bond, would the two measured bond lengths come out identical?
distractor_logic: Moving a hydrogen atom changes the molecule entirely and is not a valid resonance operation.
A single fixed structure with distinct single and double N–O bonds would predict two different bond lengths, contradicting the observation.
Dismissing the equal lengths as a 'coincidence' ignores that resonance is the well-established explanation for exactly this kind of observation.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: For the phenoxide ion, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>O<sup>−</sup> (conjugate base of phenol), which position(s) can validly carry the delocalised negative charge in a resonance structure?
options: Every ring carbon equally, including meta, in every canonical structure
Only the oxygen atom itself; the ring carbons can never carry any of the negative charge
The ortho and para ring carbons (via structures where the ring double bonds shift toward oxygen and the negative charge appears at an ortho or a para carbon)
The meta ring carbon only
questions.explanation: Pushing the oxygen's extra lone pair into the ring and shifting the ring's π electrons appropriately generates canonical structures with the negative charge localised at the ortho and para ring carbons, exactly mirroring the pattern seen for phenol's lone-pair donation; the meta position is never reached by this delocalisation pathway.
questions.hint: This is the same delocalisation pathway used for neutral phenol's ring activation — which positions does that pathway reach?
distractor_logic: Claiming all ring positions (including meta) share the charge equally ignores that resonance structures are specific, not a uniform smear across every atom.
Meta alone is incorrect since that position is never reached by this resonance pathway.
Claiming the charge can never appear on the ring contradicts the entire basis for phenoxide's delocalisation and enhanced stability relative to a simple, non-conjugated alkoxide.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: The enolate ion formed by removing an alpha hydrogen from acetone, CH<sub>3</sub>–CO–CH<sub>3</sub>, gives CH<sub>3</sub>–CO–CH<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup>. Which is a valid resonance structure of this carbanion?
options: CH<sub>3</sub>–CO–CH<sub>3</sub> with no charge at all, since the negative charge simply disappears
CH<sub>3</sub>–CH(OH)–CH<sub>3</sub>, formed by adding a hydrogen to oxygen
CH<sub>2</sub>=C(CH<sub>3</sub>)–O<sup>−</sup>, formed by moving the methyl group to a different carbon
CH<sub>3</sub>–C(–O<sup>−</sup>)=CH<sub>2</sub>
questions.explanation: The carbanion's lone pair delocalises into the adjacent C=O system, forming a new C=C π bond while the original C=O π electrons move fully onto oxygen as a lone pair (negative charge); this gives the valid enolate resonance structure CH<sub>3</sub>–C(–O<sup>−</sup>)=CH<sub>2</sub>, with all atoms in their original positions.
questions.hint: Push the carbanion's lone pair toward the adjacent carbonyl carbon and see where the C=O π electrons end up.
distractor_logic: Moving the methyl group to a different carbon changes atomic connectivity, which resonance never does.
Charge cannot simply 'disappear' in a resonance structure of a charged species — total charge is always conserved across all canonical forms.
Adding a hydrogen to oxygen produces a genuinely different, protonated molecule, not a resonance form.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: For the formate ion, HCOO<sup>−</sup>, which pair of structures correctly represents its resonance?
options: H<sub>2</sub>C=O–O<sup>−</sup>, formed by moving the hydrogen from carbon to oxygen
HCOO<sup>−</sup> has only one possible structure, since there is only one hydrogen atom in the molecule
H–C(=O)–OH, a single structure with one fixed single and one fixed double C–O bond and no charge at all
H–C(–O<sup>−</sup>)=O ↔ H–C(=O)–O<sup>−</sup>, two equivalent canonical forms differing only in which oxygen carries the double bond
questions.explanation: Like acetate, formate has two equivalent canonical structures, each placing the C=O double bond on a different oxygen while the negative charge sits on the other; the true structure is a hybrid of these two equivalent forms, giving both C–O bonds equal, intermediate character — this is the standard explanation for why carboxylate C–O bond lengths are experimentally equal.
questions.hint: Formate is structurally just like acetate at the –COO<sup>−</sup> group — how many equivalent resonance structures does a carboxylate ion typically have?
distractor_logic: The number of hydrogen atoms in the molecule has no bearing on how many resonance structures the carboxylate group can have.
Moving the hydrogen atom from carbon to oxygen would give a completely different connectivity, not a valid resonance form.
A single fixed-bond structure (formic acid itself, which is neutral, not the anion) does not represent the resonance-delocalised anion.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Rank in decreasing order of acidity: p-nitrophenol, phenol, p-cresol (p-methylphenol).
options: p-Cresol > phenol > p-nitrophenol
All three are equally acidic, since all have the same –OH group
p-Nitrophenol > phenol > p-cresol
Phenol > p-nitrophenol > p-cresol
questions.explanation: The para-nitro group withdraws electron density from the ring by both induction and resonance, stabilising the resulting phenoxide ion and making p-nitrophenol markedly more acidic than plain phenol. The para-methyl group is a weak electron donor (+I/hyperconjugation), which slightly destabilises the phenoxide relative to plain phenol, making p-cresol the weakest acid of the three.
questions.hint: Does the para substituent in each case help stabilise the negative charge that develops on the phenoxide oxygen after deprotonation, or does it push additional electron density toward it?
distractor_logic: Claiming equal acidity ignores that the para substituent's electronic character measurably shifts phenoxide stability and hence acid strength.
Placing phenol above p-nitrophenol ignores the strong stabilising effect of the nitro group on the phenoxide.
The reverse order confuses electron-withdrawing (acid-strengthening) with electron-donating (acid-weakening) substituents.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Rank in decreasing order of basicity: p-methoxyaniline, aniline, p-nitroaniline.
options: Aniline > p-methoxyaniline > p-nitroaniline
p-Nitroaniline > aniline > p-methoxyaniline
p-Methoxyaniline > aniline > p-nitroaniline
All three are equally basic, since all have an –NH<sub>2</sub> group directly on the ring
questions.explanation: A para-methoxy group modestly increases the electron density available at nitrogen relative to plain aniline, making p-methoxyaniline slightly more basic. A para-nitro group, by contrast, strongly delocalises (withdraws) the nitrogen lone pair into the ring and onto itself by resonance, dramatically reducing its availability to accept a proton, making p-nitroaniline drastically less basic than plain aniline.
questions.hint: Which para substituent tends to feed more electron density toward the ring (and, indirectly, nitrogen), and which one aggressively pulls the nitrogen lone pair away by resonance?
distractor_logic: The reverse order confuses which substituent enhances versus which severely depletes the nitrogen lone pair's availability.
Equal basicity ignores the very large, well-documented basicity-lowering effect of a strong resonance acceptor like nitro on an aromatic amine.
Placing aniline above p-methoxyaniline ignores the modest additional stabilising donor effect of the methoxy group.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Rank in decreasing order of acidity: p-nitrobenzoic acid, benzoic acid, p-methoxybenzoic acid (p-anisic acid).
options: Benzoic acid > p-nitrobenzoic acid > p-methoxybenzoic acid
p-Nitrobenzoic acid > benzoic acid > p-methoxybenzoic acid
p-Methoxybenzoic acid > benzoic acid > p-nitrobenzoic acid
All three are equally acidic, since all share the same –COOH group
questions.explanation: A para-nitro group withdraws electron density from the ring and helps stabilise the carboxylate anion formed on deprotonation, increasing acidity relative to plain benzoic acid. A para-methoxy group is a net electron donor to the ring by resonance, which somewhat destabilises the carboxylate relative to benzoic acid, making p-methoxybenzoic acid the weakest acid of the three — consistent with the experimentally observed pK<sub>a</sub> order (p-nitrobenzoic < benzoic < p-methoxybenzoic).
questions.hint: As with the phenol series, ask whether the para substituent helps or hinders stabilisation of the anion formed after the acidic proton leaves.
distractor_logic: Equal acidity ignores the real, measurable pK<sub>a</sub> differences these substituents produce.
Placing benzoic acid above p-nitrobenzoic acid ignores the stabilising effect of the nitro group on the carboxylate.
The reverse order again confuses electron-withdrawing (acid-strengthening) with electron-donating (acid-weakening) substituents.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Rank in decreasing order of basicity: ethylamine (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>), 2-fluoroethylamine (FCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>), aniline (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>).
options: 2-Fluoroethylamine > ethylamine > aniline
All three are equally basic, since all carry an unsubstituted –NH<sub>2</sub> group
Aniline > 2-fluoroethylamine > ethylamine
Ethylamine > 2-fluoroethylamine > aniline
questions.explanation: Ethylamine, with no electronic complication, is the most basic. In 2-fluoroethylamine, fluorine's −I effect withdraws a modest amount of electron density from the nitrogen lone pair through the σ framework, mildly reducing basicity. In aniline, the nitrogen lone pair is extensively delocalised into the aromatic ring by resonance, which reduces its availability far more drastically than the simple inductive pull of a nearby fluorine, making aniline by far the least basic of the three.
questions.hint: Compare a purely inductive reduction in basicity (fluorine two carbons away) with a resonance-based reduction (the lone pair delocalised into an aromatic ring) — which effect cuts basicity more severely?
distractor_logic: The reverse order ignores that both the inductive and resonance effects here reduce (not increase) basicity relative to plain ethylamine.
Equal basicity ignores that these two distinct effects (induction and resonance) each measurably change how available the nitrogen lone pair is.
Ranking 2-fluoroethylamine below ethylamine ignores that the inductive effect, though real, is far weaker than aniline's resonance-based reduction.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Rank in decreasing order of acidity: fluoroacetic acid (FCH<sub>2</sub>COOH), benzoic acid (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>COOH), acetic acid (CH<sub>3</sub>COOH).
options: Acetic acid > benzoic acid > fluoroacetic acid
All three are equally acidic, since all contain a –COOH group directly
Benzoic acid > fluoroacetic acid > acetic acid
Fluoroacetic acid > benzoic acid > acetic acid
questions.explanation: Fluorine directly on the alpha carbon withdraws electron density strongly by induction, making fluoroacetic acid the strongest acid. In benzoic acid, the –COOH group is attached directly to an sp<sup>2</sup> aromatic ring carbon; although the ring can donate some electron density back into the carbonyl by resonance, the net inductive/hybridisation character of the aromatic ring carbon (higher effective electronegativity than a simple sp<sup>3</sup> alkyl carbon) still makes benzoic acid somewhat more acidic than acetic acid, whose plain alkyl (+I) methyl group is the weakest acid of the three.
questions.hint: Fluoroacetic acid's effect is purely a close-range inductive pull; benzoic acid's ring is directly conjugated with the –COOH group, bringing resonance into play alongside the ring's inductive character — how do the two together compare with a plain alkyl group like methyl?
distractor_logic: Ranking benzoic acid above fluoroacetic acid ignores that a directly-attached, highly electronegative fluorine exerts a stronger close-range inductive pull than an aromatic ring one bond further away.
The reverse order ignores that both fluoroacetic and benzoic acid are measurably more acidic than plain acetic acid.
Equal acidity ignores the real, well-documented pK<sub>a</sub> differences among these three acids.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Rank in decreasing order of acidity: p-nitrophenol, m-nitrophenol, phenol.
options: Phenol > m-nitrophenol > p-nitrophenol
All three are equally acidic regardless of the position of the nitro group
p-Nitrophenol > m-nitrophenol > phenol
m-Nitrophenol > p-nitrophenol > phenol
questions.explanation: A nitro group at the para position directly conjugates with the ring pathway that carries negative charge to ortho/para positions in the phenoxide ion, giving the strongest stabilisation and highest acidity. At the meta position, the nitro group can only act inductively (it is not part of that resonance pathway), giving weaker stabilisation and lower acidity than the para isomer, though still more acidic than unsubstituted phenol. Plain phenol, with no electron-withdrawing substituent, is the least acidic of the three.
questions.hint: Which ring positions does the resonance delocalisation of phenoxide's negative charge actually reach — and is the meta position one of them?
distractor_logic: Ranking m-nitrophenol above p-nitrophenol ignores that direct resonance stabilisation (available only at ortho/para) is stronger than the purely inductive stabilisation available at meta.
The reverse order ignores that both nitro-substituted phenols are more acidic than plain phenol.
Claiming no positional dependence directly contradicts the well-established ortho/para versus meta distinction in resonance-based substituent effects.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: How many hyperconjugative (no-bond resonance) structures can be drawn for the sec-butyl cation, CH<sub>3</sub>–CH<sup>+</sup>–CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>3</sub>?
questions.explanation: The cationic carbon has two different alpha carbons: the methyl group (3 alpha C–H bonds) and the CH<sub>2</sub> of the ethyl portion (2 alpha C–H bonds, since one of its bonds is used connecting to the terminal CH<sub>3</sub>). Total alpha hydrogens = 3 + 2 = 5, giving 5 hyperconjugative structures.
questions.hint: Identify both alpha carbons attached to the cationic centre separately, and count the remaining C–H bonds on each one individually.
distractor_logic: 6 mistakenly assumes both alpha carbons contribute 3 hydrogens each, ignoring that the ethyl-side alpha carbon has already used one bond to connect further down the chain.
3 counts only one of the two alpha carbons.
9 substantially overcounts beyond the actual number of alpha C–H bonds present.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: How many hyperconjugative structures can be drawn for propene, CH<sub>2</sub>=CH–CH<sub>3</sub>, considering the alpha C–H bonds of the methyl group adjacent to the double bond?
questions.explanation: The alpha carbon here is the CH<sub>3</sub> group directly attached to the sp<sup>2</sup> carbon of the double bond; it contributes 3 C–H bonds, each capable of hyperconjugative overlap with the adjacent π system, giving 3 hyperconjugative structures.
questions.hint: Which single carbon in propene is 'alpha' to the C=C double bond, and how many hydrogens does it carry?
distractor_logic: 0 wrongly assumes hyperconjugation cannot occur here, when in fact this exact interaction is why propene is more stable than ethylene.
6 overcounts beyond what a single CH<sub>3</sub> group can supply.
2 undercounts the methyl group's hydrogens.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: The cyclopentyl cation has its positive charge on one ring carbon, flanked on each side by a ring –CH<sub>2</sub>– group. How many alpha hydrogens are available for hyperconjugation?
questions.explanation: The cationic ring carbon has two adjacent ring carbons, each a CH<sub>2</sub> group contributing 2 alpha hydrogens; total alpha hydrogens = 2 + 2 = 4.
questions.hint: How many ring carbons are directly adjacent to the cationic carbon, and how many hydrogens does each of those carbons carry?
distractor_logic: 2 counts only one of the two adjacent ring carbons.
6 and 8 overcount beyond what two CH<sub>2</sub> groups can actually supply (each CH<sub>2</sub> has only 2, not 3, hydrogens).

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: How many hyperconjugative structures can be drawn for the tert-butyl free radical, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C•, using the same counting method used for carbocations?
questions.explanation: Exactly as for the tert-butyl cation, each of the three methyl groups attached to the radical-bearing carbon contributes 3 alpha C–H bonds, giving 3 × 3 = 9 hyperconjugative structures in total; the same alpha-hydrogen counting method applies to radicals as to carbocations.
questions.hint: The radical centre also has an available (singly-occupied) orbital that adjacent C–H bonds can overlap with, just as an empty orbital does for a cation — so use the same counting approach.
distractor_logic: 3 counts only a single methyl group.
6 undercounts by omitting one methyl group's contribution.
12 overcounts beyond the 9 total alpha C–H bonds actually available on the three methyls.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Compare the isopropyl cation, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CH<sup>+</sup>, with the sec-butyl cation, CH<sub>3</sub>–CH<sup>+</sup>–CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, by counting alpha hydrogens. Which has more, and by how many?
options: Isopropyl cation has more, by 1 (6 versus 5)
Both have exactly the same number of alpha hydrogens (6 each)
Isopropyl cation has more, by 3 (6 versus 3)
sec-Butyl cation has more, by 1 (6 versus 5)
questions.explanation: Isopropyl cation's two alpha carbons are both methyl groups, contributing 3 + 3 = 6 alpha hydrogens. sec-Butyl cation's two alpha carbons are a methyl group (3 alpha H) and the CH<sub>2</sub> of its ethyl portion (2 alpha H, since one bond is used connecting further down the chain), totalling 5. So isopropyl cation, despite being 'smaller', actually has one more alpha hydrogen available than sec-butyl cation.
questions.hint: Both cations are secondary, but carefully count the alpha hydrogens contributed by each individual alpha carbon rather than assuming a larger cation automatically has more.
distractor_logic: Reversing which cation has more ignores the actual count (6 for isopropyl versus 5 for sec-butyl).
A difference of 3 substantially overstates the actual gap between the two counts.
Claiming equal counts ignores that sec-butyl's ethyl-side alpha carbon contributes only 2 (not 3) hydrogens.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Compare 2-methylbut-2-ene, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C=CH–CH<sub>3</sub>, with pent-1-ene, CH<sub>2</sub>=CH–CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>3</sub>, by counting the total alpha hydrogens available for hyperconjugation with each double bond, and use this to explain which alkene is more stable.
options: 2-Methylbut-2-ene has 9 alpha hydrogens (6 from its two methyls on one sp<sup>2</sup> carbon, 3 from the methyl on the other) versus only 2 for pent-1-ene (from its single adjacent CH<sub>2</sub>), so the trisubstituted alkene is more stable
Both alkenes have exactly the same number of alpha hydrogens and are equally stable
Pent-1-ene has more alpha hydrogens than 2-methylbut-2-ene and is therefore more stable
Neither alkene is stabilised by hyperconjugation, since this effect applies only to carbocations and radicals, not alkenes
questions.explanation: In 2-methylbut-2-ene, one sp<sup>2</sup> carbon bears two methyl groups (3 + 3 = 6 alpha H) and the other sp<sup>2</sup> carbon bears one methyl group (3 alpha H), for 9 total. In pent-1-ene, only the CH<sub>2</sub> group adjacent to the terminal double bond contributes alpha hydrogens (2 total). The much larger number of hyperconjugative structures available to the trisubstituted alkene explains why more highly substituted alkenes are generally more stable, consistent with Zaitsev-type stability trends.
questions.hint: Identify every sp<sup>3</sup> carbon directly attached to each double bond, and count the C–H bonds on each one.
distractor_logic: Pent-1-ene, being only monosubstituted, clearly has fewer available alpha hydrogens than the trisubstituted alkene, not more.
The counts (9 vs 2) are clearly unequal, so the alkenes are not equally stabilised.
Hyperconjugation is a well-established stabilising factor for alkenes as well as for carbocations and radicals, so denying it applies to alkenes at all is factually incorrect.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Non-polar bromine, Br<sub>2</sub>, adds across the C=C double bond of ethylene even though it is not intrinsically an ionic or highly polar reagent. How does the electromeric effect explain this?
options: The electromeric effect only applies to reagents like HBr that already contain a permanent charge; it cannot explain Br<sub>2</sub> addition at all
Br<sub>2</sub> is already strongly ionic in the gas phase, so no polarisation or electron shift is needed for the reaction to occur
The alkene's π electrons play no role in this reaction; only the inductive effect of the alkyl substituents governs the addition

As Br<sub>2</sub> approaches the electron-rich π cloud, the alkene's electron density induces a temporary polarisation of the Br–Br bond, making the nearer bromine electrophilic; the alkene's π electrons then shift toward that bromine to form a new C–Br bond, while the Br–Br electron pair moves fully onto the far bromine
questions.explanation: Even a non-polar reagent like Br<sub>2</sub> can be induced to react with an alkene because the alkene's own electron-rich π cloud polarises the approaching Br–Br bond as it gets close, making one bromine atom electrophilic; the electromeric shift of the alkene's π electrons then forms the new C–Br bond as the Br–Br bond breaks heterolytically.
questions.hint: Even though Br<sub>2</sub> starts out non-polar, can the approaching electron cloud of the alkene itself induce a temporary polarisation in the Br–Br bond?
distractor_logic: The electromeric effect is a general description of temporary π-electron shifts in the presence of any approaching reagent capable of being polarised, not limited to reagents that are already charged.
Br<sub>2</sub> is not ionic in the gas phase or in typical non-polar solvents.
Ethylene has no alkyl substituents at all, so an inductive-effect-only explanation cannot account for its reactivity toward Br<sub>2</sub>.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: What is the essential difference between the +E (positive electromeric) and −E (negative electromeric) effects?
options: +E is a shift of π electrons toward the atom being attacked by the reagent (e.g. electrophilic addition to an alkene); −E is a shift of π electrons away from the site of attack (e.g. a nucleophile attacking a carbonyl carbon, pushing the C=O electrons onto oxygen)
+E and −E both describe the same direction of electron shift; the sign is purely a matter of notation with no chemical difference
+E describes a permanent effect, while −E describes a temporary one
+E occurs only in saturated molecules, while −E occurs only in molecules with a multiple bond
questions.explanation: In +E, the π electron pair shifts toward the carbon being attacked by an electrophile, helping form the new bond directly at that site (as in alkene addition). In −E, the π electron pair shifts away from the carbon under nucleophilic attack, moving instead onto an adjacent, more electronegative atom (as in nucleophilic addition to a carbonyl, where the electrons move onto oxygen rather than toward the incoming nucleophile's point of attack).
questions.hint: Ask which atom the π electrons end up on relative to where the new bond to the reagent actually forms.
distractor_logic: Both +E and −E require a multiple bond to exist in the first place, and neither can occur in a fully saturated molecule.
Both are temporary, reagent-triggered effects, unlike the permanent inductive effect.
The two effects genuinely differ in the direction electron density moves relative to the site of attack, so they are not simply notational.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: When cyanide ion, CN<sup>−</sup>, attacks the carbonyl carbon of ethanal (CH<sub>3</sub>CHO) to form a cyanohydrin, how does the electromeric effect describe the response of the C=O bond?
options: The C=O π electron pair shifts toward the incoming CN<sup>−</sup>, forming a temporary C=N bond directly at that step
No electron shift occurs at the C=O bond; only a new σ bond forms between carbon and the nucleophile, with the carbonyl untouched
The C=O π electron pair shifts entirely onto the oxygen as CN<sup>−</sup> forms a new bond to carbon, generating an alkoxide-like oxygen with a full negative charge — an example of the −E effect
The C=O π electrons split evenly between carbon and oxygen, leaving both atoms with a partial negative charge
questions.explanation: As the nucleophile CN<sup>−</sup> attacks the electrophilic carbonyl carbon, the C=O π electron pair is completely displaced onto the oxygen (which can accommodate the negative charge well, being electronegative), generating an alkoxide-type oxygen anion as the new C–CN bond forms — a clear example of the −E effect, since the electrons move away from, not toward, the site of nucleophilic attack.
questions.hint: The nucleophile is bringing its own electron pair to bond with carbon — where do the original C=O π electrons have to go as that new bond forms?
distractor_logic: The electrons move fully onto oxygen rather than splitting evenly, which is exactly why the resulting intermediate carries a full (not partial) negative charge on oxygen.
The carbonyl clearly is affected as the mechanism proceeds, so 'no electron shift occurs' is incorrect.
The electrons cannot shift 'toward' CN<sup>−</sup> to form a new C=N bond, since CN<sup>−</sup> is the electron-donating nucleophile, not an electron acceptor at that position.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: During electrophilic addition of HCl to but-2-ene, both the electromeric effect of the C=C double bond and the (much weaker) permanent inductive effects of the surrounding alkyl groups are technically present. Which effect dominates in governing the immediate response of the double bond to the approaching H<sup>+</sup>, and why?
options: Both effects are always exactly equal in magnitude, so neither can be said to dominate
Neither effect matters; only steric factors determine how the double bond responds to HCl
The inductive effect dominates, because it is a permanent effect and therefore always stronger than any temporary effect

The electromeric effect dominates, because it is a strong, essentially instantaneous, complete transfer of π electron density triggered directly by the approaching electrophile, whereas the inductive effect is comparatively weak and too gradual to control the immediate reactive response
questions.explanation: The electromeric effect is generally a much stronger, essentially complete shift of electron density that occurs specifically in response to an approaching reagent, whereas the inductive effect is a comparatively weak, always-present background polarisation; when a multiple bond is present and a reagent approaches, the electromeric effect dominates the immediate electronic response, even though the (weaker) inductive effects of nearby alkyl groups are still technically operating in the background.
questions.hint: Compare the typical relative strengths of the electromeric effect and the inductive effect when both could, in principle, influence the same reacting centre.
distractor_logic: Steric factors can influence reaction rate and regiochemistry but do not eliminate or replace the role of these electronic effects.
Permanence does not automatically mean greater strength — the inductive effect is in fact the weaker of the two in most direct comparisons.
The two effects are not of equal magnitude, since the electromeric effect is specifically a strong, complete electron shift while the inductive effect is a weak, partial one.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: A para-nitro group is attached to a benzylic cation and, separately, to a benzylic carbanion (each compared with its own unsubstituted benzyl counterpart). How does the effect of the nitro group differ between these two intermediate types?
options: The nitro group destabilises both the cation and the carbanion, since it is electron-withdrawing in every context

The nitro group destabilises the benzylic cation (by withdrawing electron density from an already electron-poor centre) but stabilises the benzylic carbanion (by accepting/withdrawing some of the excess negative charge through resonance)
The nitro group stabilises both the cation and the carbanion equally, since it is simply a strong substituent regardless of the charge type nearby
The nitro group has no effect on either intermediate, since both are already delocalised by the aromatic ring regardless of substituents
questions.explanation: The nitro group's electron-withdrawing character (by both induction and resonance) has opposite consequences depending on the sign of the charge it is near: it worsens an already electron-deficient cation (destabilising it further) but helps neutralise/accommodate the excess electron density of a carbanion (stabilising it). The same substituent can therefore have opposite effects on stability depending on the type of charged intermediate involved.
questions.hint: Does an electron-withdrawing group help or hurt a centre that already has too little electron density (a cation)? What about a centre that already has too much (a carbanion)?
distractor_logic: Claiming it destabilises both ignores that withdrawing electron density is exactly what a carbanion needs to become more stable.
Claiming the nitro group stabilises both ignores that it clearly worsens an already electron-poor cation.
Claiming no effect on either ignores the substantial, well-established influence electron-withdrawing/donating groups have on charged benzylic intermediates.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: A para-methoxy group is attached to a benzylic cation and, separately, to a benzylic carbanion (each compared with its own unsubstituted benzyl counterpart). How does the effect of the methoxy group differ between these two intermediate types?
options: The methoxy group destabilises both the cation and the carbanion, since oxygen is highly electronegative in every context
The methoxy group has no measurable effect on either intermediate, since resonance effects only matter for neutral molecules
The methoxy group stabilises both the cation and the carbanion equally, since it is simply a resonance donor regardless of the nearby charge

The methoxy group stabilises the benzylic cation (by donating electron density into the electron-poor centre by resonance) but destabilises the benzylic carbanion (by donating even more electron density onto an already electron-rich centre)
questions.explanation: An electron-donating group like methoxy helps an electron-deficient cation by supplying additional electron density (stabilising it), but it worsens an already electron-rich carbanion by pushing even more electron density toward a centre that already has an excess (destabilising it). This is the mirror image of how an electron-withdrawing group like nitro behaves toward the same two intermediate types.
questions.hint: Does an electron-donating group help or hurt a centre that already has too little electron density? What about a centre that already has too much?
distractor_logic: Claiming equal stabilisation for both ignores that donating more density to an already-negative carbanion is unfavourable.

Oxygen's high electronegativity governs its inductive character, but here the dominant effect at the para position is resonance donation into the ring, which is stabilising (not destabilising) for the electron-poor cation.
Resonance effects clearly do matter for charged species, not just neutral molecules, as this very comparison demonstrates.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Does a para-nitro or para-methoxy substituent affect the stability of a benzylic free radical as dramatically as it affects the corresponding benzylic cation or carbanion? Explain.
options: Yes, but only for electron-withdrawing substituents; electron-donating substituents have no effect on radicals whatsoever

No — because a free radical carries no net charge, it is far less sensitive to a substituent's electron-withdrawing or -donating (polar) character; its stability is dominated instead by resonance delocalisation of the unpaired electron into the ring, which is present regardless of whether the substituent is a donor or an acceptor
Yes — the effect is exactly as large as for the cation and the carbanion, since resonance delocalisation works identically for all three intermediate types
No — because free radicals are never stabilised by resonance at all, unlike cations and carbanions
questions.explanation: Because a radical has no net electric charge, its stability is much less sensitive to whether a nearby substituent withdraws or donates electron density (the polar/charge-stabilising effects that dominate for cations and carbanions); the benzylic radical's stability instead comes predominantly from resonance delocalisation of the unpaired electron into the ring, an effect present with either type of para substituent, so the dramatic swings seen for charged intermediates are not mirrored nearly as strongly for the neutral radical.
questions.hint: Cations and carbanions are charged, so they respond strongly to whether a substituent adds or removes electron density; does a neutral radical have that same sensitivity?
distractor_logic: There is no basis for claiming donating groups have zero effect while withdrawing groups do — both have a comparatively modest effect on a neutral radical relative to their large effect on charged species.
Radicals are, in fact, well known to be resonance-stabilised (e.g. benzyl and allyl radicals), so denying any resonance stabilisation is incorrect.
The effect for radicals is measurably smaller than for the charged intermediates, not identical.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Benzene's resonance energy, estimated from its heat of hydrogenation, is about 36 kcal/mol — far larger than the few kcal/mol of stabilisation a single hyperconjugating C–H bond typically contributes to a simple alkyl carbocation. What does this comparison best illustrate?
options: The two numbers are unrelated and cannot be meaningfully compared, since one concerns a neutral molecule and the other a charged species
Resonance energy and hyperconjugative stabilisation are simply two different names for exactly the same physical effect

Resonance delocalisation across a fully conjugated, cyclic pi system generally provides substantially more stabilisation than hyperconjugative donation from a single sigma bond, consistent with resonance being the stronger of the two stabilising effects
Hyperconjugation must actually be the stronger effect, since carbocations react faster than benzene undergoes addition
questions.explanation: Both resonance and hyperconjugation are electron-delocalisation effects that lower a species' energy, but they differ enormously in magnitude: benzene's extensive, fully conjugated six-membered pi system delocalises electron density far more effectively than the comparatively weak overlap of a single adjacent sigma C-H bond with an empty orbital. Comparing their typical magnitudes (tens of kcal/mol versus only a few) is a useful, concrete way to see that resonance is generally the stronger stabilising mechanism of the two.
questions.hint: Both quantities measure 'how much more stable delocalisation makes something' — what does comparing their sizes tell you about which delocalisation pathway (an extended conjugated ring, or a single sigma bond) is more effective?
distractor_logic: Resonance and hyperconjugation are related but distinct effects (delocalisation through a conjugated pi system versus through a single sigma bond into an adjacent empty/radical orbital), not the same effect under two names.

Both stabilisation energies describe the same general phenomenon (electron delocalisation lowering energy) and are legitimately comparable in magnitude even though one system is neutral and the other charged.
Reactivity depends on many factors beyond ground-state stabilisation, so it cannot be used to reverse this comparison.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: In 1,3-butadiene, CH<sub>2</sub>=CH–CH=CH<sub>2</sub>, the central C2–C3 bond (about 1.46 Å) is measurably shorter than a typical isolated C–C single bond (about 1.54 Å, as in ethane, which joins two sp<sup>3</sup> carbons). Besides conjugative delocalisation between the two adjacent π systems, what additional, complementary factor is understood to contribute to this shortening?
options: The two carbons are actually held together by a full second bond that was simply omitted from the structural formula
The bond is shorter purely because butadiene is a smaller, lighter molecule overall than ethane, with no electronic explanation required

The C2–C3 bond joins two sp<sup>2</sup>-hybridised carbons (higher s-character, so the bonding electrons are held closer to each nucleus) rather than two sp<sup>3</sup> carbons as in ethane; both this hybridisation-linked effect and conjugation act together to shorten the bond
Hybridisation has no bearing on bond length at all; only conjugation can ever shorten a carbon–carbon single bond
questions.explanation: Conjugation (resonance delocalisation between the two π systems) is the primary, well-known explanation for the shortening, but it works alongside a second, complementary effect: the C2–C3 bond joins two sp<sup>2</sup> carbons, each with greater s-character (and therefore a more tightly held, more electronegative-acting bonding pair) than the sp<sup>3</sup> carbons of ethane; bonds between higher-s-character carbons are intrinsically shorter, so both factors together account for the observed difference.
questions.hint: Conjugation is one part of the explanation — but are the two central carbons in butadiene the same hybridisation type as the two carbons in ethane?
distractor_logic: The central bond is correctly represented as a single bond in the structural formula, with its partial double-bond character arising from delocalisation rather than a literal second bond having been left out.

Hybridisation-linked bond shortening is a real, independent, well-documented effect (seen even in non-conjugated systems comparing sp<sup>2</sup>–sp<sup>2</sup> versus sp<sup>3</sup>–sp<sup>3</sup> single bonds), so it is not true that only conjugation can shorten a bond.
Overall molecular size does not determine an individual bond's length.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Of the two pairs (a) butan-1-ol & butan-2-ol, and (b) butan-1-ol & 2-methylpropan-1-ol, which pair is related by chain isomerism, and which by position isomerism?
options: (b) is chain isomerism (the carbon skeleton changes, straight vs branched, with –OH terminal in both); (a) is position isomerism (the skeleton is unchanged, only the –OH position moves)
Both pairs show position isomerism
Both pairs show chain isomerism
(a) is chain isomerism and (b) is position isomerism
questions.explanation: In pair (b), the underlying 4-carbon skeleton changes from straight-chain to branched while –OH stays on a terminal carbon in both — the hallmark of chain isomerism. In pair (a), the skeleton (straight-chain butane) is identical in both compounds; only the locant of –OH differs (C1 vs C2) — the hallmark of position isomerism.
questions.hint: For each pair, ask separately: has the carbon skeleton itself changed shape, or has only the functional group's position on an unchanged skeleton moved?
distractor_logic: Swapping the labels confuses which pair has a changed skeleton versus which has a changed locant.
Claiming both are the same type ignores that these two pairs demonstrate two clearly distinct isomerism mechanisms.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: 2,2-Dimethylpropane (neopentane) is one of the three chain-isomeric alkanes with molecular formula C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub>. What are the IUPAC names of its two other chain isomers?
options: Butane and 2-methylbutane
2-Methylbutane and 3-methylbutane
Pentane and 3-methylbutane
Pentane and 2-methylbutane
questions.explanation: The three chain isomers of C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub> are pentane (straight chain), 2-methylbutane (one branch), and 2,2-dimethylpropane (two branches on the same carbon); relative to 2,2-dimethylpropane, the other two are pentane and 2-methylbutane.
questions.hint: List every possible way 5 carbons can be arranged into a saturated, acyclic skeleton, then name each one.
distractor_logic: '3-Methylbutane' is not a valid IUPAC name (numbering a 4-carbon parent chain from either end places the only possible branch at C2, not C3, so the name would always be written as 2-methylbutane).
'butane' has only 4 carbons, one fewer than required for this molecular formula.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>–O–CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> and CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH share the molecular formula C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O. Give the correct IUPAC name of the first compound and identify the type of isomerism relating the two.
options: Diethyl ether only (has no valid IUPAC systematic name); chain isomerism
Ethoxyethane; functional group isomerism
1,1-Diethyl ether; metamerism
Ethoxyethane; position isomerism
questions.explanation: The IUPAC name for CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>–O–CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> is ethoxyethane (an ethyl group named as the 'ethoxy' substituent prefix on an ethane parent). Since this compound is an ether and the other is an alcohol — two entirely different functional classes sharing one molecular formula — they are related by functional group isomerism.
questions.hint: Ethers ARE named systematically under IUPAC rules (as alkoxy-substituted alkanes) — 'diethyl ether' is just the common name.
distractor_logic: Position isomerism would require the same functional class with the group merely relocated, which does not describe an ether versus an alcohol.
Claiming ethers have no valid systematic IUPAC name is incorrect.
Metamerism applies only when both compounds share the same functional class (e.g. two different ethers), not an ether compared with an alcohol.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: An organic solid is first purified by recrystallisation from ethanol; 0.20 g of the purified solid is then combusted by Liebig's method, giving 0.352 g of CO<sub>2</sub> and 0.144 g of H<sub>2</sub>O. Why is the purification step essential before this analysis, and what is the percentage of carbon in the compound?
options: Purification has no bearing on the accuracy of combustion analysis; %C = 48%
Purification is required only to improve the sample's melting point, not its analytical accuracy; %C = 48%
Without purification, the sample could not combust at all; %C = 40%
Without purification, any carbon- or hydrogen-containing impurity would also combust and be counted, giving an inaccurate result; %C = 48%
questions.explanation: Mass of C = 0.352 × 12/44 = 0.096 g; %C = (0.096/0.20) × 100 = 48%. Any impurity carried into the combustion would contribute its own carbon and hydrogen to the CO<sub>2</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>O produced, making the calculated %C not truly representative of the pure compound — this is exactly why the recrystallisation step matters.
questions.hint: Combustion analysis burns everything present in the sample tube — would an impurity's own carbon content be distinguishable from the compound's?
distractor_logic: Melting point is a separate purity check unrelated to why elemental analysis specifically needs a pure sample.
Claiming purification is irrelevant to accuracy ignores that any impurity's carbon/hydrogen content would be lumped into the result.
Claiming an unpurified sample 'could not combust' is incorrect (impure samples combust fine, they just give misleading results) and also pairs it with a wrong %C figure.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: A chlorine-containing organic compound is first washed with water to remove a water-soluble inorganic chloride impurity (the organic compound itself being water-insoluble); 0.20 g of the washed, pure compound then gives 0.287 g of AgCl by the Carius method. Why was the washing step necessary, and what is %Cl in the compound?
options: Washing was needed only to improve the sample's colour, not the accuracy of the chlorine estimation; %Cl = 35.5%
Without washing, the Carius method would give no precipitate at all; %Cl = 20%
Without washing, chlorine from the inorganic impurity would also precipitate as AgCl, falsely inflating the calculated %Cl for the organic compound; %Cl = 35.5%
Washing has no effect on the Carius estimation, since AgNO<sub>3</sub> only reacts with organically bound chlorine; %Cl = 35.5%
questions.explanation: Mass of Cl = 0.287 × 35.5/143.5 = 0.0710 g; %Cl = (0.0710/0.20) × 100 ≈ 35.5%. The Carius method converts all chlorine present — from both the organic compound and any inorganic chloride impurity — into AgCl, so an unremoved inorganic chloride would make the compound appear to contain more chlorine than it actually does.
questions.hint: Does AgNO<sub>3</sub> distinguish between chlorine that came from the organic compound and chlorine that came from an inorganic salt impurity, once both have been converted to chloride ion in solution?
distractor_logic: The Carius method would still give a (misleadingly high) precipitate even without washing, not none at all.
Colour is not the relevant concern here, accuracy of the elemental result is.
AgNO<sub>3</sub> precipitates chloride ion regardless of its original source, so the claim that it only reacts with organic chlorine is incorrect.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: A volatile liquid compound is first purified by fractional distillation to remove a closely boiling by-product, then 0.15 g of the pure compound is analysed by the Dumas method, giving 22.4 mL of N<sub>2</sub> at STP. Why was fractional (rather than simple) distillation required here, and what is %N?
options: Simple distillation was avoided only because it is slower, not because it is less effective at this separation; %N ≈ 18.7%
Simple distillation cannot resolve two liquids with closely spaced boiling points, and any residual by-product would skew the measured N<sub>2</sub> volume; %N ≈ 18.7%
Fractional distillation was unnecessary, since the Dumas method automatically corrects for any impurities present; %N ≈ 18.7%
Fractional distillation was needed to remove water, which the Dumas method cannot tolerate at all; %N ≈ 18.7%
questions.explanation: %N = (28 × 22.4)/(22400 × 0.15) × 100 = 627.2/3360 × 100 ≈ 18.7%. Since the by-product boils close to the compound of interest, only fractional distillation (with its repeated vaporisation–condensation cycles) can adequately separate them; any of the by-product carried over would contribute its own nitrogen content (or dilute the sample), skewing the %N result.
questions.hint: The by-product is described as 'closely boiling' — which distillation technique is specifically designed to resolve small boiling-point differences?
distractor_logic: The Dumas method has no built-in correction for sample impurity, so purification genuinely matters.
Speed is not the reason fractional distillation is preferred here, resolving power is.
The Dumas method's KOH absorption step does address CO<sub>2</sub>, not general water intolerance, so that reasoning is incorrect.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: In CH<sub>4</sub> + Cl<sub>2</sub> → (UV light) CH<sub>3</sub>Cl + HCl, which combination of descriptions is correct: the type of fission that initiates the mechanism, the nature of the chlorine species in the propagation steps, and the overall reaction type?
options: Heterolytic fission of Cl–Cl initiates the mechanism; Cl<sup>+</sup> acts as an electrophile; the overall reaction is a substitution
Homolytic fission of Cl–Cl initiates the mechanism; Cl atoms act as free radicals (not classical electrophiles or nucleophiles) during propagation; the overall reaction is a substitution
Homolytic fission of C–H initiates the mechanism; Cl atoms act as electrophiles; the overall reaction is an elimination
Heterolytic fission of Cl–Cl initiates the mechanism; Cl<sup>−</sup> acts as a nucleophile; the overall reaction is an addition
questions.explanation: UV light supplies enough energy to homolytically cleave the non-polar Cl–Cl bond into two identical chlorine radicals; these radicals abstract a hydrogen from methane and propagate the chain as free radicals rather than as classical ionic electrophiles or nucleophiles; overall, one hydrogen atom is replaced by one chlorine atom, which is a substitution reaction (specifically, free-radical substitution).
questions.hint: UV light is the classic initiator for radical chain mechanisms — what kind of bond cleavage does it typically cause in a symmetrical, non-polar bond like Cl–Cl?
distractor_logic: The C–H bond is not the one initiating the mechanism (it reacts with a chlorine radical, but is not itself the bond that first breaks under UV light).
Heterolytic fission of the non-polar, symmetric Cl–Cl bond is not chemically sensible, since there is no reason for both electrons to favour one identical chlorine over the other.
The overall transformation clearly replaces one H with one Cl (substitution), not addition or elimination.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: In CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br + KCN → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CN + KBr, which combination is correct: the role of CN<sup>−</sup>, the type of fission at the C–Br bond, and the overall reaction type?
options: CN<sup>−</sup> acts as a nucleophile; the C–Br bond undergoes heterolytic fission (Br leaving with both bonding electrons); the overall reaction is a substitution
CN<sup>−</sup> acts as a nucleophile; the C–Br bond undergoes homolytic fission; the overall reaction is a substitution
CN<sup>−</sup> acts as a free radical; the C–Br bond undergoes heterolytic fission; the overall reaction is an elimination
CN<sup>−</sup> acts as an electrophile; the C–Br bond undergoes homolytic fission; the overall reaction is an addition
questions.explanation: CN<sup>−</sup> is negatively charged with a lone pair available to donate, making it a nucleophile that attacks the electrophilic carbon; as the new C–CN bond forms, the C–Br bond breaks heterolytically, with both electrons leaving as Br<sup>−</sup>; since –Br is simply replaced by –CN, the overall reaction is a substitution.
questions.hint: Is CN<sup>−</sup> electron-seeking or electron-donating? And does the C–Br bond break evenly or unevenly as the new bond forms?
distractor_logic: One group (–Br) is clearly replaced by another (–CN), which is the definition of substitution, not addition or elimination.
A negatively charged species with a lone pair to donate is a nucleophile, not an electrophile, and has all its electrons paired, so it is not a radical either.
Ionic substitution mechanisms of this kind proceed through heterolytic, not homolytic, bond cleavage.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: In (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C–Cl + H<sub>2</sub>O → (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C–OH + HCl, proceeding through a carbocation intermediate, which combination is correct: the type of fission at C–Cl, the role water plays toward the carbocation, and the overall reaction type?
options: Heterolytic fission of C–Cl forms (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C<sup>−</sup> and Cl<sup>+</sup>; water acts as a nucleophile; the overall reaction is a substitution
Heterolytic fission of C–Cl forms (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>−</sup>; water acts as an electrophile; the overall reaction is an elimination
Homolytic fission of C–Cl forms two radicals; water acts as an electrophile; the overall reaction is an addition

Heterolytic fission of C–Cl forms (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>−</sup>; water acts as a nucleophile, attacking the electron-deficient carbocation with its oxygen lone pair; the overall reaction is a substitution
questions.explanation: Chlorine, being more electronegative, takes both bonding electrons as the C–Cl bond breaks heterolytically, forming the tertiary carbocation (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>−</sup>; water then attacks the electron-poor carbocation using a lone pair on oxygen, acting as a nucleophile; since –Cl is ultimately replaced by –OH, the overall transformation is a substitution.
questions.hint: Which atom keeps both electrons of the C–Cl bond as it breaks? And does water donate or accept electron density when it attacks the resulting cation?
distractor_logic: Homolytic fission would give neutral radicals, not the charged carbocation intermediate described.
Reversing the charges on carbon and chlorine ignores that chlorine, not carbon, is the more electronegative atom and keeps the electron pair.
Water's oxygen lone pair makes it electron-donating (nucleophilic), not electron-accepting (electrophilic), toward the electron-poor cation.
The net transformation replaces one group with another (substitution), not eliminates atoms to form a multiple bond.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Cyclohexanol consists of a saturated six-membered carbon ring bearing an –OH group. How should the ring system be classified, and which suffix does the principal characteristic group contribute to its IUPAC name?
options: Heterocyclic; the suffix '-one'
Alicyclic (a saturated, non-aromatic ring); the suffix '-ol'
Alicyclic; the suffix '-one'
Aromatic; the suffix '-ol'
questions.explanation: The ring contains only carbon atoms and has no delocalised aromatic π system, so it is classified as alicyclic. The principal characteristic group is –OH, contributing the suffix '-ol' (cyclohexane + -ol = cyclohexanol), exactly as the compound is named.
questions.hint: Does the ring contain a non-carbon atom, or a benzene-like delocalised π system? And which functional group is actually present, an alcohol or a ketone?
distractor_logic: '-one' is the ketone suffix, which does not apply here since the compound has an –OH group, not a C=O.
Heterocyclic is incorrect since every ring atom is carbon.
Aromatic is incorrect since there is no delocalised, benzene-like π system in a saturated ring.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Pyridine is a six-membered aromatic ring containing one nitrogen atom in place of a CH unit. How is it classified, and is 'pyridine' itself a systematically built IUPAC name (root + suffix, as with acyclic compounds) or a retained (accepted trivial-origin) name?
options: It is a heterocyclic aromatic compound; 'pyridine' is a fully systematic substitutive name built the same way as 'hexanol'
It is a heterocyclic aromatic compound; 'pyridine' is a retained name officially accepted by IUPAC, not built by the usual substitutive root-plus-suffix method
It is an aromatic hydrocarbon; 'pyridine' is a retained name
It is an alicyclic compound; 'pyridine' is a fully systematic substitutive name
questions.explanation: The ring contains a non-carbon atom (nitrogen) and has a delocalised, aromatic π system, making pyridine a heterocyclic aromatic compound. Unlike acyclic names built systematically from a root chain and a suffix, 'pyridine' is one of a set of ring names IUPAC has chosen to retain from traditional (trivial) nomenclature rather than construct from scratch.
questions.hint: Compare how 'pyridine' is formed with how a name like 'hexan-1-ol' is built from a root and a suffix — does 'pyridine' follow that same pattern?
distractor_logic: Alicyclic would ignore both the heteroatom and the aromatic character of the ring.
Claiming 'pyridine' is built the same way as an acyclic substitutive name ignores that ring names like this are specifically retained, not constructed.
Calling it an aromatic hydrocarbon ignores that a hydrocarbon by definition contains only carbon and hydrogen, whereas pyridine contains nitrogen.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: But-3-enoic acid, CH<sub>2</sub>=CH–CH<sub>2</sub>–COOH, is classified as what type of carbon skeleton, and does its suffix '-enoic acid' correctly cite both the double bond and the principal characteristic group within a single systematic name?
options: It is an alicyclic compound; yes, the suffix is correctly combined

It is an open-chain (acyclic), unsaturated compound; yes — '-en-' signals the C=C double bond and '-oic acid' signals the principal carboxylic acid group, both combined in one suffix string as IUPAC rules require
It is an open-chain, unsaturated compound; no, unsaturation and the principal group can never be cited together in a single suffix
It is an aromatic compound; the suffix is incomplete without an additional locant for the acid group
questions.explanation: The molecule has no ring, so it is open-chain (acyclic), and it contains a C=C double bond, making it unsaturated. IUPAC rules allow (and require) citing unsaturation and the principal characteristic group together within one combined suffix, exactly as seen in '-enoic acid', '-enal', or '-enone'.
questions.hint: Trace the carbon chain of the formula as written — is there a ring anywhere? And does the compound's name combine an '-en-' infix with the '-oic acid' suffix in one word?
distractor_logic: The compound is not aromatic (no benzene-type ring is present), and the suffix as given already fully specifies both the double bond's presence and the acid group without needing an extra locant beyond what combined citation provides.
IUPAC nomenclature specifically does allow combining an unsaturation infix with the principal-group suffix in one name, so claiming this is never possible is incorrect.
There is no ring in this structure, so 'alicyclic' is incorrect.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Ethylene glycol (HOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH, two –OH groups) has a much higher boiling point than ethanol (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH, one –OH group), even though the two molecules are of comparable size. Explain via hydrogen bonding, and state which technique would most directly exploit this boiling-point gap to separate a mixture of the two.
options: Ethylene glycol can form roughly twice as many intermolecular hydrogen bonds per molecule as ethanol, creating a far more extensive hydrogen-bonded network that requires much more energy to break; (fractional) distillation would exploit the resulting large boiling-point gap
The two compounds actually have very similar boiling points, so no purification technique based on boiling point would work
Ethylene glycol has a higher boiling point purely because it has a larger molecular mass, unrelated to hydrogen bonding; sublimation would be the appropriate technique
Ethanol forms more hydrogen bonds than ethylene glycol, which is why it has the lower boiling point; crystallisation would be the appropriate technique
questions.explanation: With two –OH groups instead of one, each ethylene glycol molecule can donate and accept more hydrogen bonds than ethanol, linking molecules into a more extensive network; breaking this network to vaporise the liquid requires substantially more energy, giving ethylene glycol a much higher boiling point. This large boiling-point difference is exactly the kind of gap that (fractional) distillation is well suited to exploit.
questions.hint: How many –OH groups does each molecule have available for hydrogen bonding, and how does that affect the extent of the hydrogen-bonded network in the liquid?
distractor_logic: The boiling points of these two compounds are, in fact, very different (ethylene glycol boils roughly 100 °C higher).

While molecular mass does play some role in boiling point generally, the dominant factor for these two similarly-sized molecules is the number of hydrogen-bonding sites, not mass alone, and sublimation applies to solids subliming directly to vapour, not to separating two liquids.
Ethanol, having only one –OH group, forms fewer (not more) hydrogen bonds per molecule than ethylene glycol.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Two isomeric alcohols are to be separated by simple distillation: one can form an intramolecular hydrogen bond (chelation), the other only intermolecular hydrogen bonds. Which one distils over first (at the lower temperature), and why?
options: The intramolecularly hydrogen-bonded (chelated) isomer, because its hydrogen bond is 'used up' within the single molecule and cannot extensively link separate molecules together, unlike the isomer relying on intermolecular hydrogen bonding
The intramolecularly hydrogen-bonded isomer distils over last, because chelation always increases boiling point
Both isomers distil over at exactly the same temperature, since both contain the same number of hydrogen-bonding groups
The intermolecularly hydrogen-bonded isomer, because intermolecular hydrogen bonds always lower boiling point relative to intramolecular ones
questions.explanation: This mirrors the classic ortho- versus para-nitrophenol comparison: the chelated isomer's hydrogen bond stays within the molecule, preventing it from linking extensively with neighbouring molecules the way the intermolecularly hydrogen-bonded isomer can; with a weaker overall intermolecular network, the chelated isomer requires less energy to vaporise and distils over at the lower temperature, i.e. first.
questions.hint: Which isomer's hydrogen bond is available to link separate molecules together, and which one has already 'spent' its hydrogen bond internally?
distractor_logic: The claim that chelation 'always increases' boiling point is backwards — chelation generally lowers boiling point relative to the intermolecularly bonded isomer.
Intermolecular hydrogen bonding is what raises boiling point by linking many molecules, so it does not lower it.
Equal boiling points would ignore the well-established, measurable difference chelation makes.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Simple ethers, despite having an oxygen atom capable of accepting a hydrogen bond, generally have boiling points much closer to comparable alkanes than to isomeric alcohols. Explain why, and state what this implies about separating an ether from its isomeric alcohol by distillation.
options: Ethers cannot accept or donate hydrogen bonds at all, which is why their boiling points are so much lower than alcohols; distillation would not work to separate them
Ethers and their isomeric alcohols always have nearly identical boiling points, making distillation an unsuitable separation technique
Ethers form even stronger hydrogen bonds than alcohols, which is why they should have higher, not lower, boiling points

An ether's oxygen has no attached hydrogen, so it cannot donate a hydrogen bond (only accept one), preventing the extensive mutual donor–acceptor network alcohols form; this typically leaves a large, easily exploitable boiling-point gap between an ether and its isomeric alcohol, so simple distillation readily separates them
questions.explanation: Because an ether oxygen has no O–H bond, it can only accept a hydrogen bond from another molecule that has one to offer, but cannot donate one itself; this rules out the kind of mutual, extensive hydrogen-bonded network that alcohols (with both a donor and acceptor O–H) can form with each other, keeping ether boiling points much closer to a comparable non-hydrogen-bonding alkane. Since this typically creates a substantial boiling-point gap between an ether and its isomeric alcohol, straightforward (simple) distillation is usually sufficient to separate the two.
questions.hint: An ether's oxygen can accept a hydrogen bond from a molecule that has an O–H or N–H group — but can the ether itself supply the hydrogen needed to donate one?
distractor_logic: Ethers can still accept hydrogen bonds from suitable donors (e.g. from water or an alcohol), so claiming zero hydrogen-bonding capability at all is too strong.
Ethers and their isomeric alcohols in fact typically show a substantial boiling-point gap, which is exactly why distillation works well here.
Ethers do not form stronger hydrogen bonds than alcohols — quite the opposite, since they lack a donor O–H bond.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: CH<sub>3</sub>–CH=CH<sub>2</sub> + HBr → CH<sub>3</sub>–CHBr–CH<sub>3</sub> proceeds through a carbocation intermediate. Identify the overall reaction type and the specific intermediate formed (including its degree of substitution).
options: Substitution reaction; a secondary carbocation
Elimination reaction; a tertiary carbocation
Addition reaction; a secondary carbocation, CH<sub>3</sub>–CH<sup>+</sup>–CH<sub>3</sub> (isopropyl cation)
Addition reaction; a primary carbocation, CH<sub>3</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>
questions.explanation: H<sup>+</sup> and Br<sup>−</sup> add across the C=C double bond with no atoms lost, making this an addition reaction. Following Markovnikov's rule, the proton adds to the terminal carbon, generating the more stable secondary carbocation, CH<sub>3</sub>–CH<sup>+</sup>–CH<sub>3</sub>, which Br<sup>−</sup> then attacks to give the final product.
questions.hint: Are atoms being added across a multiple bond here, or is something being removed/replaced? And which carbon ends up positively charged after Markovnikov-style protonation?
distractor_logic: No group is being replaced here, ruling out substitution.
The proton adds to the less-substituted terminal carbon (not the internal one), so the resulting cation is secondary, not primary.
No atoms are being eliminated to form a new multiple bond, ruling out elimination, and there is no tertiary carbon available in propene at all.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C–Br + OH<sup>−</sup> (alcoholic, heated) → (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C=CH<sub>2</sub> + Br<sup>−</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>O. Identify the overall reaction type, and state whether OH<sup>−</sup> is acting primarily as a nucleophile or as a base in this particular transformation.
options: Elimination reaction; OH<sup>−</sup> acts as an electrophile, accepting electron density from the C–H bond
Substitution reaction; OH<sup>−</sup> acts primarily as a nucleophile, attacking the carbon bearing bromine
Addition reaction; OH<sup>−</sup> acts as an electrophile
Elimination reaction; OH<sup>−</sup> acts primarily as a base here, removing a beta-hydrogen rather than attacking carbon
questions.explanation: A hydrogen and the bromine are removed from adjacent carbons to form a new C=C double bond, which is elimination (dehydrohalogenation). In this pathway, OH<sup>−</sup> removes a proton from a carbon adjacent to the one bearing bromine, acting as a Brønsted base rather than attacking the carbon bearing the leaving group as a nucleophile (the nucleophilic pathway would instead give the substitution product, tert-butanol).
questions.hint: The product is an alkene, formed by losing HBr overall — is OH<sup>−</sup> attacking carbon here, or removing a proton from a neighbouring carbon?
distractor_logic: There is no multiple bond present in the reactant for OH<sup>−</sup> to add across, ruling out addition.
OH<sup>−</sup> is electron-rich (it has lone pairs to donate), making it an electron donor (nucleophile/base), never an electrophile (electron acceptor).
The alkene product, formed by loss of atoms rather than replacement of one group by another, rules out simple substitution.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH + HBr → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br + H<sub>2</sub>O proceeds by protonation of the alcohol oxygen followed by loss of water. Identify the overall reaction type, and state the role water plays as it departs.
options: Elimination reaction; water acts as an electrophile as it departs
Substitution reaction; water acts as an electrophile, accepting a proton from HBr directly
Addition reaction; water acts as a nucleophile as it departs
Substitution reaction; water departs simply as a leaving group (a neutral, stable molecule taking the bonding electron pair with it), not itself acting as a nucleophile or electrophile in that step
questions.explanation: The –OH group (after protonation, as –OH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>, a much better leaving group) is ultimately replaced by –Br, making this a substitution reaction. As it leaves, water is simply the leaving group, departing with the bonding electron pair as a stable, neutral molecule; it is not itself functioning as a nucleophile (electron donor to a new centre) or an electrophile (electron acceptor) in that specific step.
questions.hint: A 'leaving group' is a distinct mechanistic role from 'nucleophile' or 'electrophile' — which role does the departing water molecule actually play here?
