distractor_logic: No multiple bond is present to add across, ruling out addition, and no new multiple bond is formed by loss of atoms in this net transformation, ruling out elimination.

Describing water as accepting a proton 'directly' from HBr misrepresents the accepted stepwise mechanism, in which the alcohol oxygen is protonated first, and this mischaracterises water's role as the (later) leaving group rather than as an electrophile.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: A compound gives a positive Lassaigne test for both nitrogen (Prussian blue) and sulfur (black precipitate with lead acetate). If 0.15 g of this compound is then analysed by the Dumas method and gives 25.2 mL of N<sub>2</sub> at STP, calculate %N.
questions.hint: Plug the given volume and mass directly into the Dumas formula and simplify step by step, exactly as in the single-element case — the qualitative test simply tells you nitrogen (and separately, sulfur) is present, but the quantitative calculation proceeds the same way regardless.
distractor_logic: 25.2% simply restates the given volume figure without applying the formula.
15% restates the sample mass.
28% comes from using the numerator (28) without correctly completing the division.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: A compound tests negative for nitrogen (no Prussian blue) but positive for a halogen (a white precipitate with AgNO<sub>3</sub>, insoluble in dilute HNO<sub>3</sub>). If 0.20 g of this compound gives 0.36 g of AgCl by the Carius method, calculate %Cl, and state whether this is consistent with the qualitative test result.
options: %Cl ≈ 44.5%; yes, this substantial non-zero value is consistent with a positive qualitative halogen test
%Cl ≈ 44.5%; no, a positive qualitative test should have given exactly 100% chlorine
%Cl ≈ 35.5%; yes, consistent with the qualitative test
%Cl ≈ 44.5%; this result is inconsistent with the negative nitrogen test and suggests an error
questions.explanation: Mass of Cl = 0.36 × 35.5/143.5 = 0.0891 g; %Cl = (0.0891/0.20) × 100 ≈ 44.5%. A substantial, clearly non-zero %Cl is exactly what a positive qualitative halogen test predicts; the negative nitrogen test and the halogen result are entirely independent tests for two different elements and are not expected to be related to each other.
questions.hint: First carry out the standard Carius %Cl calculation, then ask simply: does a non-trivial percentage of chlorine match what a positive qualitative silver nitrate test would lead you to expect?
distractor_logic: The negative nitrogen test and the chlorine content are unrelated pieces of information and do not indicate any error when both are considered together.
35.5% comes from a calculation error (mistaking the atomic mass of chlorine itself for the final percentage).
A qualitative positive test only indicates presence, not 100% composition, so expecting exactly 100% chlorine is a misunderstanding of what the qualitative test measures.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: A compound gives negative results for both nitrogen and sulfur in Lassaigne's test. 0.25 g of it yields 0.55 g of CO<sub>2</sub> and 0.225 g of H<sub>2</sub>O on combustion (Liebig's method), with carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen (by difference) as the only elements present. Calculate %C, %H, and %O.
questions.explanation: Mass of C = 0.55 × 12/44 = 0.15 g → %C = (0.15/0.25) × 100 = 60%. Mass of H = 0.225 × 2/18 = 0.025 g → %H = (0.025/0.25) × 100 = 10%. %O (by difference, since the negative qualitative tests confirm no N or S) = 100 − 60 − 10 = 30%.
questions.hint: Find %C and %H from the combustion products exactly as usual, then use the qualitative test results to justify assigning the remainder entirely to oxygen.
distractor_logic: The 44%/10%/46% option applies the mass ratios backwards, understating %C and overstating %O.
The 55%/22.5%/22.5% option simply restates the raw CO<sub>2</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>O masses as percentages without applying the correct 12/44 and 2/18 mass-ratio conversions.
The 60%/25%/15% option keeps the correct %C but uses an incorrectly inflated %H.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Cyclopropane and propene share the molecular formula C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub> but belong to different structural classes (one alicyclic/ring, one open-chain/unsaturated). What type of isomerism relates them?
options: Position isomerism
They are not isomers at all, since they belong to different classes of compound
Ring-chain isomerism (a specific case of functional/structural isomerism, where a ring and an open unsaturated chain share the same molecular formula)
Metamerism
questions.explanation: Cyclopropane (a saturated 3-membered ring) and propene (an open-chain compound with one C=C double bond) both satisfy the same molecular formula, C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>, via two different structural strategies for accounting for the same degree of unsaturation (a ring counts the same as one double bond); this specific ring-versus-open-chain relationship is called ring-chain isomerism.
questions.hint: Both a ring and a double bond independently account for one 'degree of unsaturation' relative to a fully saturated open chain — does that let two very differently shaped molecules share one molecular formula?
distractor_logic: Position isomerism requires an identical skeleton with a group merely relocated, which does not describe a ring versus an open chain.
Sharing an identical molecular formula while differing in structure is precisely the definition of isomers, so denying they are isomers at all is incorrect.
Metamerism requires the same functional class with different alkyl groups, which also does not apply here.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Cyclobutane and but-1-ene both have molecular formula C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>. Name the type of isomerism relating them, and state how many degrees of unsaturation each compound has.
options: Position isomerism; cyclobutane has 0 degrees of unsaturation and but-1-ene has 1
Ring-chain isomerism; cyclobutane has 2 degrees of unsaturation and but-1-ene has 1
Functional group isomerism; both have 0 degrees of unsaturation
Ring-chain isomerism; each has exactly 1 degree of unsaturation (the ring in cyclobutane, the C=C double bond in but-1-ene)
questions.explanation: A ring and a C=C double bond each independently account for exactly one degree of unsaturation relative to the fully saturated acyclic formula (C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+2</sub>); since both cyclobutane (a ring) and but-1-ene (a double bond) have formula C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub> (two hydrogens short of C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>), each has exactly 1 degree of unsaturation, and their ring-versus-chain relationship is ring-chain isomerism.
questions.hint: Compare each formula (C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>) with the fully saturated acyclic formula for 4 carbons (C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>) — how many 'pairs of hydrogens' short is each one?
distractor_logic: A single ring contributes exactly 1 degree of unsaturation, not 2.
Cyclobutane is not fully saturated relative to butane, so assigning it 0 degrees of unsaturation is incorrect.
Both compounds clearly have some unsaturation (the ring, the double bond), so claiming both have 0 degrees is inconsistent with their molecular formula.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Toluene (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>–CH<sub>3</sub>) and cycloheptatriene (a seven-membered ring with three double bonds) share the molecular formula C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>8</sub> but belong to very different structural classes (one aromatic, one non-aromatic polyene ring). Are they isomers, and if so, what general category of isomerism applies?
options: No — compounds with different degrees of aromaticity can never be considered isomers of each other
Yes — they are structural isomers, since they share a molecular formula but differ fundamentally in structure and class
No — their molecular formulas are actually different once the ring sizes are properly accounted for
Yes, but only stereoisomers, since both are cyclic
questions.explanation: Sharing an identical molecular formula (C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>8</sub>) while having fundamentally different structures (an aromatic ring with a methyl substituent versus a non-aromatic seven-membered triene ring) is exactly what defines structural (constitutional) isomers, regardless of how different their bonding patterns or classes are.
questions.hint: The definition of isomers depends only on sharing a molecular formula while differing in structure — does that definition care whether the two structures happen to be aromatic or not?
distractor_logic: These are constitutional (structural) isomers, not stereoisomers, since their atom-to-atom connectivity is different, not just their spatial arrangement.
Nothing in the definition of isomerism excludes comparing an aromatic and a non-aromatic compound.
Both molecules genuinely share the formula C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>8</sub>, so claiming the formulas actually differ is factually incorrect.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: A compound rapidly decolorises bromine water (indicating unsaturation) and also gives a positive Lassaigne test for nitrogen. What reaction type would this compound undergo with Br<sub>2</sub>, and what does the positive nitrogen test tell you about its composition?
options: An addition reaction (Br<sub>2</sub> adds across the C=C double bond responsible for decolorisation); the positive nitrogen test indicates a covalently bound nitrogen atom is present elsewhere in the molecule, unrelated to the unsaturation
An addition reaction; the nitrogen test indicates the double bond itself must contain a nitrogen atom
A substitution reaction; the nitrogen test indicates the compound is entirely composed of nitrogen with no carbon skeleton
An elimination reaction; the nitrogen test result has no chemical meaning here and can be disregarded
questions.explanation: Rapid decolorisation of bromine water is the classic test for a C=C (or C≡C) double/triple bond reacting by addition; a separate, positive Lassaigne nitrogen test (Prussian blue) confirms that the molecule also contains covalently bound nitrogen somewhere in its structure (converted to NaCN during sodium fusion), a completely independent structural feature from the site of unsaturation.
questions.hint: Bromine water addition tests specifically for a carbon–carbon multiple bond; Lassaigne's test specifically detects certain heteroatoms — do these two tests need to be probing the same part of the molecule?
distractor_logic: Decolorisation of bromine water is a hallmark of addition, not substitution.
A positive nitrogen test never implies the compound is 'entirely nitrogen' with no carbon skeleton, since Lassaigne's test is performed on organic (carbon-containing) compounds specifically.
A genuine qualitative test result always carries chemical meaning and should not be disregarded.
The double bond itself, in this generic scenario, need not contain the nitrogen atom at all — nitrogen could be located anywhere else in the molecule.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: A mixture of coloured plant pigments decomposes when heated, ruling out heating-based purification methods such as distillation or sublimation. Which technique is most appropriate to separate the mixture, and why?
options: Simple distillation, since it can always be performed at a low enough temperature to avoid decomposition
Steam distillation, since it is the only technique capable of separating coloured compounds
Sublimation, since coloured compounds always sublime cleanly regardless of thermal stability
Column (adsorption) chromatography, since it requires no heating and separates based on differential adsorption rather than volatility or boiling point
questions.explanation: Chromatography separates components by exploiting differences in how strongly each is adsorbed onto a stationary phase as a mobile phase carries them along, a process that requires no heating at all — making it ideally suited to thermally unstable, heat-sensitive mixtures such as plant pigments (historically, in fact, exactly how adsorption chromatography was first developed and named).
questions.hint: Which of these techniques does not require heating the sample at all?
distractor_logic: Sublimation requires heating and also depends on the compound's ability to vaporise directly, which is unrelated to colour.
Simple distillation still requires heating to at least some elevated temperature, which the premise explicitly rules out for this thermally unstable mixture.
Steam distillation still involves heating (to generate steam) and is not uniquely tied to separating coloured compounds specifically.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: A chemist wants to both confirm the presence of a halogen in a compound and obtain a precise measure of how much halogen it contains. Name the two distinct techniques used for each purpose, and state the key difference in what each tells you.
options: Lassaigne's test (qualitative, sodium fusion followed by AgNO<sub>3</sub>) tells you only whether halogen is present or absent; the Carius method (quantitative) tells you the precise percentage by mass of halogen present
The Carius method is used to detect presence/absence, while Lassaigne's test is used to measure the exact percentage
Both purposes are served equally well by Lassaigne's test alone; the Carius method is unnecessary
Both techniques give only a yes/no answer; neither can provide a precise percentage of halogen
questions.explanation: Lassaigne's test converts covalently bound halogen into a simple halide ion that gives a characteristic precipitate with AgNO<sub>3</sub>, answering only a yes/no question about presence. The Carius method, by contrast, precisely weighs the AgX precipitate formed from a known mass of sample, allowing calculation of the exact percentage composition — a quantitative result Lassaigne's test cannot provide.
questions.hint: One of these two tests gives a simple precipitate-or-no-precipitate result; the other involves carefully weighing a precipitate to calculate a percentage — which is which?
distractor_logic: The option claiming Carius detects presence/absence while Lassaigne's measures the percentage has the two methods' roles reversed (Carius is the quantitative one, Lassaigne's the qualitative one, not the other way around).
The Carius method very much does provide a precise percentage by mass, contrary to the claim that neither technique can.
Lassaigne's test alone cannot provide a percentage, so it cannot serve both purposes.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Phenol reacts with bromine water rapidly, without needing a catalyst, unlike benzene, which requires a Lewis acid catalyst for the same kind of reaction. Classify the overall reaction type, and explain why phenol reacts so much faster.
options: Addition reaction; the –OH group adds directly across the incoming bromine molecule
Nucleophilic substitution; phenol's –OH group acts as a leaving group, accelerating the reaction

Electrophilic substitution; the oxygen lone pair's resonance donation into the ring raises electron density (especially at ortho/para positions), making the ring far more reactive toward the electrophile without needing a catalyst to generate one
Electrophilic substitution; phenol reacts faster only because of steric effects, with no electronic contribution from the –OH group
questions.explanation: Bromination of an aromatic ring (replacing a ring hydrogen with bromine) is an electrophilic substitution. Phenol's oxygen lone pair delocalises into the ring by resonance, substantially raising the electron density at the ortho and para positions; this makes the ring nucleophilic enough to react directly with the (relatively weak) electrophile Br<sub>2</sub> without the Lewis acid catalyst benzene requires to generate a stronger electrophilic species.
questions.hint: Reaction with bromine that replaces a ring hydrogen, on an aromatic ring, is what type of reaction in general? And what electronic feature does phenol have that plain benzene lacks?
distractor_logic: No addition across a multiple bond by –OH is occurring, since the ring itself remains aromatic and only a ring hydrogen is replaced.
The –OH group is not acting as a leaving group here (it remains on the ring after the reaction).
The rate enhancement is a well-documented electronic (resonance donation) effect, not merely a steric one.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Nitrobenzene undergoes electrophilic substitution reactions much more slowly than benzene itself. Classify the reaction type under discussion, and explain the electronic basis for nitrobenzene's reduced reactivity.
options: Electrophilic substitution; –NO<sub>2</sub> has no electronic effect on the ring, and the slower rate is due only to the larger size of the substituent

Electrophilic substitution; the –NO<sub>2</sub> group withdraws electron density from the ring by both induction and resonance, lowering the ring's overall electron density and making it a poorer target for electrophilic attack
Nucleophilic substitution; –NO<sub>2</sub> makes the ring a better leaving group
Electrophilic addition; –NO<sub>2</sub> prevents the ring's double bonds from reacting at all
questions.explanation: This is still electrophilic aromatic substitution, but –NO<sub>2</sub> is a strong electron-withdrawing group by both induction and resonance, pulling electron density away from the ring (especially at ortho/para positions) and leaving the ring far less nucleophilic toward an approaching electrophile than plain benzene, hence the much slower reaction rate — the opposite behaviour to an activating group like –OH.
questions.hint: Is –NO<sub>2</sub> an electron donor or an electron acceptor relative to the ring, and how would that affect the ring's attractiveness to an electrophile?
distractor_logic: The rate reduction here has a well-established electronic origin (induction and resonance withdrawal), not merely a steric size effect.
The ring itself is not a 'leaving group' in this substitution, and this is not a nucleophilic substitution mechanism at all.
Benzene rings do still react with electrophiles even when substituted with –NO<sub>2</sub>, just more slowly, so claiming the double bonds 'cannot react at all' is too strong.

questions.chapter_name: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: During addition of HBr to an alkene, the initial polarisation of the C=C bond is governed mainly by the electromeric effect, while the choice of which carbocation intermediate actually forms (and hence the final product's regiochemistry) is governed by relative carbocation stability, explainable via inductive and hyperconjugative effects. Classify the overall reaction type, and state how these three effects contribute to different stages of the mechanism.
options: Addition; the electromeric effect determines the final product's regiochemistry, while inductive and hyperconjugative effects govern the initial response of the π bond, the reverse of the correct order

Addition (electrophilic addition); the electromeric effect drives the initial, reagent-triggered response of the π bond (enabling carbocation formation), while inductive and hyperconjugative effects determine which possible carbocation is more stable and therefore preferentially formed, governing the Markovnikov regiochemistry of the final product
Substitution; all three effects act simultaneously at exactly the same stage of the mechanism, with no distinction between them
Elimination; only the inductive effect plays any role, with electromeric and hyperconjugative effects being irrelevant to this reaction
questions.explanation: HBr adds across the alkene's C=C bond (addition). The electromeric effect describes the immediate, complete shift of π electrons that occurs specifically because an electrophile (H<sup>+</sup>) is approaching — this is what makes the initial carbocation-forming step happen at all. Once two different carbocations are possible, it is the inductive (+I of alkyl groups) and hyperconjugative (alpha C–H donation) effects that determine which of those possible cations is more stable, and therefore which one preferentially forms and dictates the major (Markovnikov) product.
questions.hint: Separate the mechanism into two conceptual stages: what triggers the very first electron shift as the reagent approaches, and what determines which of several possible intermediate structures is preferred once formed?
distractor_logic: Claiming all three effects act 'simultaneously with no distinction' ignores that they genuinely operate at conceptually distinct stages of the mechanism.

No group is being replaced here, so this is not a substitution reaction, and no atoms are eliminated to form a new multiple bond, so it is not an elimination reaction either (a multiple bond is being consumed, not created).

Reversing which effect governs which stage swaps the roles of the electromeric effect (initial π-bond response) and the inductive/hyperconjugative effects (intermediate stability), which is backwards.

topics.name: Classification of Organic Compounds
topics.summary: Organic compounds are first sorted by their carbon skeleton. Open-chain (acyclic) compounds have carbon atoms linked in a continuous or branched chain with no ring, like butane. Alicyclic compounds have a ring of carbon atoms that behaves chemically like an open chain — no delocalised π system — as in cyclohexane. Aromatic compounds have a planar, cyclic, fully conjugated ring obeying the (4n+2) π-electron rule, the defining example being benzene; larger fused-ring systems like naphthalene are polycyclic aromatics. Heterocyclic compounds have at least one non-carbon atom (commonly O, N, or S) as a ring member, and can themselves be aromatic (pyridine, furan) or non-aromatic. These categories are not mutually exclusive along every axis — a compound is classified along the acyclic/alicyclic/aromatic axis and separately checked for heteroatoms. The key skill is reading a structure and asking, in order: is there a ring at all? does it contain a non-carbon atom? does it have a fully delocalised, planar π system?
key_formulas: Open-chain (acyclic): no ring present
Alicyclic: saturated or non-aromatic ring, all-carbon
Aromatic: planar, cyclic, fully conjugated, (4n+2) π electrons
Heterocyclic: ring contains ≥1 non-carbon atom (may be aromatic or not)
topics.worked_example: Classify cyclohexane, benzene, furan, and butane. Cyclohexane: all-carbon, saturated ring → alicyclic. Benzene: all-carbon, aromatic ring → aromatic. Furan: one ring oxygen, aromatic → heterocyclic aromatic. Butane: no ring at all → open-chain (acyclic).
common_mistakes: Assuming every ring is automatically aromatic (cyclohexane is not).
Forgetting that a heterocyclic compound can still be aromatic (furan, pyridine) rather than treating 'heterocyclic' and 'aromatic' as mutually exclusive labels.
Misclassifying fused polycyclic hydrocarbons like naphthalene as anything other than aromatic.

topics.name: IUPAC Nomenclature of Hydrocarbons
topics.summary: Naming an alkane, alkene, or alkyne starts with finding the parent chain: the longest continuous carbon chain, and if there is a tie, the one containing the maximum number of multiple bonds. The parent's saturation is shown by the suffix — -ane for all single bonds, -ene for a C=C, -yne for a C≡C — with a locant showing where the multiple bond starts (the lower-numbered carbon of the two). Numbering runs in whichever direction gives the multiple bond (and then any substituents) the lowest possible locant. A very common trap is stopping at the first 'long-looking' chain without checking whether continuing through a branch (especially an ethyl or larger substituent) actually gives an even longer chain — IUPAC rules always require the genuinely longest possible chain to be the parent, even if that means what looked like a simple substituent is actually part of the main chain and the name has to be rebuilt with a different, longer chain and different substituents.
key_formulas: Suffixes: -ane (all single bonds) / -ene (C=C) / -yne (C≡C)
Parent chain selection order: longest chain > more multiple bonds (on a tie) > more substituents (on a further tie)
Numbering: lowest locant to the multiple bond first when no principal characteristic group is present
topics.worked_example: CH<sub>2</sub>=CH–CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>3</sub>: 4-carbon chain, double bond between C1 and C2 (numbering from the end nearer the double bond) → but-1-ene.
common_mistakes: Not checking whether a branch (especially an ethyl group or longer) actually extends the true longest chain, as in mistakenly naming an 8-carbon alkane '2-ethyl-3-methylpentane' instead of the correct '3,4-dimethylhexane'.
Numbering from the wrong end and giving the multiple bond a higher locant than necessary.

topics.name: IUPAC Nomenclature of Substituted Compounds
topics.summary: When a molecule carries a functional group beyond simple unsaturation, IUPAC rules require picking one principal characteristic group to be the suffix; every other group present is cited only as a prefix. The seniority order (high to low, abbreviated) runs: carboxylic acids > esters > amides > nitriles > aldehydes > ketones > alcohols/phenols > amines > ethers. Numbering is then applied in strict priority: the principal group gets the lowest locant first; only if a choice remains do multiple bonds, then substituents, get considered. Prefixes for non-principal groups (hydroxy-, oxo-, chloro-, amino-, etc.) are cited in alphabetical order in the final name, each with its own locant. A frequent source of error is assuming a compound's more 'obvious' or first-drawn functional group is automatically the suffix, when seniority is fixed by the table regardless of drawing order — for instance, a ketone always outranks an alcohol, so a hydroxy-ketone is always named as an '-one' with a 'hydroxy-' prefix, never the reverse.
key_formulas: Seniority (high→low, common groups): carboxylic acid > ester > amide > nitrile > aldehyde > ketone > alcohol/phenol > amine > ether
Only the most senior group present is the suffix; all others become prefixes
Numbering priority: principal group lowest locant > multiple bonds > substituents
topics.worked_example: CH<sub>3</sub>–CO–CH<sub>2</sub>–CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)–CH<sub>2</sub>–OH: ketone outranks alcohol, so number to give the ketone the lowest locant (from the methyl end): 5-hydroxy-4-methylpentan-2-one.
common_mistakes: Assuming an alcohol is senior to a ketone (it is not — ketone outranks alcohol in the standard seniority table).
Numbering from the end that minimises a substituent's locant instead of the principal group's locant.
Forgetting to alphabetise multiple prefixes in the final name.

topics.name: Structural Isomerism
topics.summary: Structural (constitutional) isomers share a molecular formula but differ in how their atoms are connected. Chain isomerism arises from a different carbon-skeleton arrangement with the same functional character (n-butane vs isobutane). Position isomerism keeps the skeleton and functional group fixed but moves the group to a different carbon (propan-1-ol vs propan-2-ol). Functional group isomerism changes the functional class entirely while keeping the molecular formula (an ether vs an alcohol, or an aldehyde vs a ketone). Metamerism is a narrower case: two compounds of the same functional class (typically ethers, ketones, or secondary/tertiary amines) that differ only in how straight, unbranched alkyl groups are distributed on either side of the functional group (diethyl ether vs methyl propyl ether). A special case worth knowing by name is ring-chain isomerism, where a saturated ring and an open-chain compound with one double bond share a formula (cyclopropane vs propene), since a ring and a double bond each account for one degree of unsaturation.
key_formulas: Chain isomerism: same functional class, different carbon skeleton
Position isomerism: same skeleton & functional group, different locant
Functional group isomerism: different functional class, same molecular formula
Metamerism: same functional class, different (unbranched) alkyl groups around the functional group
Ring-chain isomerism: a ring and an open-chain double bond sharing one formula (each = 1 degree of unsaturation)
topics.worked_example: Diethyl ether and methyl propyl ether (both C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O ethers) are metamers; dimethyl ether and ethanol (also both C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O) are functional group isomers, since one is an ether and the other an alcohol.
common_mistakes: Calling any two isomers with the same functional group 'metamers' even when one has a branched skeleton (branching makes it chain isomerism instead).
Confusing functional group isomerism (different class) with position isomerism (same class, group just relocated).

topics.name: Inductive Effect
topics.summary: The inductive effect is a permanent, relatively weak polarisation transmitted through the σ-bond framework of a molecule, caused by an electronegativity difference between bonded atoms. An electronegative substituent pulls electron density toward itself (−I effect), while an alkyl group, being comparatively electron-releasing relative to hydrogen, pushes density away from itself (+I effect). Because it acts through σ bonds rather than through space or a π system, the inductive effect weakens sharply with distance, becoming largely negligible beyond about three bonds from the substituent. −I strength broadly tracks electronegativity (F is the strongest common −I halogen), while +I strength among simple alkyl groups increases with branching (tert-butyl > isopropyl > ethyl > methyl). The inductive effect explains many trends in acid/base strength: a nearby −I substituent stabilises the conjugate base of an acid (increasing acidity) or destabilises a lone pair's availability on an amine (decreasing basicity), and these effects are additive when more than one such substituent is present.
key_formulas: −I strength (decreasing): –NO<sub>2</sub> > –CN > –COOH > –F > –Cl > –Br > –I > –OH > –OCH<sub>3</sub> > –C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub> > –H
+I strength (decreasing): –C(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub> > –CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> > –C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub> > –CH<sub>3</sub> > –H
Effect strength falls off sharply with the number of bonds separating substituent and reaction centre
topics.worked_example: Trichloroacetic acid > dichloroacetic acid > chloroacetic acid > acetic acid in acid strength, since each additional chlorine adds its own cumulative −I withdrawal, stabilising the conjugate base further.
common_mistakes: Treating the inductive effect as equally strong regardless of distance.
Confusing the direction of +I and −I.
Forgetting that multiple −I or +I substituents on the same carbon have an additive, not merely repeated, effect.

topics.name: Resonance and Mesomeric Effect
topics.summary: Resonance describes a molecule or ion whose true electronic structure cannot be captured by a single Lewis structure; instead it is represented as a hybrid of several canonical (resonance) structures that differ only in the arrangement of electrons — every atomic nucleus stays in exactly the same position across all of them. More stable (major) contributors have more covalent bonds, less separation of unlike charges, and negative charge (if any) on the more electronegative atom. Resonance explains why the two C–O bonds of a carboxylate or the two N–O bonds of a nitro group are experimentally equal and intermediate in length between single and double bonds, why the amide C–N bond has restricted rotation, and why substituents like –OH or –NH2 attached directly to an aromatic ring donate electron density specifically to the ring's ortho and para positions (never meta) by delocalising a lone pair into the π system. The overall stabilisation a fully delocalised system enjoys relative to a hypothetical localised structure is called its resonance (delocalisation) energy, and can be estimated experimentally, as with benzene's unusually small heat of hydrogenation.
key_formulas: A more stable canonical structure has: more covalent bonds, less charge separation, negative charge on the more electronegative atom, no adjacent like charges
topics.worked_example: Acetate ion, CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>−</sup>, has two equivalent canonical structures (C=O on each oxygen in turn); the true hybrid gives both C–O bonds equal, intermediate length — confirmed experimentally.
common_mistakes: Thinking resonance structures interconvert rapidly in real time (the real molecule is a single, static hybrid, not a mixture in equilibrium).
Moving an atom's position between 'resonance structures' (this makes them different molecules, not resonance forms).
Forgetting that ring donation reaches only ortho/para, never meta.

topics.name: Electromeric Effect
topics.summary: The electromeric effect is a temporary, much stronger electronic shift that occurs only in molecules containing a multiple bond (C=C, C=O, etc.) and only at the moment an attacking reagent approaches. The shared π electron pair is completely transferred to one of the two multiply-bonded atoms, and the effect disappears entirely once the reagent is removed — contrasting sharply with the permanent, always-present inductive effect. It is denoted +E when the π electrons move toward the atom that ends up bonded to the attacking electrophile (as in electrophilic addition to an alkene, where the shift generates a carbocation on the other carbon), and −E when the electrons move away from the site of attack instead, typically onto a more electronegative atom such as oxygen (as when a nucleophile attacks a carbonyl carbon, pushing the C=O electrons fully onto oxygen). Because it is a strong, complete, instantaneous shift, the electromeric effect generally dominates over the comparatively weak, permanent inductive effect whenever both could, in principle, influence the same reacting centre.
key_formulas: +E: π electrons shift toward the atom being attacked (e.g. HX addition to an alkene)
−E: π electrons shift away from the site of attack, onto a more electronegative atom (e.g. nucleophilic attack on a carbonyl)
topics.worked_example: HBr addition to propene: the electromeric shift lets H<sup>+</sup> bond to the terminal carbon, leaving the more stable secondary carbocation at C2 — Markovnikov addition.
common_mistakes: Confusing the electromeric effect with the (permanent, weaker) inductive effect.
Forgetting it strictly requires a multiple bond and an approaching reagent, so it cannot be invoked for a fully saturated molecule at rest.

topics.name: Hyperconjugation
topics.summary: Hyperconjugation, sometimes called no-bond resonance, is the delocalisation of electron density from a σ bond (almost always a C–H, occasionally a C–C bond) on a carbon directly attached (the alpha carbon) to an electron-deficient centre (a carbocation), a radical, or an adjacent π system, into the empty or partially filled orbital there. One of its canonical structures literally shows that C–H bond broken, with the electrons drawn as a new π bond and a bare proton left over — hence 'no-bond' resonance. The number of possible hyperconjugative structures equals the number of alpha C–H bonds available, and more such structures mean more stabilisation; this is why cation/radical/alkene stability generally increases with the degree of substitution (methyl < primary < secondary < tertiary). A key subtlety: only alpha hydrogens count. A carbon that is highly branched but is not itself directly attached to the reactive centre (for example, the far end of a neopentyl group) contributes nothing, however bulky it looks, if the actual alpha carbon in between has no spare C–H bonds left.
key_formulas: Number of hyperconjugative structures = number of alpha C–H (or C–C) bonds on the carbon(s) directly attached to the cationic/radical/unsaturated centre
tert-Butyl cation, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C<sup>+</sup>: 3 methyls × 3 alpha H each = 9 hyperconjugative structures
topics.worked_example: Ethyl cation, CH<sub>3</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>: alpha carbon is the single CH<sub>3</sub>, contributing 3 alpha H — 3 hyperconjugative structures.
common_mistakes: Counting hydrogens on a carbon that is not directly (alpha) attached to the reactive centre.
Assuming a more heavily branched substituent always means more hyperconjugation, without checking how many spare C–H bonds the actual alpha carbon(s) have left.

topics.name: Hydrogen Bonding
topics.summary: Hydrogen bonding is a relatively strong intermolecular attraction that requires a hydrogen atom covalently bonded to a small, highly electronegative atom — classically F, O, or N — so the hydrogen carries a significant partial positive charge able to interact with a lone pair on a nearby electronegative atom. Intermolecular hydrogen bonding links separate molecules into an extended network, substantially raising boiling point, melting point, and often water solubility relative to a similarly sized molecule without this capability (this is why ethanol boils far higher than its isomer dimethyl ether, which has no O–H to donate). Intramolecular hydrogen bonding (chelation) instead forms a ring within a single molecule, as in ortho-nitrophenol; because the donor and acceptor are 'used up' internally, chelated molecules cannot link as extensively with their neighbours, giving them a distinctly lower boiling point, melting point, and water solubility than an isomer capable of intermolecular hydrogen bonding, such as para-nitrophenol.
topics.worked_example: ortho-Nitrophenol (intramolecular H-bond/chelation) has a markedly lower boiling point than para-nitrophenol (intermolecular H-bonding), even though both are structural isomers with identical formula.
common_mistakes: Assuming any electronegative atom (e.g. Cl, S) supports classic hydrogen bonding — only F, O, and N are small and electronegative enough.
Forgetting that chelation lowers, rather than raises, boiling point relative to the intermolecularly bonded isomer.

topics.name: Homolytic and Heterolytic Fission
topics.summary: A covalent bond can break in two fundamentally different ways. Homolytic fission splits the shared electron pair symmetrically, with one electron going to each fragment; because both resulting species are neutral with a single unpaired electron, this always produces two free radicals, and is typical of non-polar bonds broken under energetic conditions like UV light or heat (Cl2 → 2Cl•). Heterolytic fission instead sends both electrons of the pair to just one fragment — almost always the more electronegative or better-stabilising atom — producing a cation and an anion; this is typical of polar bonds breaking in a polar solvent, such as the ionisation of a tertiary alkyl halide to a carbocation and a halide ion. Recognising which type of fission a given bond-breaking step represents is the first move in predicting whether the resulting intermediate will be a radical (and therefore likely to propagate a chain mechanism) or an ion (and therefore likely to react through classic electrophile/nucleophile pathways).
key_formulas: Homolytic: A:B → A• + B• (equal split → two neutral free radicals)
Heterolytic: A:B → A<sup>+</sup> + B<sup>−</sup> (unequal split, both electrons to the more electronegative/stabilising atom → a cation and an anion)
topics.worked_example: (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C–Cl ionising in water: heterolytic fission, both electrons go to the more electronegative chlorine, giving (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>−</sup>.
common_mistakes: Assuming any bond-breaking event under heat or light must be heterolytic.
Forgetting that homolytic fission requires (and produces) exactly one unpaired electron per fragment, never a full charge.

topics.name: Carbocations
topics.summary: A carbocation is a carbon bearing a formal positive charge with only three bonds; it is sp2 hybridised and planar, with an empty, unhybridised p orbital perpendicular to the plane of the three σ bonds. Stability increases with anything that can feed electron density into that empty orbital: alkyl substitution (via +I induction and hyperconjugative donation of alpha C–H bonds), giving the familiar order methyl < 1° < 2° < 3°, and especially resonance delocalisation when the cation is allylic or benzylic, which typically outranks even a simple tertiary alkyl cation. A directly attached heteroatom lone pair (as in an oxocarbenium ion) can be an even stronger stabiliser than alkyl hyperconjugation alone. Electron-withdrawing substituents (−I or −M, such as –NO2) destabilise a nearby cation by worsening its already low electron density, while electron-donating substituents (+I or +M, such as –OCH3) stabilise it — and this effect is strongest when the donor/acceptor is positioned at a site (ortho/para on a benzylic system) that is actually reached by the resonance delocalisation pathway.
key_formulas: Simple alkyl stability: methyl < 1° < 2° < 3°
Overall (typical teaching order): benzylic/allylic > 3° > 2° > 1° > methyl
EWG (–I/–M) destabilises; EDG (+I/+M) stabilises, especially at resonance-connected (ortho/para) positions
topics.worked_example: p-Methoxybenzyl cation > benzyl cation > p-nitrobenzyl cation, since –OCH<sub>3</sub> donates (stabilises) and –NO<sub>2</sub> withdraws (destabilises) exactly at a resonance-connected ring position.
common_mistakes: Forgetting that a resonance-stabilised (allylic/benzylic) cation, even if formally primary or secondary, often outranks a purely hyperconjugative tertiary alkyl cation.
Applying an EWG/EDG substituent's effect at a ring position not actually reached by the resonance pathway (e.g. meta).

topics.name: Carbanions
topics.summary: A carbanion is a carbon bearing a lone pair and a formal negative charge with three bonds; it is roughly sp3 hybridised and pyramidal, similar in shape to ammonia. Because alkyl groups are electron-donating (+I), adding more of them to an already electron-rich carbanion centre intensifies the negative charge and destabilises it — the opposite substitution trend to carbocations: methyl > 1° > 2° > 3° among simple alkyl carbanions. Electron-withdrawing groups (−I and, especially, resonance-accepting groups like –NO2 or a carbonyl) strongly stabilise an adjacent carbanion by pulling away and/or delocalising the excess negative charge, which is why an enolate (carbanion next to C=O) or a nitro-stabilised carbanion is far more stable than a plain alkyl carbanion; conversely, electron-donating groups like –OCH3 destabilise a nearby carbanion by pushing yet more density toward an already negative centre. Resonance-delocalised carbanions (benzylic, allylic, or adjacent to a carbonyl/nitro group) are always more stable than a comparable simple alkyl carbanion with no such delocalisation available.
key_formulas: Simple alkyl stability: methyl > 1° > 2° > 3° (reverse of carbocation trend)
EWG (–I/resonance acceptor) stabilises; EDG destabilises a carbanion
Resonance-accepting groups rank (typical teaching order): –NO<sub>2</sub> > C=O (enolate) > C≡N > phenyl > none
topics.worked_example: O<sub>2</sub>N–CH<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup> > C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup> > CH<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>, since the nitro group both withdraws and resonance-accepts the negative charge more effectively than a phenyl ring, and plain methyl carbanion has no stabilisation at all.
common_mistakes: Applying the carbocation substitution trend (more alkyl = more stable) directly to carbanions, when it is in fact reversed.
Forgetting that an electron-withdrawing group stabilises (not destabilises) an adjacent carbanion.

topics.name: Free Radicals
topics.summary: A free radical is a neutral species with a single unpaired electron, formed by homolytic fission; because that unpaired electron creates a net magnetic moment, radicals are paramagnetic. Radical stability follows largely the same substitution and resonance trends as carbocations: more alkyl substitution stabilises via +I and hyperconjugative donation into the singly-occupied orbital (methyl < 1° < 2° < 3°), and resonance-delocalised radicals (allylic, benzylic, and especially the classic, extensively-delocalised triphenylmethyl radical) are generally more stable still, often outranking a simple tertiary alkyl radical. Unlike carbocations and carbanions, however, a neutral radical carries no net charge, so it is far less sensitive to whether a nearby substituent is electron-withdrawing or electron-donating; radical stability is dominated by degree of substitution and resonance delocalisation rather than by the strong polar (EWG/EDG) effects that dramatically swing cation and carbanion stability. As with any hyperconjugation-based comparison, it is the number of genuine alpha C–H bonds — not overall molecular bulk — that determines the stabilisation a given radical receives.
key_formulas: Simple alkyl stability: methyl < 1° < 2° < 3°
Overall (typical teaching order): triphenylmethyl/benzylic > allylic > 3° > 2° > 1° > methyl
Radicals are comparatively insensitive to EWG/EDG polar effects relative to charged intermediates
topics.worked_example: Allyl radical (CH<sub>2</sub>=CH–CH<sub>2</sub>•) is more stable than tert-butyl radical, since resonance delocalisation over two carbons generally outweighs purely hyperconjugative tertiary stabilisation.
common_mistakes: Assuming a strongly electron-withdrawing or -donating substituent swings radical stability as dramatically as it would for a cation or carbanion.
Judging hyperconjugative stabilisation by how 'bulky' a substituent looks rather than by actually counting alpha C–H bonds.

topics.name: Electrophiles and Nucleophiles
topics.summary: An electrophile ('electron-loving') is any electron-deficient species — a cation, or a neutral molecule with an incomplete octet or a polarised, electron-poor atom — that seeks out and attacks a region of high electron density; common examples include H+, carbocations, and neutral Lewis acids like BF3 (boron has only six electrons). A nucleophile ('nucleus-loving') is an electron-rich species — an anion, or a neutral molecule with an available lone pair — that donates electron density to an electron-poor centre; examples include CN−, OH−, and neutral species like NH3 or H2O. Overall charge is a useful clue but not the deciding factor: many good nucleophiles are neutral (water, ammonia), and the same species can sometimes act as a nucleophile in one reaction (attacking carbon in a substitution) and as a simple Brønsted base in another (removing a proton in an elimination) — the distinguishing question is always where the electron pair ends up and what bond is being formed or broken.
topics.worked_example: BF<sub>3</sub> (incomplete octet on boron) is an electrophile; CN<sup>−</sup> (lone pair on carbon, negatively charged) is a nucleophile.
common_mistakes: Assuming only charged species can be electrophiles or nucleophiles (many important examples of both are neutral).
Confusing a species acting as a nucleophile (attacking carbon) with the same species acting as a base (removing a proton) in a different reaction pathway.

topics.name: Types of Organic Reactions
topics.summary: Organic reactions are broadly sorted by what happens to the atoms present. A substitution reaction replaces one atom or group with another, with no multiple bond created or destroyed (CH3CH2OH + HBr → CH3CH2Br + H2O). An addition reaction combines two or more molecules across a multiple bond, with no atoms lost (HBr adding across an alkene's C=C). An elimination reaction removes atoms or groups from adjacent carbons to create a new multiple bond — essentially the reverse of addition (dehydrohalogenation of an alkyl halide with alcoholic KOH to give an alkene). Aromatic rings, despite containing formal double bonds, characteristically undergo electrophilic substitution rather than addition, because addition would destroy the ring's aromatic stabilisation; substituents already on the ring (like activating –OH or deactivating –NO2) speed up or slow down this substitution by raising or lowering the ring's electron density through resonance and induction. Correctly classifying a reaction requires tracking exactly which atoms are gained, lost, or simply relocated between reactants and products.
topics.worked_example: CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br + KOH (alcoholic, heated) → CH<sub>2</sub>=CH<sub>2</sub> + KBr + H<sub>2</sub>O is elimination (H and Br removed from adjacent carbons to form a new C=C).
common_mistakes: Confusing addition and elimination as simple opposites without checking which direction the specific reaction actually runs.
Treating aromatic ring reactions as addition reactions rather than recognising them as (electrophilic) substitution.

topics.name: Sublimation and Crystallisation
topics.summary: Sublimation purifies a solid that passes directly from solid to vapour on gentle heating (without an intervening liquid phase), such as camphor, naphthalene, or ammonium chloride; heating the impure solid lets the pure compound vaporise and recondense elsewhere, leaving non-volatile impurities behind in the residue — but it only works if the compound genuinely sublimes cleanly and does not decompose first. Crystallisation instead exploits differences in solubility, typically as a function of temperature: a compound is dissolved in a hot solvent close to saturation, and as the solution cools, the compound (being far less soluble cold) crystallises out in pure form while soluble impurities stay in solution (or vice versa, depending on which component is more soluble). Crystallisation only discriminates well when the compound and its impurities have genuinely different solubility behaviour; if two components have very similar solubility profiles in every available solvent, crystallisation will not separate them effectively no matter how carefully the temperature is controlled.
topics.worked_example: A crude solid containing a sublimable impurity, the target compound (soluble hot, sparingly soluble cold in ethanol), and a water-soluble salt: sublime off the volatile impurity, wash away the salt with water, then recrystallise from hot ethanol.
common_mistakes: Assuming every solid can be purified by sublimation regardless of thermal stability.
Using crystallisation when the compound and impurity have nearly identical solubility, mistakenly expecting a melting-point difference alone to help.

topics.name: Distillation and Differential Extraction
topics.summary: Simple distillation separates two miscible liquids whose boiling points differ substantially (conventionally by at least about 25 °C); when boiling points are closer together, a single vaporisation-condensation step cannot cleanly separate them, and fractional distillation (using a fractionating column for repeated vaporisation-condensation cycles) is required instead. Steam distillation purifies a water-immiscible liquid that would decompose at its own normal boiling point: because the mixture boils once the combined vapour pressures of water and the compound equal atmospheric pressure, the compound distils over at a temperature below 100 °C and well below its own decomposition point. Differential (solvent) extraction is a liquid–liquid technique: a compound distributes unevenly between two immiscible solvents according to its relative solubility in each, so shaking the mixture with a chosen solvent in a separating funnel transfers most of the compound into whichever layer it prefers, letting the two layers then be separated cleanly.
key_formulas: Simple distillation is reliable when boiling points differ by roughly ≥ 25 °C; otherwise use fractional distillation
Steam distillation: mixture boils once the combined vapour pressures of water and the compound equal atmospheric pressure (below either pure component's own boiling point)
topics.worked_example: A thermally unstable, water-immiscible liquid that decomposes at its normal boiling point is purified by steam distillation, distilling over below 100 °C without reaching its decomposition temperature.
common_mistakes: Trying to use simple distillation on liquids with closely spaced boiling points instead of fractional distillation.
Forgetting that steam distillation requires the compound to be immiscible with water and to have some appreciable vapour pressure at temperatures below 100 °C.

topics.name: Chromatography
topics.summary: Chromatography separates a mixture's components based on differences in how strongly each is adsorbed onto a stationary phase (commonly alumina or silica) as a mobile phase (an eluant) is passed continuously over/through it. Components that interact weakly with the stationary phase are carried along fastest by the mobile phase and elute (come off the column) first; strongly adsorbed components are repeatedly held back and elute later. More polar compounds generally interact more strongly with a polar stationary phase like alumina than non-polar compounds do, so increasing the polarity of the mobile phase can help displace and elute a strongly retained polar compound sooner. Because it requires no heating at all, chromatography is especially well suited to separating thermally unstable or heat-sensitive mixtures — historically, in fact, the technique was first developed and named for separating coloured, heat-sensitive plant pigments on a column, which is also why it remains a good example for illustrating elution order.
topics.worked_example: In column chromatography, a weakly adsorbed compound elutes before a strongly adsorbed one; increasing the mobile phase's polarity can speed up elution of a strongly retained polar compound.
common_mistakes: Assuming the more strongly adsorbed compound elutes first (it is, in fact, the last to come off).
Overlooking chromatography as the go-to purification method whenever heating-based techniques are ruled out by thermal instability.

topics.name: Qualitative Analysis of Elements
topics.summary: Lassaigne's test (sodium fusion) is the standard qualitative method for detecting nitrogen, sulfur, and halogens in an organic compound: fusing the compound with sodium metal converts these covalently bound elements into simple, water-soluble ionic sodium salts (NaCN, Na2S, NaX) that can then be tested with everyday ionic reagents. Nitrogen is confirmed by treating the extract with FeSO4/FeCl3 and dilute acid to form Prussian blue, Fe4[Fe(CN)6]3. Sulfur is confirmed by a black precipitate of lead sulfide with lead acetate (or a violet colour with sodium nitroprusside). Halogens are confirmed by a precipitate with AgNO3 (checked for insolubility in dilute HNO3 to rule out other anions), with the precipitate's colour indicating which halogen. Phosphorus requires a separate oxidative fusion and is confirmed by a yellow precipitate of ammonium phosphomolybdate. Each of these gives only a yes/no answer about presence — the corresponding quantitative method must be used to determine how much of the element is actually present.
topics.worked_example: A Lassaigne extract giving Prussian blue with FeSO<sub>4</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, but no precipitate with AgNO<sub>3</sub> and no black precipitate with lead acetate, indicates nitrogen is present but no halogen or sulfur.
common_mistakes: Forgetting that sodium fusion must first convert covalent N/S/halogen into ionic form before any of the standard tests will work.
Mixing up which reagent confirms which element (e.g. confusing the sulfur and halogen tests).

topics.name: Quantitative Analysis of Elements
topics.summary: Liebig's method determines carbon and hydrogen by completely combusting a weighed sample and separately weighing the CO2 and H2O produced, from which the mass (and hence percentage) of each element is calculated. Nitrogen is estimated either by the Dumas method (converting nitrogen to N2 gas and measuring its volume at STP after CO2 is absorbed by KOH) or by Kjeldahl's method (converting nitrogen to NH3, absorbing it in a known excess of standard acid, then back-titrating the unreacted acid with standard alkali). Halogens, sulfur, and phosphorus are estimated by the Carius method: oxidative fusion converts the element into a simple ion that is precipitated as AgX (for halogens), BaSO4 (for sulfur), or a similar gravimetrically weighable compound, and the element's mass is back-calculated from the precipitate's mass using the appropriate molar-mass ratio. Every one of these calculations follows the same two-step logic: convert the mass of the measured product into the mass of the element it contains, then express that as a percentage of the original sample mass.
key_formulas: %C = (mass CO<sub>2</sub> × 12/44) / mass of sample × 100
%H = (mass H<sub>2</sub>O × 2/18) / mass of sample × 100
%N (Dumas) = 28 × V(N<sub>2</sub>, STP, mL) / (22400 × mass of sample) × 100
%N (Kjeldahl) = 1.4 × N × (V<sub>1</sub> − V<sub>2</sub>) / mass of sample
%X (Carius, halogen) = mass AgX × (atomic mass X / molar mass AgX) / mass of sample × 100
%S (Carius) = mass BaSO<sub>4</sub> × (32/233) / mass of sample × 100
topics.worked_example: 0.30 g sample gives 0.44 g CO<sub>2</sub> and 0.18 g H<sub>2</sub>O: %C = (0.44×12/44)/0.30×100 = 40%; %H = (0.18×2/18)/0.30×100 ≈ 6.7%.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to convert the mass of the measured product (CO<sub>2</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>O, AgX, BaSO<sub>4</sub>) into the mass of the actual element before dividing by the sample mass.
Mixing up the Dumas (gas-volumetric) and Kjeldahl (acid–base titration) formulas for nitrogen.
